articles.title: Press review: Western plan drives Zelensky’s warning as US, Iran exchange strikes anew
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. Russia believes a Western concerted action may be behind Vladimir Zelensky’s threat to civil aviation as the conflict between the United States and Iran resumes after a month-long lull. Meanwhile, Romania declines to discuss measures aimed at reducing drone incident risks in the Black Sea. These stories topped Thursday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Western plan may be behind Zelensky’s warning about Russian skies
Kiev has issued a warning to international airlines to steer clear of Russian airspace. That may involve a coordinated action by European countries in an attempt to set their own terms of negotiations, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. The Transport Ministry said it would avert any major disruptions in the functioning of civil aviation, while experts deem a complete closure of Russian skies unlikely. Despite the escalation of rhetoric, Moscow remains ready for a settlement as it still awaits negotiators from the United States.
As Russian troops make gains on the battlefield, Ukraine issued yet another threat that Russian President Vladimir Putin slammed as a "bid for state terrorism." Vladimir Zelensky’s warning came hours after relations between Russia and Germany deteriorated: Germany formally blamed Russia for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport that took place in early August. Moscow dismissed the accusations as unsubstantiated.
"I think this is a concerted action. Zelensky was likely instructed to act within this framework in order to put as much pressure on Russia as possible. Actually, what Zelensky is doing is making threats to the civilian population. And that is already a war crime," the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told Izvestia.
Zelensky’s latest statement largely amounts to an attempt to achieve a media impact, while in fact the situation on the front is developing to the advantage of the Russian Armed Forces, according to Yevgeny Semibratov, deputy director of the Institute for Strategic Studies and Forecasts at Peoples' Friendship University of Russia. At the same time, Kiev's threats should not be completely ignored as Ukraine is consistently enhancing its drone capabilities.
Vladimir Popov, a merited military pilot, said Russia’s Air Force and air defenses have considerably diminished the Ukrainian army’s ability to use aircraft in the immediate vicinity of the combat zone. Therefore, the Ukrainians are trying to make up for the lack of aviation capabilities with the massive use of UAVs. According to calculations based on reports from the Russian Defense Ministry, in the summer of 2026, between 750 and 800 drones were reported daily, with the intensity rate increasing to 960 drones by August. During the peak periods of July and August, Russian forces destroyed between 4,500 and 8,000 drones per week.
Nevertheless, Russia remains willing to negotiate, Grigory Karasin, the head of the Russian Federation Council Committee on International Affairs, told Izvestia. However, with his recent statements, Zelensky has undermined his credibility as a responsible politician and he poses a threat to international stability, the senator added.
Vedomosti: US, Iran exchange strikes again after a month-long lull
For the first time since late July, the United States and Iran carried out large-scale strikes against each other’s positions in the Middle East. Early on Wednesday morning, units from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched missiles and drones against US military facilities in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and the Kurdish autonomous region in northern Iraq in response to the US bombing of coastal Iranian cities. At the same time, the IRGC said two tankers struck mines in the Hormuz Strait as they attempted to use what Tehran called an unauthorized route there.
The United States and Iran have reached the stage of managed escalation in the Middle East conflict, Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. According to him, the two sides will continue to exchange military, rhetorical and economic attacks for a certain period. "As the American and Iranian leaderships view it, willingness to make concessions represents a sign of weakness. At the same time, the sides would hate a repetition of the spiral of violence that occurred in late February. Both the Americans and the Iranians are quite satisfied with how things currently stand and they will have enough resources to continue this confrontation for a very long time," the expert in American studies maintained.
Trump’s mid-term goal is to keep a plateau of managed confrontation for another two years until the next presidential election, Koshkin believes: "Therefore Trump now finds it important to demonstrate a tough and resolute approach to Tehran. Both sides are escalating tensions in the information space which does not automatically mean a military confrontation."
The sides will continue to escalate the situation as differences between the United States and Iran, including over the status of the Strait of Hormuz, have not disappeared, Senior Research Fellow at the Center for Analysis of Strategies and Technologies Yury Lyamin argued. On the one hand, Washington is trying to bring more Middle East oil onto the global market, and on the other hand, Tehran is trying to use the problem with the waterways as a key political bargaining chip, he said. "The Americans are still trying to demine certain sectors of the route, which is provoking Iranian retaliation. This standoff was there during the ceasefire, so any incidents may cause further escalation, a scenario that is taking place now," the analyst added.
At present, the US economic pressure stemming from the naval blockade poses the main threat to Iran’s security, Lyamin continued. "In this regard, Tehran is prepared to escalate to step up pressure on global markets and the United States. Overnight American attacks on Iranian tankers gave the Iranian leadership a pretext for retaliatory strikes against tankers of the Gulf Arab states," the expert added.
Izvestia: Romania hampers measures toward Black Sea security
Romania is reluctant to discuss measures that would reduce the risk of incidents in the Black Sea and along the border with Ukraine, the Russian embassy in Bucharest told Izvestia. The growing frequency of drone attacks and attacks on civilian vessels have heightened tensions in the region. Despite the recent change of government, neighboring Bulgaria, too, still follows NATO’s strict bloc discipline and is boosting its military presence in the Black Sea.
Against this background, Turkey has sought to act as a key mediator in talks on safe navigation. On September 1, Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Turkish counterpart, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, held a one-on-one meeting at the SCO summit in Bishkek. Earlier, Turkey’s top diplomat, Hakan Fidan, said Ankara is maintaining contact with both Moscow and Kiev as it expects to formulate new safe navigation rules. However, NATO’s other Black Sea allies have dismissed dialogue. Romania, for one, is not planning to address this issue with Russia, the Russian embassy in Bucharest told Izvestia.
For Romania, the Black Sea is a space of strategic rivalry with Russia rather than a zone where it should establish a sustainable mechanism of interaction, according to Artyom Perchun, a researcher at the Faculty of World Economy and International Affairs at the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies of the National Research University Higher School of Economics. Any compromises would contradict NATO’s current strategy designed not to build trust with Moscow but focused on a military buildup since 2022.
The policy course pursued by Romania’s neighbor, Bulgaria, is also contributing to regional tensions. "Even in the absence of explicitly Russophobic rhetoric, Sofia continues to follow Western guidelines in our direction, including in the context of `strengthening NATO’s defense capabilities,’ which inevitably leads to militarization of the Black Sea region," the Russian embassy in Bulgaria told Izvestia.
Meanwhile, Romania has in fact been the main route of weapons supplies to Ukraine, Andrey Kortunov, an expert with the Valdai Discussion Club, noted. If in 2022-2024 Poland’s Rzeszow served as a key and almost uncontested hub for NATO, by 2026 the alliance deliberately turned Romania into its second largest military logistics hub on the eastern flank, he said.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Moscow, Yerevan move closer to parting ways
Late on Tuesday evening, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan held talks on the future of Yerevan in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). On the whole, the Russian and Armenian leaders focused on whether Armenia’s course toward European integration would conflict with its EAEU membership during the public part of their conversation. Putin sees this as a problem as he suggested the Armenian PM hold a referendum so as not to escalate the situation. Apparently, he suspects that the majority of Armenians will vote against, given the latest developments, and that would be the end of the matter. In turn, Pashinyan is not even trying to hide that his nation is not yet ready to make what he views as the correct decision, so there will be no plebiscite.
On September 2, the EU Council approved trade measures to support Armenia. The trade relief measures will apply for two years and cover 80% of Armenian exports amid Russian restrictions on Armenian supplies, Brussels emphasized.
The latest measures will hardly have any positive effect in 2026 as the fruit and vegetables season is coming to a close, but they may produce a result next year, Sergey Melkonyan, a research fellow at the Applied Policy Research Institute of Armenia, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The decision by Brussels will not heighten the conflict between Armenia and the EAEU as Armenian exports to the EU do not undermine the Eurasian organization’s interests, he argued.
"As regards the talks, Pashinyan and Putin agreed to reassess the Armenian-Russian relationship," Melkonyan noted as he highlighted this as the main piece of positive news which was also mentioned by the Armenian head of government.
At the same time, the expert continued, Yerevan has adopted a course for downgrading the level of cooperation with Russia which would affect the defense, energy, transport infrastructure and trade spheres. "As regards Moscow, it will need to decide whether it would like to retain its influence in the South Caucasus or is ready for a divorce. <…> Much will perhaps depend on the next round of talks. Perhaps in order to reduce risks, Pashinyan may want to meet with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev who should visit Yerevan in October. After that, we could reach some conclusions regarding what will happen at the EAEU summit in December," Melkonyan concluded.
Kommersant: Russian diesel export ban fuels US exports
The global diesel shortage, caused by the Russian export ban and disruptions to supplies from the Middle East, has enabled US producers to increase exports to a record level and driven prices higher. Russian companies may be forced to offer discounts to reclaim their share after exports resume.
Amid geopolitical tensions and as Russian exports were suspended in August, US diesel exports rose to a record high of 54.2 million barrels, a 16.3% increase from July, a report by S&P Global showed. And spot prices for ultra-low sulfur diesel (ULSD) on Mexico’s East Coast surged to $4.7 per gallon, the highest since S&P Global began to issue reports in May 2006. According to the latest report, the key factor that prompted the sharp rise in prices was Russia’s move to extend the diesel export ban to September 30.
The situation now favors diesel producers and exporters, Igor Yushkov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, noted: in addition to the complete suspension of petroleum product supplies from the Persian Gulf countries, shipments of crude to major refiners such as India have also declined. Consequently, they too are cutting diesel fuel exports, the analyst said. The other reason for the global shortage is linked to the halted Russian exports. According to Yushkov, American suppliers are taking the place of Russian, Middle Eastern, and Indian producers in this situation.
Dmitry Skryabin, a portfolio manager at Alfa-Capital brokerage, recalled that Russia has historically been the world's second-largest diesel exporter after the United States, and therefore it could swiftly restore its position in the global market. The key issue, the analyst continued, is not so much maintaining physical market share as the pricing parameters of export contracts, as a reshuffle in supply chains and a return to the market could alter the final cost of supplies.

articles.title: AFRL Seeks Payload-Agnostic, Affordable Hypersonic Cruise Missile
articles.body:
The Air Force Research Laboratory has signaled to industry it wants to develop a low-cost hypersonic cruise missile to deliver a wide range of payloads at a range up to 500 nautical miles.
In a brief one-page notice released Sept. 1, posted on Sam.gov, AFRL gave the broad outlines of its new project, which falls under the broader Pioneering Aerospace Capabilities, Engineering & Research program.
“Offerors are encouraged to consider modular open systems architectures, together with aggressive application of digital engineering advanced manufacturing techniques,” according to the note.
That note signals an openness to using 3D printing as a way to make a more affordable hypersonic missile than the Air Force has pursued in other programs, such as its two other hypersonic weapons, the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile and the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon.
HACM is an ongoing Air Force effort with RTX to build a scramjet-powered, air-breathing hypersonic missile to reach and maintain speeds of Mach 5 or greater, capable of being carried on tactical fighters and bombers; Northrop Grumman developed the engine.
ARRW is a Lockheed Martin-built, boost-glide, air-launched hypersonic weapon designed primarily to be carried by bombers.
Payload
The new AFRL project has “no specific payload requirement,” according to the notice.
That agnostic payload approach differs from HACM, which from the outset was based around a kinetic warhead to strike heavily defended targets. The new project’s lack of specific warhead requirements means it could carry kinetic strike options, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance payloads, or electronic warfare gear.
But the strike option remains.
“It could provide new ‘middle ground’ options for precision strikes against time-sensitive targets,” retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, director of future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “Depending on its seekers and warhead variants, a 500-nautical mile hypersonic weapon could be used against ground fixed and relocatable targets, moving maritime targets, and possibly even high-value airborne targets like [Airborne Early Warning & Control] aircraft.”
More Options
Such a weapon would given Air Force planners a wider range of options, especially in far-flung regions of the Pacific, where an adversary such as the Chinese military uses complex anti-access, area-denial systems, Gunzinger said.
The hypersonic focus is also crucial for overcoming much of the Chinese military’s capabilities, he said.
“The capability and capacity to conduct prompt maritime strikes against moving targets such as the [People’s Liberation Army Navy] Type 055 Renhai class cruisers and Type 52D Luyang-III class destroyers will be critical to defeating an assault on Taiwan or other scenario,” Gunzinger said. “I would also stress the value of using hypersonic class weapons to counter high-value airborne aircraft like KJ-500/600 AEW&C aircraft, which will be key to countering the PLA Air Force’s long-range kill chains.”
And, if right-sized, that kind of missile could be used across a variety of platforms, such as the F-15EX, as well as the B-21, B-2, F-47 and even the F-35, he said.
“Frankly, sixth-generation stealth aircraft will not need 500 [nautical mile] standoff, but it would increase their ability to avoid the highest risk threat areas and expand areas it can attack in a single sortie,” the retired colonel and former B-52 pilot said.
While the Air Force is still working to field HACM, Gunzinger sees the potential of a low-cost cruise missile as an added, not replacement, capability. Especially, he said, if the future weapon could carry EW payloads, which are critical for suppression of enemy air defenses.
Scaling Hypersonics and Cost
The 3D-printing option might give the Air Force a way to scale the weapons in a way that Gunzinger and Mitchell have long advocated.
“Affordability can be a barrier to fielding hypersonic weapons at scale—the Army’s ‘Dark Eagle’ ground-launched boost-glide weapon that costs $40 million or more for a single warhead is a good example of this,” Gunzinger said. “So, an air-launched weapon that costs low single-digit millions of dollars each would increase the potential to acquire them at scale.”
The Air Force is seeking $1.96 billion in hypersonic funding for HACM and ARRW in its fiscal 2027 budget request, currently winding its way through Congress.
Most of that, about $1.2 billion, is for HACM: $404 million to buy the first operational lot of missiles and $806 million for continued dollars for research, development, test, and evaluation.
The service is also seeking around $748 million for ARRW—$452 million for procurement and $296 million for an Increment 2 version of the weapon work to be adapted for long-range counter-maritime missions.
But even beyond hypersonics, the Air Force is keenly interested in developing cheaper munitions. It is pursuing many of them through its Family of Affordable Mass Munitions program, which seeks to field 28,000 low-cost cruise missiles over the next five years. The Pentagon announced in July it was awarding multiyear contracts with companies Anduril, CoAspire and Zone 5 Technologies to produce those non-hypersonic weapons at a quick clip, starting in 2027.
The Project
The affordable hypersonic missile project will consist of two rounds. The first will have AFRL accept white paper submissions from industry, followed by a second round in which industry will submit full technical and cost proposals.
The lab first posted a notice for a potential “focused call” or technology demonstration competition in January, titled “Rapid Maturation and Demonstration of Hypersonic Weapon Concepts.” Then on March 16, it released a call for “Hypersonic Affordable Mass Weapon Concepts,” Molly Lachance, an AFRL spokesperson, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
“Following internal reviews and refined program requirements for the Hypersonic Affordable Mass Weapon Concepts (HAMWC) effort, we updated key project parameters to better align with mission priorities. Because these adjustments represented a material change to the original scope, a resolicitation was required,” Lachance wrote.
For the Sept. 1 notice, AFRL expects to post amendments within 30 days, according to the notice.

articles.title: B-52s Deploy for Bomber Task Force to Australia’s New BUFF Base
articles.body:
Air Force B-52 Stratofortress bombers landed at a northern Australian air base this week, a major display of the U.S. military’s ability to project force in the Pacific.
Multiple B-52s landed at Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal in the country’s Northern Territory on Sept. 1, according to official Air Force imagery released Sept. 3.
The joint military-civilian airfield near the town of Katherine, which the Pentagon plans to use as a launching pad for operations in the Pacific, has undergone a $1.1 billion upgrade in recent years.
That work enables it to support the deployment of a half-dozen B-52s, giving the U.S. more locations to stage bombers in the region amid China’s growing military might.
The base also houses Australian F-35A Lightning stealth fighter jets and MQ-4C Triton remotely piloted surveillance aircraft.
Australia is south of the U.S. territory of Guam, where Andersen Air Force Base serves as America’s current bomber hub in the Western Pacific. RAAF Base Tindal would give the U.S. Air Force more basing options for long-range missions in the region.
“Operating from RAAF Base Tindal marks our ability to project, sustain, and regenerate decisive airpower across an expanding extended network,” states one photo caption released by Pacific Air Forces. The deployment from the base “deepens our partnership and interoperability” and “highlights our shared commitment to regional stability, ensuring our forces remain agile and responsive in support of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” PACAF added in other captions.
Air Force Global Strike Command and the Eighth Air Force, which oversees the nation’s bomber force, declined to comment, citing operational security, and referred questions to Pacific Air Forces on Sept. 2 when asked about the deployment. PACAF did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It is unclear how long the bombers will be deployed to the region and how many aircraft are operating from Australia. The bombers hail from the 2nd Bomb Wing at Barksdale Air Force Base, La.
Multiple wargames on potential conflicts with China have highlighted the strategic and operational value of Australia’s airbases and naval facilities, said retired Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot and deputy assistant secretary of defense for forces transformation and resources.
“That has been a constant in our wargames: using Australia’s multiple airfields—and not just in northern Australia but in the south too—to generate long-range bomber strikes and tanker sorties to support bomber and fighter operations,” said Gunzinger, the Director of Future Concepts and Capability Assessments at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“China has a limited number of very long-range ballistic missiles that can reach U.S. air forces stationed at Diego Garcia, in Australia, and other air bases that are not located along the First Island Chain.” Bombers’ longer ranges would allow them to be stationed at airfields even further from China if necessary, Gunzinger added.
Washington and Canberra are increasingly aligned under the AUKUS security pact, which also includes the United Kingdom. The agreement will give U.S. nuclear-powered subs to Australia and allow the U.S. to stage subs out of Australia starting next year. Conceived under the Biden administration, AUKUS has also been embraced by the second Trump administration.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 2 to commemorate the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS Treaty, a mutual defense pact, during which the two defense chiefs “discussed how both nations will continue to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific.”
“The Secretary noted the alignment between U.S. and Australian National Defense Strategies and also acknowledged that Canberra recognizes the gravity of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the region to ensure that both countries remain safe and prosperous,” the Pentagon said in a readout provided from the meeting. “Both leaders agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises.”
The U.S. has operated fighters and bombers from other Royal Australian Air Force Bases, such as RAAF Base Amberley, and the two countries conduct the biennial Talisman Saber, one of the largest and most complex military training exercises held. By 2030, the U.S. Navy expects some 2,300 Americans to be based in Western Australia.
“What we’re seeing is a real increase in U.S. posture in Australia,” said Zack Cooper, a senior fellow and expert on U.S. strategy in Asia at the American Enterprise Institute. “Sometimes it can take a really long time to build out the infrastructure, but in this case, I think we’re seeing the U.S. and Australia move pretty quickly on both the air and the naval side. I think it’s emblematic of the step-up in effort we’re seeing from both Canberra and Washington.”
“The U.S. needs to diversify the locations from which it can operate air and naval assets. Australia’s northern bases do that on the air side and the naval facilities in Perth are critical on the nuclear submarine side,” he added.
Equipping a base to handle large bombers with heavy payloads is no small task: runways must be long, sturdy, and adequate, with ramp space, fuel infrastructure, and safe weapons storage facilities.
“That can all drive some considerable investment in airfields, which Australia has made and continues to invest in to bolster regional deterrence,” Gunzinger said.

articles.title: Why Russia’s Iskander-M Missile Still Relies on Western Chips for Its Most Critical Functions
articles.body:

Why Russia’s Iskander-M Missile Still Relies on Western Chips for Its Most Critical Functions
About 78% of the identified components in the inertial navigation system of Russia's 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missile are US-made, an independent analysis has found.
The Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO) reached that figure after examining the missile's inertial navigation system, a core element that fixes the weapon's position and tracks its movement in flight. The share applies to the components identified within that single analyzed system, not to the missile as a whole.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The parts NAKO traced are not peripheral. According to the commission, the chips perform critical functions—signal processing, analog-to-digital conversion, digital isolation, power management, and memory.
Where the components come from
Two US firms account for most of the American share. NAKO traced almost 40% of the identified US components to Analog Devices and roughly 12% to Texas Instruments, with the remaining 48% spread across 11 other manufacturers.
American suppliers were the largest but not the only foreign source. NAKO's breakdown of the identified components by origin ran as follows:
- American manufacturers accounted for 78% of the parts;
- Japanese suppliers made up 9.4%;
- Taiwanese firms, 6.3%;
- Swiss firms, 6.3%.
Russia's "import substitution"
Moscow has pressed import substitution across its defense industry, and NAKO acknowledged that Russia has replaced some foreign parts—mostly simpler, less sophisticated ones. The commission described the Oreshnik as its most localized missile to date.
Where systems demand high-precision signal processing and data conversion, though, the reliance on Western components persists.
That unevenness, NAKO argued, matters for sanctions design. Rather than trying to choke off every electronic part reaching Russia, the commission urged a focus on the components that specific weapons cannot function without.
Not an isolated case
The Iskander missile is not the only weapon of its kind. On August 10, 2026, specialists from Ukraine’s Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) demonstrated foreign components extracted from Russian missiles, drones, and other weaponry to Ukrainian diplomats.
As of August 2026, the directorate had identified 5,816 foreign components across 202 Russian weapons systems, it reported, alongside numerous Russian and Belarusian parts.
Among the samples were an American Nvidia Jetson Orin microcomputer taken from a Russian S-71M cruise missile and an inertial module carrying parts from Texas Instruments and Japan's TDK.
A presentation at the Office of the President of Ukraine last week underscored the same dependency. Ukraine's presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, pointed to the Kometa navigation module and components of autonomous inertial systems as critical units. The reliance extends beyond electronics to imported rocket-fuel components, carbon fiber, specialized resins, aluminum and titanium alloys, and high-precision machine tools.
Why it matters for sanctions
Russia’s access to Western microelectronics has come under greater scrutiny as its ballistic missile campaign expands.
Since the start of 2026, Russia has fired more than 500 ballistic missiles at Ukraine while also deploying North Korean KN-23 systems.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has assessed that Russia can build up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year and already holds 600 to 630 in its arsenal. He emphasized that Ukraine's forces are working to blunt Russia's military machine, though he acknowledged that the strikes continue.

articles.title: Pentagon extends MidEast deployments into 2027 even as Trump mulls declaring war over - report
articles.body:
The US military is extending deployments across the Middle East as the Trump administration prepares for the possibility that its conflict with Iran could continue well into 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
At the same time, US officials told the WSJ that US President Donald Trump has privately discussed with senior aides whether he should declare the Iran war over, arguing that sustained economic pressure could eventually compel Tehran to dismantle its nuclear program or bring about the collapse of the regime.
“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” Trump wrote on social media.
What Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth originally presented as a short, decisive military effort has grown exponentially, with Washington now maintaining about 50,000 troops in the region, along with 19 warships, fighter squadrons, air-defense units, and paratroopers, according to the report.
Sources said the military presence is intended to preserve President Donald Trump's ability to choose between continued economic pressure, limited military operations, and broader escalation.
Some aides have warned Trump that expanding the conflict beyond the recent exchanges of strikes could hurt Republican candidates in the November midterm elections, according to the report. Trump has maintained that electoral considerations are not guiding his military decisions.
The Pentagon's sizable regional deployment is designed in part to keep alternative courses of action available.
Trump was briefed last month on potential military options that included intensified airstrikes and deploying ground troops to capture Iranian islands near the Strait of Hormuz, according to the WSJ. Another potential target was Pickaxe Mountain, the site near Natanz that US and Israeli officials have spotlighted over concerns about possible Iranian nuclear activity.
The possibility of such operations requires the US to retain significant offensive capabilities in the region even while Trump tests whether economic pressure can produce a diplomatic result.
Longer deployments cause intense strain on US troops overseas
The deployments are increasingly straining US service members, their families, and military equipment, however. Extended missions are contributing to maintenance delays that could take years to resolve, according to the report.
The strain is most felt by Army air-defense personnel responsible for intercepting Iranian missiles and drones, whose standard deployment period has increased from nine months to 12 months, one person familiar with the matter told the WSJ.
Some units originally assigned to Europe or the Pacific have already spent more than a year deployed after being redirected to the Middle East.
Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, warned that the increased operational tempo could exhaust personnel, postpone maintenance and interfere with longer-term modernization efforts.
Pressure on US Navy continues to grow as well
The Navy is facing similar pressures, as 19 US warships are currently operating in Middle Eastern waters, including two aircraft carriers and 13 guided-missile destroyers, according to a Navy official cited by the WSJ.
Destroyers including the USS Delbert D. Black and USS Spruance, which were deployed for the opening stages of the Iran war, are now helping enforce the blockade. Some of the ships, with crews of roughly 300, are spending several consecutive months at sea rather than receiving more regular breaks.
The deployments underscore the contradiction at the heart of Washington's current strategy: Trump is signaling interest in winding down the conflict while preserving the military capability to rapidly intensify it.
The challenges the extended deployments bring are further compounded by extensive Iranian attacks on American assets, and analysts have indicated that the IRGC is continuing to target US bases and assets as part of an effort to push Washington out of the region.
Despite this, Trump on Wednesday stressed that the US remained prepared to strike Iran again following an Iranian attempt to deploy new mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
“We see everything that they’re doing,” Trump told reporters. “They can’t go to the bathroom without us seeing it.”

articles.title: Agents of chaos: Zelensky’s security services trade accusations after Kiev gunfights
articles.body:
Agents of chaos: Zelensky’s security services trade accusations after Kiev gunfights
The gang-warfare-style clash between Ukrainian security agencies that left three troops shot in Kiev and shocked the country is being spun into competing narratives by the rival parties involved.
Depending on which one of Vladimir Zelensky’s security agencies is speaking, the central figure in the conflict is either a hired gun working for Moscow, or a brave Ukrainian combat officer who was illegally detained for over a week by rogue Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) agents.
What triggered the scandal?
The gunfight on Wednesday morning followed the disappearance on August 23 of Stepan Kaplunov, a reported white supremacist and senior officer in the so-called Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), a militia commanded by notorious neo-Nazi Denis “White Rex” Kapustin, under the patronage of the Ukrainian Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
This week, armed SBU and HUR combat units exchanged gunfire in eastern Kiev, in what was later revealed to have been a standoff over an alleged SBU search of the missing RDK officer’s apartment.
What excuses has the SBU offered for taking the HUR’s man?
On Thursday, as the scandal over the shooting escalated, the SBU accused Kaplunov of participating in a Russian government plot to assassinate a “leader of Russian opposition movement” on Ukraine’s Independence Day, which was marked on August 24.
The agency released a video in which Kaplunov, wearing sunglasses, “confessed” to cooperating with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), along with several screenshots it claimed had been taken from a messaging app on his phone.
Despite claiming to have foiled the alleged plot, the SBU said it chose not to seek Kaplunov’s formal arrest – a striking admission given that he was effectively being accused of treason.
What did Kaplunov claim he discussed with the “Russians”?
If authentic, the screenshots show the RDK officer – wanted for terrorism in Russia – discussing contract killings in Ukraine.
A test job worth $50,000 targeting “not a general or a politician” could have secured him a retainer that would pay him as much as $300,000 per week, his interlocutor wrote.
The alleged Russian connection was described as a “businessman from border areas” who was the son of someone important, “deals with FSB, etc.” and knew the client.
Where is Kaplunov now?
Kaplunov is presumably at a HUR safehouse, having been released after the debacle erupted across social media. In keeping with standard PR procedure, he subsequently gave an interview to a Ukrainian media outlet.
A decorated officer who has fought with Ukrainian units since 2014 and joined the RDK in 2023, where he serves as the RDK’s deputy commander for combat operations, Kaplunov now claims that the SBU had forced the confession from him, to manufacture legal grounds for searching his apartment.
He claims to have spent ten days in two secret SBU detention facilities, bound, blindfolded, and held incommunicado. He credited a HUR formation nicknamed “Timur’s special unit” – reportedly an umbrella structure for the RDK and several other militia groups working for military intelligence – with securing his release “by force.”
All three personnel injured in the shooting were Timur’s men, Kaplunov said.
“Timur” is the callsign of a man Kaplunov identified as Dmitry Ivanov. He stressed that Ivanov, rather than White Rex, is his direct commander.
“We are all a big family, and ‘Timur’ himself, our commander, will never leave anyone behind, not a soldier nor a commander, he will stand up for everyone,” Kaplunov said.
He blamed “historic competition” between the SBU and HUR for the confrontation and alleged that his “abduction” had been intended as a way to get to Ivanov.
What has the HUR said?
HUR has warned it is being targeted by a smear campaign and urged journalists who receive “dubious information” to report the leaks to law enforcement.
In an interview while wearing a face mask, “Timur,” accused the SBU of unlawfully detaining Kaplunov. He claimed that HUR personnel and the SBU’s Alfa commando unit had peacefully resolved the confrontation before another group of SBU agents arrived at the scene and opened fire.
Were there any repercussions for the agencies?
An embarrassed Zelensky, facing military, economic, demographic, and reputational collapse, fired Oleg Khramov from his position as head of the SBU section responsible for protecting state secrets, although it was not immediately clear whether he had any involvement in the scandal.
Both agencies have suffered a serious reputational blow for the second time this year.
Earlier, Ukrainian investigators accused an active HUR operative and a police officer reportedly serving clandestinely for the SBU of masterminding the Monaco bombing that seriously injured exiled Ukrainian businessman Vadim Ermolaev and members of his family in June.
The principal perpetrator was allegedly murdered by the masterminds after she returned to Ukraine.
Are SBU and HUR rivals?
Both agencies were overhauled with CIA assistance following the Western-backed armed coup in Kiev in 2014, according to media reports.
The SBU is currently run by Aleksandr Poklad, the agency’s acting head and former deputy head, whose promotion has yet to be confirmed by parliament.
Kirill Budanov, now the head of Zelensky’s office, previously commanded HUR before a corruption scandal forced the Ukrainian leader’s previous chief of staff, Andrey Yermak, to resign last year.
Budanov and Poklad reportedly have had strong personal animosity since 2022, when the SBU summarily executed banker Denis Kireev, an undercover HUR agent. Poklad allegedly orchestrated the killing.
Is Zelensky in control of SBU and HUR?
Zelensky’s ability to maintain control over Ukraine’s competing centers of power remains in question. His presidential term expired in 2024, and he has remained in office under martial law without holding another election.
The Ukrainian government has been battered by corruption allegations, with Western-backed anti-graft investigators regularly bringing cases against people close to Zelensky.
In the most recent example, last month a deputy head of Zelensky’s office was accused of laundering several bags of cash to pay bail for a former energy minister who himself faces graft allegations in a separate case.
The Ukrainian military is also under increasing strain as Zelensky has failed to secure additional supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles, the weapons Kiev badly needs to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
Despite the shortage, he ordered mass strikes in July on Russian cargo ships and retail warehouses, prompting overwhelming retaliatory strikes.
This week, Zelensky also threatened foreign airlines operating in Russia, claiming that Russian airspace belongs to Ukrainian kamikaze drones now.
With the situation rapidly unraveling, it remains unclear what people trained to spy, sabotage, abduct, and kill on behalf of the state might choose to do next.

articles.title: Japan and Germany are forgetting the lessons of 1945
articles.body:
Japan and Germany are forgetting the lessons of 1945
The anniversary of victory over militarist Japan is more than a commemoration of a distant war. It is an opportunity to ask uncomfortable questions: What exactly was defeated in 1945 and what lessons were meant to survive the victory?
What was supposed to end in 1945?
Japan’s surrender ended a catastrophic war in Asia and the Pacific. Germany’s defeat ended an equally catastrophic war in Europe. In both cases, military power had ceased to be merely an instrument of state policy and had become a force shaping policy itself. Countries were destroyed and tens of millions were dead as a consequence.
After the war, Japan was forced to embraced a high degree of military self-restraint, symbolized by Article 9 of its constitution and by the deliberately defensive character of its armed forces. Germany followed a different path but reached a similar conclusion: Military power requires strict limits and could not be treated as the normal measure of national strength.
Neither country ended up completely defenseless. Both retained armed forces and entered alliance structures. But for decades, there was an underlying recognition that more weapons did not necessarily mean more security.
Today, that recognition is fading. Japan is undertaking its most extensive military buildup since World War II. Germany is carrying out the most consequential rearmament of its postwar history. Both are increasing military spending, expanding defense-industrial capacity, acquiring more powerful strike capabilities, and deepening strategic cooperation. More ominously, both are reassessing their relationship with nuclear weapons.
The justification is simple. The Japanese are told to fear China. The Germans are told to fear Russia.
But what if these threats are being systematically inflated – and politically manufactured? What if the preparations supposedly intended to prevent war are making a larger war increasingly likely?
Japan is being told to fear China
Japan’s transformation is historically significant, because its postwar restraint was a conscious reaction to the disaster of the first half of the 20th century. Today, however, restraint is increasingly presented as an obsolete luxury in an age of geopolitical competition.
Japan is expanding its defense budget, strengthening its naval and air capabilities, acquiring long-range missiles, and developing what it calls “counterstrike capabilities.” It is strengthening its military infrastructure and integrating more closely into wider regional military planning. All of this is still framed as defensive measures, but that doesn’t change the fact that Japan is becoming a powerful military actor.
The relentlessly repeated justification is that China is growing stronger, therefore Japan must rearm. China is expanding its naval forces, therefore Japan must expand its own. China possesses increasingly sophisticated missiles, therefore Japan requires long-range strike capabilities.
But this narrative usually omits the strategic environment from which China’s own military policies emerge.
China is not surrounded by Chinese military bases. Instead, it faces a dense US-centered network of bases, alliances, intelligence systems, and military partnerships operating along its maritime periphery. US forces are stationed in Japan and elsewhere across the region. Japan is expanding its own military role and acquiring new offensive-range capabilities. Beijing’s response to this environment is then cited as proof that the original buildup was necessary, creating a vicious cycle of artificial reasoning.
China, like any major power, does pursue its own interests and take part in the global competition for influence. But the idea that China is simply a disguised aggressor waiting for an opportunity to attack Japan ignores both the elementary logic of power politics and Chinese strategic culture.
Why would China deliberately initiate a major war against Japan, knowing that this could bring it into direct conflict with the US and its allies? The more plausible scenario is the opposite, that China will increasingly prepare for a conflict because it sees one being prepared against it.
Germany is being told to fear Russia
Germany is undergoing a parallel transformation. The army is expanding, military procurement is accelerating, arms production is being encouraged, and Germany is openly aspiring to a much larger role in EU military security.
The entire project rests upon a single dominant assumption: Russia is preparing to threaten Europe, and Europe must therefore prepare for war with Russia. Every day, the Europeans are being told that Russia intends to attack Germany or conquer Europe. These claims are absurd.
Russia’s strategic concerns have long centered on the military configuration along its borders and the expansion of hostile infrastructure toward them. These concerns are being consistently ignored, and all it does is show an unwillingness to understand how Moscow calculates risk.
The dangerous habit of contemporary Western policy is to assign cause and effect selectively. NATO’s expansion and military buildup are described as defensive. Russia’s response is described as proof of inherent aggression. More NATO deployments become necessary because of that response. Another example of circular logic.
Portraying Russia as an inherently expansionist force with no intelligible security interests creates the intellectual conditions in which permanent confrontation becomes inevitable. And permanent confrontation is increasingly becoming the organizing principle of German policy.
China and Russia have become indispensable threats for those advocating a historic expansion of Japanese and German military power. Without the Chinese threat, Japan’s transformation would be much harder to justify. Without the Russian threat, Germany’s rearmament would lose its central political rationale.
An external threat is useful to unlock budgets, strengthen arms industries, create political urgency, and marginalize those who ask whether another course is possible. But history repeatedly demonstrates that exaggerated threats can produce genuine catastrophes.
From rearmament to nuclear strategy
The nuclear dimension makes the parallel German-Japanese rearmament even more disturbing.
Germany has long taken part in NATO’s nuclear-sharing arrangements, but discussion is now moving beyond passive acceptance of an existing framework. Berlin is increasingly involved in debates about a broader European nuclear architecture and closer strategic coordination with France. The question is no longer merely whether Germany lives under an allied nuclear umbrella, but how deeply it should take part in planning and arrangements surrounding nuclear deterrence.
Japan’s case is even more historically charged. The only country to have suffered nuclear attacks, Japan built an important part of its postwar identity around the Three Non-Nuclear Principles: not possessing, producing, or permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons. Now, questions regarding nuclear sharing, extended deterrence, and the practical limits of Japan’s non-nuclear commitments are being discussed more openly than before.
This should concern the entire world. Once countries with Germany’s and Japan’s histories begin moving closer to nuclear strategy, a critical psychological barrier is weakened. Nuclear weapons become increasingly normalized as instruments of security policy rather than recognized for what they are: weapons whose actual use would represent a failure of civilization on an unimaginable scale.
Berlin and Tokyo are drawing closer
In March, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius proposed a Reciprocal Access Agreement with Japan during talks with his counterpart, Shinjiro Koizumi.
This agreement would reduce legal and bureaucratic obstacles to the movement of German and Japanese military personnel onto each other’s territory, facilitating joint training, exercises, and potentially operations.
The proposal would give the Berlin-Tokyo military relationship a more permanent operational structure. Germany has already increased its military activity in the Indo-Pacific through deployments and exercises; a reciprocal access framework would make cooperation easier and more routine.
The symbolism is difficult to miss: Countries whose military histories were forcibly ended in 1945 are now building new structures for military access, deployment, and cooperation with each other.
And growing pressure generates resistance. Military blocs generate opposing alignments. The world is once again being divided into increasingly rigid strategic camps – and the countries that spent decades demonstrating the value of military restraint are now helping accelerate this process.
The lesson the world should draw from 1945
Military strength itself is not the problem. States have legitimate security interests and legitimate reasons to maintain capable armed forces. The decisive question is what political leadership does with that power. A strong military under prudent leadership can deter conflict. A rapidly expanding military under leadership convinced that confrontation is inevitable can accelerate it.
China, Russia, Japan, and Germany all have legitimate security concerns. So do their neighbors.
The task of serious statecraft is not to declare one side’s fears legitimate and another’s imaginary. It is to prevent competing security concerns from becoming a machinery of permanent escalation.
Eighty-one years after victory in 1945, Japan and Germany should remember that lesson particularly well. Their postwar restraint was not weakness – it was an understanding born from catastrophe.
Today, Japan is rearming against a supposedly inevitable Chinese threat. Germany is rearming against a supposedly inevitable Russian threat. Both are moving closer to nuclear strategy. Both are expanding military partnerships. Both are being told that there is no alternative.
This is perhaps the most dangerous phrase in international politics. There is always an alternative before war begins.

articles.title: 'We will be asking for that money' — Trump says Europe should repay US for Ukraine aid
articles.body:
'We will be asking for that money' — Trump says Europe should repay US for Ukraine aid
U.S. President Donald Trump claimed on Sept. 3 that he will ask European countries to repay Washington for ammunition and military aid given to Ukraine under former President Joe Biden.
The demand comes amid Trump's growing fury with European and NATO countries for their refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran, which has dragged on for six months. Hostilities flared again in recent days after the U.S. launched 100 strikes against Iran on Sept. 1."(T)he Biden Administration gave far more Munitions away to Ukraine, at no cost to them, whatsoever, than we have used in Iran," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
"Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for — If they were only asked, but we will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly." 
In the post, Trump also lambasted media reports that the U.S. military was running low on missile stocks due to the war against Iran. 
"For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place," wrote the American Commander-in-Chief. 
The new post is the latest instance of Trump bristling over U.S. aid to Ukraine and NATO, which he has frequently both exaggerated and decried.

It is not clear where Trump's "$300 billion" figure comes from — previously, Trump claimed Biden sent Ukraine $500 billion in aid, while Zelensky has said the total is around $100 billion.

"We're asking for rare earth and oil — anything we can get."
Under the Trump administration, U.S. aid to Ukraine has ground to a halt, leaving Europe and NATO countries to shoulder the financial burden of supporting Kyiv amid Russia's full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Ukraine is experiencing a severe shortage of "air-to-air" missiles for F-16s - media
articles.body:
Ukraine is experiencing a severe shortage of "air-to-air" missiles for F-16s - media
Kyiv • UNN
Due to the acute shortage of "air-to-air" missiles, Ukrainian F-16s sometimes rely solely on guns. Weapons supplies are being rationed.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots are facing such an acute shortage of air-to-air missiles that during some daytime sorties they rely exclusively on the fighters’ internal cannon to counter Russian aerial threats. This was reported by a journalist who recently spoke with a senior commander of Ukraine’s Air Force, UNN reports, citing the TWZ Newsletter.
The publication notes that the shortage of air-to-air missiles means that available weapons stocks are currently being rationed.
This information offers a striking insight into the everyday reality of Ukrainian F-16 operations. Although aircraft may be available, pilots may be ready, and Russian drones and cruise missiles may be approaching, there may simply not be enough missiles to equip the fighters.
According to Newsmax journalist Shelby Wilder, Ukraine’s Air Force can track missile shipments as they cross the country’s border, with personnel counting not only the hours but also the minutes until the weapons reach the aircraft. The concern is whether the missiles will arrive in time for the next Russian airstrike.
A Ukrainian commander who identified himself by the call sign "Phantom" and said he was the commander of the 107th Wing confirmed the fundamental problem when asked directly whether Ukraine was experiencing an acute shortage of missiles for its F-16s.
"Yes, it is true. Any aircraft without weapons… is useless," Phantom said.
The publication notes that this straightforward assessment is particularly striking given the tasks Ukraine assigns to its F-16s and the relentless Russian bombing of Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
We would add
The fighters have become an important part of Ukraine’s multilayered air defense system, hunting Russian drones and cruise missiles, as well as providing a potential counter to Russian combat aircraft and conducting sorties against ground targets. Ukraine has operated F-16s since the summer of 2024.
"We are focused on protecting our airspace from Russian drones in order to protect our infrastructure inside the country," Phantom said. "Our priority target is cruise missiles."
Missiles are needed to destroy as many of the approaching threats as possible before they reach Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, and the F-16 fighter is primarily armed with medium-range AIM-120 (AMRAAM) air-to-air missiles and shorter-range AIM-9 Sidewinders.

articles.title: NATO warns Russia over submarine build up ‘We see them’
articles.body:
NATO says it is closely monitoring the expansion and modernisation of Russia’s submarine force in the High North, including new-generation nuclear-powered cruise missile submarines operating from the Kola Peninsula, according to Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum.
In a statement published on X, the NATO command drew attention to developments around Russia’s Northern Fleet and said the Alliance was treating the growth of its undersea forces seriously.
Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum stated: “Something is moving beneath the surface. Russia is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet.”
The Kola Peninsula in north-west Russia contains several of the Northern Fleet’s principal naval bases and provides access to the Barents Sea and wider North Atlantic. The area is central to Russian submarine operations in northern waters and hosts both nuclear-powered attack submarines and strategic ballistic missile submarines.
NATO specifically referred to the development of newer nuclear-powered guided missile submarines, saying: “Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial capabilities into the High North.”
Something is moving beneath the surface. 🌊
Russia 🇷🇺 is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet.
Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial… pic.twitter.com/UneKonlDon
— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) September 2, 2026
SSGN is the designation commonly used for nuclear-powered submarines equipped primarily for cruise missile operations. Russian boats in this category can be employed against surface ships and land targets, depending on their weapons fit and tasking, while retaining the endurance associated with nuclear propulsion.
The command stated: “They may be invisible beneath the waves. But not for us. We see them, we watch the developments closely and yes, we take these developments seriously.”
The Northern Fleet is responsible for Russian naval activity across the Arctic and High North and operates from bases concentrated around the Kola Peninsula. Its submarines can reach the Norwegian Sea and North Atlantic through waters bordering NATO members Norway and Iceland and areas routinely monitored by allied maritime patrol aircraft, surface vessels and submarines.
Undersea activity in the High North has remained an important part of NATO maritime planning because the region connects Russia’s northern bases with the wider Atlantic. Allied forces regularly conduct anti-submarine warfare training in northern European waters, while maritime patrol aircraft and naval units contribute to surveillance and tracking activity.
Joint Force Command Brunssum is one of NATO’s operational-level joint headquarters and is responsible for planning and conducting activities across part of the Alliance’s northern and eastern area.

articles.title: ‘I Wouldn’t Call it a War’: Vance Downplays Conflict With Iran, Even as Strikes Continue
articles.body:
Vice President J.D. Vance said Thursday that he would not characterize the United States as being at war with Iran, even as the two countries have exchanged strikes in recent days and the Trump Administration has declined to say when a conflict now stretching beyond six months might finally end.
“I wouldn’t call it a war,” Vance told reporters at a White House press briefing, the first since Karoline Leavitt stepped down as press secretary last month. “Right now, there is no active shooting.”
The distinction was striking after a renewed burst of hostilities this week, including American strikes inside Iran and Iranian attacks in the region. But it echoed an argument that President Trump and other Republicans made in the earliest days of the conflict: that the United States was carrying out a limited military operation rather than embarking on another prolonged Middle Eastern war, which, under the Constitution, would require congressional approval.
More than six months later, that distinction has become increasingly difficult to sustain. The United States has repeatedly bombed targets inside Iran as Tehran attacks commercial shipping vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, contributing to higher energy prices.
Vance acknowledged what he called a recent “flare-up” but argued that the most intensive phase of the American campaign had ended long ago. “Major combat operations are currently not ongoing, and they haven’t been ongoing in a very long time,” he said.
He said Operation Epic Fury, the large-scale campaign that followed last year’s Operation Midnight Hammer, lasted roughly six weeks. The earlier operation, he said, destroyed Iranian nuclear facilities, while Epic Fury severely damaged Iran’s conventional military and its ability to produce weapons and rebuild its nuclear program.
But Vance offered little indication of when the broader confrontation might end, saying the Administration would not commit itself to a timeline while Iran continued threatening commercial shipping and global energy supplies. Asked whether the conflict would be over before November’s midterm elections, Vance said he did not know. “You would have to ask the Iranians,” he said, adding: “When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?”
The answer underscored the open-ended nature of a conflict that Trump and others in the Administration repeatedly predicted would be brief. As recently as Wednesday, the President said he did not believe it would last “much longer.” But his Administration is simultaneously intensifying economic pressure on Iran, maintaining a naval blockade, and reserving the option of further military strikes if Iran attacks American interests or interferes with commercial shipping.
History of avoiding the word “war”
Presidents have long resisted the “war” label in conflicts undertaken without a formal declaration of war. Harry Truman called the American intervention in Korea a United Nations “police action,” while Bill Clinton avoided describing NATO’s bombing campaign in Kosovo as a war. Barack Obama similarly argued that the 2011 intervention in Libya did not constitute a “war” requiring congressional authorization.
In March, Trump openly acknowledged that referring to the conflict as “war” carried legal significance because Congress had not authorized it. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say, if you use the word war, that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” he told House Republicans at the time. “They don’t like the word ‘war,’ because you’re supposed to get approval, so I’ll use the word ‘military operation,’ which is really what it is.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson similarly insisted shortly after the initial strikes that the country was “not at war,” describing the campaign instead as “a very specific, clear mission.” Democrats have rejected that characterization and repeatedly tried to force votes requiring congressional authorization for continued hostilities. Those efforts have failed largely along party lines. The dispute has revived a decades-old argument over presidential war powers and the extent to which a president can sustain military operations abroad without explicit approval from Congress.
Economic and military pressure
Vance said Thursday that the administration would not rely on Iran to negotiate in good faith and would instead use whatever tools it considered necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and to protect global energy markets.
He argued that Iran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was “effectively gone” and that oil traffic through the crucial waterway was nearing its pre-conflict level. Shipping data, however, shows traffic remains well below where it stood before the fighting began. The Administration has made restoring commercial traffic through the strait a central objective as energy prices have become an increasing political liability ahead of the midterms.
Vance acknowledged the pain of higher gasoline prices but argued that they could have risen substantially more without American intervention in Iran. “Gas, frankly, could have been much, much higher were it not for our efforts,” he said. He declined to predict when prices might return to around $3 a gallon, saying the more important objective was ensuring “that Iran doesn’t have a nuclear weapon.”
The Administration is now pursuing what amounts to a strategy of intermittent military force combined with sustained economic pressure. Last week, it announced “Operation Economic Outcast,” an effort to further isolate Iran from its remaining trading partners. But the campaign has so far produced limited results, and imposing sanctions aggressive enough to cripple Iranian trade could require confronting countries including China, India, and Russia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that the Administration expected the principal pressure on Iran going forward to be economic, while reserving the right to use military force when necessary.
Iranian uprising
Trump himself has resumed publicly encouraged Iranians to challenge the regime, writing on Truth Social on Tuesday, “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”
When asked by TIME on Thursday whether the Trump Administration was considering arming Iranian dissidents or providing them with other direct assistance, Vance declined to provide more details. “Everything that could happen is on the table: economic pressure, military pressure, diplomatic pressure, covert pressure,” he said. “Of course, these are tools in the President's toolkit.”
Iranian leaders, meanwhile, have shown little sign of capitulating. Its leadership remains divided between officials advocating negotiations and hard-liners pressing for confrontation, and Tehran has continued striking American interests and allies in response to U.S. attacks.
The renewed American bombing has also brought fresh scrutiny of civilian casualties. Iranian authorities said a U.S. strike this week hit a wedding celebration in Sirik in southern Iran, killing at least five people and wounding scores more, including women and children. A New York Times visual analysis and a weapons expert concluded that the wedding was struck by a bomb released by American forces during attacks in the area.
Vance said the episode was under investigation but expressed deep skepticism about Iran’s account. “The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,” he said. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”
“Obviously, sometimes things happen,” he added. “When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them, so we’re investigating it very fully.”

articles.title: JD Vance reacts to airstrike that killed four at Iran wedding: ‘Things happen’
articles.body:
The US vice-president, JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” when asked on Thursday whether an American strike was responsible for killing four people, including a child, at a wedding celebration in southern Iran this week.
The strike hit Kuhestak, a town in Sirik county on the strait of Hormuz. The toll was reported not by the Iranian government but by the Iranian Red Crescent, a member of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement that operates independently of Tehran and is generally treated by international monitors as a credible source on casualty figures.
Asked at a White House press briefing whether the US was responsible, Vance dismissed the reporting.
“I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this,” he said, offering no acknowledgment that the killings had been confirmed by an internationally recognized humanitarian body.
“What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance continued. “We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen.”
Vance told reporters that he had no new information on the specific strike, but that the US was investigating and, unlike Iran, learns from its mistakes.
He also said that the conflict between the US and Iran, which has now stretched into a seventh month and led to the deaths of 18 US service members, was not presently “a war”. The comment sparked immediate backlash from Democrats and critics.
“It’s unbelievable gaslighting,” congressman Ro Khanna, a Democrat from California, said in a video posted to X.
“This is war,” he added. “You know who understands it’s a war? Donald Trump. He claims that we’re winning the war.”
Earlier on Thursday, Trump claimed in a social media post that the US had “virtually unlimited” amounts of mid- to high-grade munitions, and called journalists who have reported on the Pentagon’s dwindling stockpiles “treasonous SCUM”.
The remarks come amid a broader US-Iran war that continues with no sign of a lasting peace despite months of halting negotiations.
The US and Iran exchanged fire earlier this week, renewing fears of greater escalation across the region. US Central Command (Centcom) has said the broader strike package that Tuesday night targeted Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and communications facilities, without specifying whether the wedding venue was among the intended targets. The Red Crescent said shrapnel from the US missile strike hit the residential home where the wedding celebration was under way, killing four people and wounding more than 50 others.
Iranian authorities have previously put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures that outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated.
The strike also revives scrutiny of a 28 February US attack roughly 23 miles away, in Minab, that hit a school compound and killed at least 156 people, most of them schoolchildren. A preliminary US military inquiry reportedly found that the strike resulted from a targeting error, after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of an adjacent Revolutionary Guard naval base. The Pentagon said at the time it was investigating; a full report has not been made public.

articles.title: Iran strike leaves U.S. Navy with a serious supply problem
articles.body:
- The Navy has about 20 ships and 20,000 personnel in the Middle East, resupplying at sea every five to six days since Iran struck its Bahrain logistics base on February 28.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln spent most of nine months deployed without a port call before docking in Thailand this week en route to San Diego.
The U.S. Navy is running open-ended combat deployments in the Middle East without access to most of its regional supply bases, forcing ships to resupply at sea roughly every five to six days rather than pulling into port, The New York Times reported.
Iran struck the Navy’s logistics hub in Bahrain on February 28, the first day of the current war, according to the Times. Other regional ports large enough to handle an aircraft carrier or a supply ship remain within range of Iranian missiles and drones, making them effectively off-limits.
With nearby bases unavailable, Navy supply ships now sail 2,200 miles to Diego Garcia, a small island in the Indian Ocean, to load food, fuel and other goods before returning to the fleet. The next-closest option is Singapore, 3,700 miles away, a route that requires passing through the Strait of Malacca, one of the world’s busiest commercial shipping corridors.
The Navy currently has about 20 ships and 20,000 sailors and Marines deployed in the Middle East, according to the Times. That includes two aircraft carriers, the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) and the USS George Washington (CVN 73), along with 12 destroyers carrying roughly 3,700 personnel combined, and a three-ship amphibious ready group carrying about 5,000 Marines and sailors. Keeping that force fed and fueled requires more than 420,000 meals and about 8 million gallons of fuel every week, the Times reported. A single carrier’s air wing alone burns roughly 2 million gallons of fuel weekly, even though the ship itself is nuclear-powered.
Resupply at sea requires the receiving ship and the supply ship to sail together on identical course and speed, often for hours, while staying within roughly 150 feet of each other despite wind, waves and current. Sailors fire lines across to the other vessel using rifles, then connect the ships with steel cables that carry fuel lines and pallets of supplies. Helicopters simultaneously ferry additional pallets of food, spare parts and mail between the ships in slung cargo nets.
These deployments have no fixed end date. Ships remain on station until the president and the defense secretary decide otherwise, according to the Times, a practice the newspaper described as unsustainable.
The Navy operates 11 aircraft carriers in total and has sent four of them to the Middle East during the war. Some of the remaining carriers are undergoing extended shipyard repairs and will not be available to deploy again for years, the Times reported.
One of those four carriers, the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72), spent most of its nine months at sea without a single port call, well beyond the roughly monthly port visits the Navy typically allows crews for rest. The USS George Washington relieved the Lincoln on August 20. The Lincoln docked in Thailand on Wednesday morning, where its crew will get several days of shore leave before the ship continues across the Pacific to its home port in San Diego.

Trump will demand that Europe pay for weapons provided to Ukraine during Biden's presidency
Kyiv • UNN
Trump said that the United States would ask Europe to reimburse the costs of weapons and ammunition provided to Ukraine. He also reported on increasing production.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he would ask European countries to reimburse the United States for the cost of military aid and ammunition previously sent to Ukraine amid the war with Russia, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
In a social media post, Trump also criticized reports that U.S. ammunition stockpiles had been significantly depleted amid a separate war in Iran, adding that the United States was ramping up production and stockpiling ammunition.
"We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S., instead of selling them to others, but sales to allies will resume soon," Trump wrote.
"Hundreds of billions of dollars were given to Ukraine and NATO for free, which Europe would have paid for—if only they had been asked, but we will be asking for that money, albeit somewhat belatedly!" he added, blaming the administration of his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden.
We will add
