articles.title: US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
articles.body:
US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
Former White House staffer calls for espionage and cyber options as Washington prepares for a potential Chinese breakthrough
Jacob Stokes, deputy director of the Indo-Pacific Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS), said at an online event on Thursday that various US agencies, including the Department of Defense and the National Security Agency, should begin assessing what intelligence they need to justify taking such actions.
“Trying to think through the particulars of that will be especially important, in part because it will help policymakers … start to work backwards based on the unique nature of the technology, in the same way that in a past era, policymakers would learn about nuclear weapons and … work backwards from the science to the policy implications,” he said.
In a new CNAS report published last week, the former Obama administration national security staffer called for the US government to consider the feasibility of diplomatic, espionage, cyber and kinetic measures to prevent China from achieving AGI first.

articles.title: General Dynamics gets $194M deal on nuclear missile program
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded General Dynamics Missions Systems a $194.1 million contract modification for fire control engineering support on the SLCM-N nuclear missile program.
- The Navy has set a 2034 target date for delivering the missile, which Congress kept funded after the Biden administration sought to cancel it in 2022.
The U.S. Navy has awarded General Dynamics Missions Systems a $194.1 million contract modification for engineering support work on the Nuclear-Armed, Sea-Launched Cruise Missile program, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee modification adds to a previously awarded unpriced letter contract and covers technical and engineering support for the missile’s Fire Control Subsystem. The $194.1 million figure includes optional line items that may or may not ultimately be exercised. Work will be split between General Dynamics’ facility in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, which will handle 75% of the effort, and a facility in Manassas, Virginia, handling the remaining 25%. The contract is scheduled to run through September 30, 2028.
The Navy is obligating $135.3 million in fiscal 2025 reconciliation research, development, test and evaluation funds at the time of award, none of which will expire at the end of the current fiscal year. The Navy awarded the contract sole source under federal acquisition law, after previously publishing notice of the pending award on the government’s SAM.gov contracting portal. Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office in Washington, D.C., that oversees the service’s ballistic and cruise missile programs, is managing the contract.
The missile at the center of the contract, known as SLCM-N, is a Navy program to develop a low-yield, non-strategic nuclear warhead mounted on a sea-launched cruise missile, intended for deployment on attack submarines and potentially surface ships. The concept was first formally recommended in the Trump administration’s 2018 Nuclear Posture Review as a way to restore a capability the Navy retired in 2010, when it withdrew the nuclear-armed Tomahawk Land Attack Missile from service.
The Biden administration’s 2022 Nuclear Posture Review recommended canceling SLCM-N, citing cost and questions about the adequacy of the existing nuclear arsenal. Congress rejected that recommendation and continued funding the program through subsequent defense authorization bills, establishing it as a formal program of record in the fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act.
Rear Adm. Randy Wolfe, director of the Navy’s Strategic Systems Programs, testified before Congress in May 2025 that the program had spent the prior year working to define the missile’s overall system architecture, an effort spanning the missile itself, its fire control system, launcher system, platform integration, warhead integration, and associated support equipment and training materials. Wolfe said at the time that the Navy expected to deliver the capability in 2034. Sandia National Laboratories announced in January that the program would use the W80-5 warhead variant.

articles.title: Kiev loses some 1,510 troops along engagement line in past day — Russia’s top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,510 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 315 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, over 210 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and more than 205 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost over 385 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, more than 340 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and up to 55 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russian air defenses intercept 998 Ukrainian UAVs, two smart bombs over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 998 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and two smart bombs over the past 24 hours, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down two guided aerial bombs, three rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system and 998 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces take control of Vasilevka, Blagodatnoye, Dolzhanka in Kharkov Region
Over the past 24 hours, Russian troops have taken control of the settlements of Vasilevka, Blagodatnoye, and Dolzhanka in the Kharkov Region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of decisive actions, units of the Battlegroup North have taken control of the settlements of Vasilevka, Blagodatnoye, and Dolzhanka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike logistics center for military cargo in Kiev Region
Russian troops used droned to strike Ukraine’s logistics center in Velikaya Aleksandrovka, Kiev Region, used for the storage and distribution of military cargo, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The Russian Armed Forces continue to carry out coordinated strikes against Ukrainian logistics facilities used in the interests of the armed forces of Ukraine. Overnight, attack drones struck the Biokon logistics center in the Velikaya Aleksandrovka settlement in the Kiev Region, which was used for the storage and distribution of military cargoes," the ministry said in a statement.
Battlegroup North destroys over 240 Ukrainian dugouts, deployment sites near Kharkov
Unmanned systems units of the Russian Battlegroup North’s 11th Army Corps have destroyed over 240 dugout shelters and temporary field deployment sites of the Ukrainian armed forces in the Kharkov region during August, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operator with the call sign Grif told TASS.
"UAV operators of the Battlegroup North’s 11th Army Corps identified and destroyed over 240 Ukrainian dugouts and temporary field deployment sites in the Kharkov Region in August. The destruction of dugouts and temporary field deployment sites disrupts the deployment of enemy troops, reduces their activity, and hinders the supply of frontline positions," the soldier said.
According to him, Battlegroup North strikes the Ukrainian armed forces’ dugouts and temporary deployment sites using attack UAVs, including FPV drones. "Operators track targets from the air, verify the data received, and monitor the results of the crews’ operations," he added.
Russian forces strike facilities used by Ukrainian army -- Defense Ministry
Russian forces struck transport and energy facilities used by the Ukrainian army over the past day, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Russia’s tactical aircraft, attack drones, missile forces and artillery struck Ukraine’s logistics hubs, fuel and energy facilities and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian army, as well as production and storage sites for unmanned aerial vehicles and their components and temporary deployment points of Ukrainian troops and foreign mercenaries in 155 areas," the statement reads.
Russian Black Sea Fleet destroys six Ukrainian Navy unmanned boats
The Black Sea Fleet has destroyed six unmanned boats operated by the Ukrainian Navy, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"Black Sea Fleet forces destroyed six unmanned boats operated by the Ukrainian Navy in the Black Sea," the Defense Ministry said.
Russian forces liberate Izhevka settlement in Donetsk People’s Republic
Russian forces liberated the Izhevka settlement in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units liberated the settlement of Izhevka in the Donetsk People’s Republic through active operations," the ministry said in a statement.
Ukrainian forces sustain heavy losses in Vasilevka, Kharkov Region
Units of a separate motorized infantry brigade of the Ukrainian armed forces sustained heavy casualties in the fighting for Vasilevka in the Kharkov region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"To hold the [Vasilevka] settlement, the enemy deployed units from a separate motorized infantry brigade, but as a result of artillery fire, Ukrainian militants suffered heavy losses and were forced to leave the settlement and withdraw from their positions," the ministry said in a statement. On September 3, the ministry reported that assault troops of the Russian Battlegroup North’s 126th Motorized Rifle Regiment, 71st Guards Motorized Rifle Division, took control of the Vasilevka settlement in the Kharkov Region.

articles.title: When Drone Swarms Leave Seconds to React, Germany’s New IRIS-T Packs Eight Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
When Drone Swarms Leave Seconds to React, Germany’s New IRIS-T Packs Eight Missiles
German defense manufacturer Diehl Defence unveiled the IRIS-T SLS MK 4, a next-generation short-range air defense system, at the ILA 2026 air show in Berlin on September 3, according to ArmyInform, which cited analysts from the Belgian defense center Army Recognition Group.
The system is presented as the fourth generation of the combat-proven IRIS-T SLS platform. Diehl Defence, headquartered in Überlingen in western Germany, described it on its official website as a direct evolution of a system already tested in battlefield conditions—an implicit reference to its use in Ukraine's defense against Russian strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Diehl Defence's official product release, the IRIS-T SLS MK 4 "is a further development of the combat-proven IRIS-T SLS system" and represents a "high-performance solution in dynamic threat scenarios."
The IRIS-T SLS MK 4 consolidates radar, command-and-control systems, and a launch unit onto a single highly mobile vehicle.
Its effective engagement range reaches 12 kilometers, with altitude coverage up to 6 kilometers. The architecture is vehicle-independent, allowing the system to be mounted on different platforms to meet varied customer requirements, Diehl Defence noted on its official portal.
A key upgrade in the MK 4 standard is the increase in the number of ready-to-fire missiles from four to eight, effectively doubling engagement capacity compared with previous configurations.
ArmyInform, citing Army Recognition Group analysts, reported that this improvement is particularly relevant for countering swarm attacks involving drones and loitering munitions—scenarios in which reaction windows are measured in seconds.
Automation is another defining feature of the new system. Automated target detection, tracking, engagement planning, and firing sequencing reduce crew requirements while accelerating response times, according to Army Recognition Group specialists cited by ArmyInform.
This capability is described as especially critical against modern aerial threats such as cruise missiles and strike drones.
Defence Industry Europe, also cited by ArmyInform, reported that the missile hardware itself remains unchanged in the MK 4 variant. The system is expected to gain a fire-on-the-move capability in the future, allowing missile launches while the vehicle is in motion—a feature that would further compress response times in mobile operations.
The MK 4 standard was developed in alignment with NATO requirements and operational specifications, reflecting the alliance's growing emphasis on integrated, rapidly deployable short-range air defense.
The SLS system is already incorporated into the Ukrainian layered air defense concept and can integrate additional effectors, including the unmanned armed missile system or a combat station.

articles.title: Spy planes swarm Russia’s borders in rare surge
articles.body:
Two RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft, at least two P-8A Poseidons and American tanker support are operating across the High North in a concentration of intelligence-gathering flights rare in both scale and composition, according to open-source tracking.
The account DefenceGeek, run by one of our team members Jon, logged the aircraft operating from the United Kingdom and Iceland, watching across the border into Russia. Among them were the Royal Air Force Rivet Joint ZZ666 using the callsign ASCOT 7202, an American RC-135W as JAKE 17, and a KC-135R tanker as RAKE 67 providing refuelling.
A United States Air Force Rivet Joint is operating within the European Command area for the first time in a while, flying near Russia’s naval base complex at Murmansk. It is likely to be operating with fighter escort given an active tanker bridge in the area. A second Rivet Joint, this one British, was tracked along the border between Russia and Finland, with a Poseidon monitoring the Baltic at low altitude. American Rivet Joint aircraft have concentrated elsewhere in recent years, which is what makes an appearance over the Barents notable.
NATO Eyes on Russia Continues
Two RC-135 “Rivet Joint” SIGINT platforms and at least 2 P-8A “Poseidon” aircraft are operating out of the UK & Iceland today in the high north, watching across the border into Russia, supported by US tankers:
🇬🇧 RC-135W “ASCOT7202” ZZ666 #43C39D… pic.twitter.com/dqKU3KIQuv
— DefenceGeek 🇬🇧 (@DefenceGeek) September 2, 2026
What they are looking at
Murmansk and the wider Kola Peninsula hold the Russian Northern Fleet, including the ballistic missile submarines that carry the sea-based portion of the Russian deterrent, along with the attack boats that transit south into the Atlantic. It is the single most concentrated collection of Russian naval power anywhere, and the point from which any submarine deployment towards the Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom gap begins.
The RC-135W does not take photographs, no, it is an electronic surveillance aircraft, and its crews survey the electromagnetic spectrum to collect communications, radar emissions and other signals, building a picture of what is switched on, where it is, and how it behaves. Flying a track along a border allows the aircraft to map air defence radars and communications networks without entering the airspace they cover.
The P-8A Poseidon does a different job, of course. It hunts submarines, using sonobuoys dropped into the water and its own radar and acoustic processing, and the Royal Air Force operates nine of them from RAF Lossiemouth in Moray. A Poseidon working the Baltic at low altitude is looking at what is on and under the surface.
Britain operates three Rivet Joints from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, converted from KC-135 airframes under a co-operative programme with the United States Air Force, which flies a larger fleet of the type from Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska.
The flights come at the end of a fortnight of unusually heavy allied air activity along the Russian frontier. Around 25 aircraft from several nations operated over the Baltic region on 18 August in a package overseen by the United States, including an EA-37B Compass Call electronic attack aircraft and an ARTEMIS II intelligence platform, with further flights on the two days following. NATO E-3A Sentry aircraft and Multinational MRTT Fleet tankers have been operating over Lithuania and Poland since.
Germany formally attributed the attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russian intelligence on Tuesday, announcing the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn along with new sanctions and entry restrictions, in a step Estonia’s prime minister described as Russia taking its hybrid attacks in Europe to a new and dangerous level.
Surveillance flights of this kind are deliberately visible, as readers will know. Aircraft on these missions generally transmit, and their tracks appear on civilian monitoring platforms, which is a choice rather than an oversight.
The Russian Navy has meanwhile had no presence in the Mediterranean since June, with a NATO official telling us last week that allied warships outnumber Russian vessels in European waters by roughly three to one.
Neither the Ministry of Defence nor United States Air Forces in Europe comments on individual intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sorties.

articles.title: How 9/11 Shaped My Life
articles.body:
Twenty-five years later, Sept. 11 remains a watershed moment, one with both personal and global implications. To mark the anniversary, TIME spoke to people with very different connections to the day, to hear about what they experienced at the time as well as the ripple effects. For some, the legacy of the date is one of profound loss. Others know about the tragedy mostly from history class. One thing is clear: The attacks that changed the world also changed lives.
I was 4½ when my dad died. I have only brief memories of that day. I remember my mom taking my twin brother and me out of preschool. I remember watching the TV at home and then going over to one of her friends’, whose husband was also a firefighter, and watching it there. We were so young, we didn’t really grasp what was actually going on. But as you get older, you start to realize what you’ve missed out on. It’s not quite the same as being sad because you miss someone close to you. It’s more like you’re sad because you didn’t really get to be close to them.
My dad was a cop for 12 years and a firefighter for only 18 months, but joining the FDNY was always his plan. For as long as I can remember, I also wanted to be a firefighter. I did the entry exam when I was 18, even though they don’t take anyone until 21. I went to college, but I think I was just killing time. I dropped out after two years, as the process ramped up. My mom kept encouraging me to consider other things, but she knew I had put all my eggs in that basket. I loved the routine and discipline of the academy, and I really tried to earn my spot; I didn’t want to feel like I was getting special treatment.
A lot of things about the fire department don’t change, and I remember thinking my dad might have stood right where I was standing, worrying about getting yelled at by some drill instructor for having a button undone. I don’t have many shared memories with him, but that came close. He worked in Brooklyn, just on the other side of the tunnel from the World Trade Center. I wanted to go to a different firehouse, to let the guys make up their mind about me without having known his reputation, so I’m in the Bronx. The firefighters I meet that knew him, I feel like they're happy to see that I'm on the job.
On 9/11 I usually go to Mass at my firehouse and then drop by Ladder 101, where Dad worked. Last year for the first time I met someone who was actually riding that day, and he gave me the full rundown. They were staged at the mouth of the tunnel right under the towers, and as they sat there on the rigs, they watched the second plane come in. They could feel the impact and then they went straight in. From what I understand, his group went up a way, came back down, and were in the lobby when the building collapsed.
Dad was also a lifeguard at Overlook Beach in Long Island, and the lifeguards there put up a little memorial for him. My mom is not big on going to the firehouse or the ceremonies in the city on the anniversaries. I think it’s just too overwhelming. So we do a more casual gathering in the afternoon. It’s less somber, more a reason for everyone to just get together.
Sometimes the attention that comes with being a legacy firefighter is uncomfortable, but not for the reasons you might think. I don’t have trouble talking about it; it was something that happened when I was young, but I had a happy childhood and a very fortunate life. I’m not looking for sympathy—I feel lucky to have had that role model of selflessness and self-sacrifice. On the other hand, I do miss having had a real relationship with my dad.
Do I wish he was still alive? Of course. I sometimes wonder if I’d be different if I’d known my dad. But that event shaped my way of thinking and shaped me. I’m very proud of what he did, and I think it’s a very admirable and honorable way to die. And I wouldn’t want someone else to have been in his place because I don’t think that’s what he would have wanted. –As told to Belinda Luscombe
Kelsey Griffin
My journey of becoming a pilot started when I was 14, when I went to a youth summer camp sponsored by the Organization of Black Aerospace Professionals (OBAP). When I first told my parents that I wanted to be a pilot, of course they were a little bit concerned about the dangers that come with flight training at a young age, but they were also very supportive.
I took my first discovery flight with an instructor in 2022. At first I was definitely nervous, because there was so much going on in the plane at once. But once we were at around 2,000 feet, everything became incredibly peaceful. Looking down at the scenery gave me a sense of freedom that I never really experienced anywhere else. I knew at a young age that I never wanted to work a traditional nine-to-five job. I was also really big on traveling, and that discovery flight showed me that being a pilot was something I could do every day and enjoy. I took my first solo fight in 2024.
Flight training is expensive, but my parents made sacrifices to support me financially as I sought out scholarships and opportunities. I was drawn to the LeRoy W. Homer Jr. Foundation Scholarship, because of their mission to empower future aviators. He was an African American pilot, and a first officer for United Airlines on Flight 93. I wasn’t alive when 9/11 happened, so my understanding comes from learning about it through documentaries and conversations with my parents and grandparents and others.
The tragedies definitely impacted not only the lives of everyday people, but also caused major disruption in the aviation industry. When my mentor just started his career as a pilot, he got furloughed soon after 9/11 because the airline industry was completely devastated over Americans’ fear of flying. I have a family member that is still afraid to fly on aircrafts.
Before I went to college, I became a private pilot and a licensed drone pilot. I briefly stopped my training after one of my friends passed away, but getting the scholarship lifted my spirits and gave me an extra push to continue my goal. The scholarship exists because of somebody who lived with courage, professionalism, and commitment to serving others. Knowing that I’m representing his legacy motivates me to work harder and fly with integrity, and never take opportunities for granted.
At Middle Georgia State University, I'm enrolled in aviation courses to finish out my remaining ratings and license and also to, as we call it in the industry, time build. I have to get at least 1,000 flight hours before I can go to a regional airline. It will probably take me about six more years of training to become a major airline pilot. African American women make up less than 1% of professional pilots in the U.S. I have had the privilege of connecting with several of them through organizations such as Sisters of the Skies, OBAP, Aviation Career Enrichment, Pink STEM, and Youth in Aviation. Having this support gives me a sense of comfort and understanding that through hard work, I can also achieve it. –As told to Philip Wang
Alka Pradhan
I was infamous as an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins for choosing classes in the afternoon so I could sleep all morning. My more diligent roommate would try to wake me so she’d have someone to talk to. On 9/11, I thought that’s what she was doing. Maybe a minute or so after she got me to the TV, the second plane hit. It was terrifying.
Even at 19, I was on track to study the intersection of human-rights law and international humanitarian law. When it became clear in early October that we, the U.S., were going to strike Afghanistan in a way that seemed not entirely targeted and seemed to conflate the Taliban with al-Qaeda, that began my interest in all this. But to me, our actions didn't seem to comply with the law of war that I had been studying. I really did not anticipate that I would eventually use my specialization to litigate as hard as I possibly could against my own government. But that is what I have done for the past 13ish years in my work at Guantánamo.
I was already working with Guantánamo detainees when, in 2015, I got a call from a friend at the Department of Defense, who said the military commissions, which are prosecuting those actually alleged to have organized the attacks on 9/11, were hiring civilians. He asked if I’d be interested in representing Ammar al-Baluchi, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed’s nephew. I thought, well, there's nothing I can do that is deeper in the heart of this morass than the military commissions, because the CIA torture programs are at the heart of these cases. So I've been a defense attorney for Ammar al-Baluchi’s 9/11 case since 2015. It has been in pretrial hearings for 14 years.
For 9/11, the actual fact allegations against al-Baluchi are that he transferred money to people who ended up being the hijackers. We have never contested the fact that he transferred money. He was in Dubai, he was asked to transfer money, he transferred money. The $10,000 question is: What did he know at the time? And the government has no evidence that is not derived from torture that indicates he had any knowledge of what was happening on Sept. 11.
The 9/11 case really is all day, every day. It is the biggest criminal case in U.S. history. I hold a top-secret security clearance, and I still don’t have all the information I need about the torture at the black sites that impacted how Ammar is today and the statements he gave later. The trial has just been scheduled for June 2028, but I don’t know if it will ever happen, and I think that is a very hard truth, particularly for the victims’ family members. Witnesses have passed away, evidence has been destroyed by the government. The men themselves are deteriorating because the U.S. refuses to give them the medical care they need as undisputed torture victims. Millions and millions of dollars have been wasted on this exercise so far. It’s the Jarndyce v Jarndyce of the United States.
However I also think this is one of the most important things I will ever do because it shows fellow Americans that this is what dissent looks like, and I know it sounds trite, but this is also what patriotism looks like. I am both grateful for and have great contempt for what the Department of Defense has done over these 25 years. On 9/11 I will reach out to the victims’ family members who I am in touch with and convey my very deep sadness and anger over what happened. I will watch the commemorations. I will contemplate. Then I will start speaking again about everything that we are continuing to do wrong. –As told to B.L.
Jukay Hsu
I was student-body president at Stuyvesant High, three blocks from the World Trade Center. I had an early meeting that day with the principal about the plans for the year. So normally I’d be walking to school when the first plane hit. We evacuated, I think, just as the first tower fell, and I remember looking through these two-story plate-glass windows at this billowing black-gray kind of fog coming from one way as we went out the other way into a sunny sky.
I grew up in Queens. My mother was a social worker. I was lucky to get full financial aid to Harvard, and signed up for ROTC, then went to Iraq. I always thought service was public service. I was a second lieutenant leading a platoon of 40 men in Salahuddin province, kind of at the mid-end of the surge. Even with combat patrols, I ended up doing a lot around civil governance because counterinsurgency involves that. It was a very different kind of learning.
When I got out of the military, all my classmates were going into tech. I was like, If New York is going to become a tech sector, how can more people be included in that? All the soldiers I worked with never went to college. That's the difference between officer and soldier. Even though my platoon sergeant was 20 years older than me, I was in charge because I went to college. It really got you thinking: All these companies and jobs and wealth are being created, but two-thirds of Americans and two-thirds of New Yorkers don’t have a four-year college degree. In 2011, I ended up creating Pursuit. Our idea was to train working-class people in the skills tech companies tell us they need. The average student arrived making $16,000 and a year later has a job paying $94,000.
I left Pursuit to start a research organization called Bright Future to focus on AI alignment for the benefit of humanity. There’s this idea that AI is going to be so dominant, so superpowerful, not just tools, but creating a being—we’re trying to create like a god, essentially, right? It's kind of crazy. So what does that mean for humans? This year I also joined the New York City Economic Development Board, which oversees and shapes AI policy.
Perhaps the future is not college versus noncollege. Perhaps it’s going to be AI and non-AI. But hopefully, there’s a way to democratize that and enable cooperation. We're creating these new digital minds, so you have to consider their power and impact. Early on in high school, it was imprinted on me that what’s most important is what happens to all of us. And the ability to have agency in that. 9/11 helped cement that. Important critical junctures really can bring out the best in humanity, if we choose to respond.
Marc Rivera
I was born in Puerto Rico but have lived all but the first three months of my life on the Lower East Side of Manhattan. Next year, it will be 50 years that I'm pastoring down here. Primitive Church is within eyeshot of the towers. On 9/11, I saw the towers fall and then didn’t set foot outside lower Manhattan until March the following year.
I had just dropped my younger son at high school a block away from the Trade Center and I was going into the church office when I saw my secretary outside. She simply says, “Look.” Sure enough, there was a gaping hole in the north tower. I could see what I thought was debris falling. Later on, I discovered it may have been people. I turned around to get my son, but the police wouldn’t let me through, so I went back to the church, and all of a sudden, a sea of people filled with soot and stuff came walking down our street. We opened the church to them. We had four landlines that were somehow still working. Eventually my son walked in with a bunch of friends, all covered in soot. My older son also arrived from midtown. That was a rebirth moment for me. I was able to shift my attention to helping the helpers and healing the healers.
By day two after the collapse, I was doing what I've always done: galvanizing people and starting to help individuals, raising money to pay people's rent and medical bills and for funerals. We established the Ground Zero Clergy Task Force, which was simply clergy of different faiths, denominations, and traditions who gathered together to help at the site and to coordinate churches with FEMA and the New York City government. Every day, anywhere from 15 to 50 clergy would meet in the sanctuary, and then go down to the hole, to ground zero, to see what we could do. About a year afterward, I established a Northeast Clergy Group, which was broader and longer-standing. It tried to run the same program for people at the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania.
We closed those organizations eventually, but through them I saw the importance of not being so rigid or immovable in my theological training. Many religious people, regardless of faith tradition, tend to think that we have the patent on truth. This event broadened my perspective and really challenged me to make that change intellectually and also in my practice. When tragedy strikes, no one cares how much training you have, how many books you have written, how large your congregation is. Because the bottom line is love. I saw a fireman who looked so tired and I asked if I could pray for him. I didn’t ask what he believed first.
The most painful consequence for me personally was that my oldest son, Tim, was diagnosed with Stage IV colorectal cancer, one of the cancers that is covered by the 9/11 fund. He fought it courageously for three years, but this September will mark one year since his passing. He would have been 46. We believe he probably got it because we live down here.
One of my greatest concerns today is that there are still people in our congregation and in this community who may qualify for assistance through the 9/11 fund that the federal government set up, but some remain reluctant to apply. They’re more afraid of the system than they are of getting sick. So, more than two decades later, part of our ministry is still helping people understand that the consequences of Sept. 11 did not end on Sept. 11. We are still caring for people. We are still encouraging people to seek the help that is available to them. And we are still learning what that terrible day taught us from the very beginning: when people are hurting, our first responsibility is to love them.
Connie Stevanus
That day, I was working at a bank, and as I went from department to department, they were bringing this up on their computers. On my way home, it’s just a two-lane country road, and there was so much traffic. Cars were passing me in either direction. They were state police cars. When I finally got home, I see my husband picking things out of the yard, and I didn’t know what he was doing until I went to pull into our driveway. It was black, totally black, with small pieces of burnt debris. And it just hit me then what I was looking at. Flight 93 carried mail. We had mail in our trees, in our yard. The neighbor across the road from us had a piece of the United Airlines magazine in her yard.
We started volunteering at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pa., after my husband had retired from work, like five years after 9/11. People come from all over—Europe, Australia, different countries. They like to tell you where they were and their experiences of that day. And then they always ask, “Where were you when this happened?” We get a lot of school students, and they're very alert to what happened here, so they're usually very quiet and very respectful. My 21-year-old grandson wasn't born yet. And when he was in eighth grade, I think it was, his school came out.
I never get tired of talking about it. Probably 99% of them still feel the pain and show their emotions easily when we're talking. Sometimes it’s a little hard to be there, because I’m that person—I might not be able to say the right thing to you, but I can cry right alongside of you. At the Visitor Center, we have those three phone messages. You know that some of the passengers on Flight 93 had to leave messages because they didn’t get an answer? Those are very powerful.
Can I share one little story with you? This was just after they were done with the excavation and the road opened up. So it was about two weeks later. My husband and I stopped there after work one evening. And it was just like the day of 9/11. Sunny, bright blue sky, not a cloud in the sky. There was nobody around, just me and my husband. We looked down through the field, and you could just see where the crash site was, the fresh soil that covered that area. And we just stood there. And all you could hear were birds, the rustling of the high grass, and just silence. And there wasn't a flag. There was nothing where you would think something like this happened. You could see the little fence that they had around the debris field. But that is a moment that I'll never forget. –As told to Karl Vick
Shams Frough
I was going into fifth grade when 9/11 happened. I remember, because it was two days after a famous Northern Alliance commander was assassinated. Obviously, there was no TV in Kabul, but our ears were wide open and we did hear about it on the radio. (From a very young age, I was listening to BBC Persian.) Then came the bombings, and life in Kabul became a bit hard, so for a short period, I went back to my village, Kapisa, which is 100 km from Kabul, where I had shepherding duties. I remember very well the big difference when we returned to school; girls were going too, and we no longer had to wear black turbans. Everybody wanted the Taliban to go, but we didn’t know that eventually all these American soldiers would come and there would be a hot war again. We all thought the Northern Alliance would take over.
My mother died when I was young, and my father really worked to make sure his children did not have to work on the farm. I went to an elite Turkish-run high school; out of 6,000 applicants, only 100 were accepted—and some of those places were reserved for the children of government ministers. Most lessons were in English, but we also learned Turkish. I wanted to go to medical school, but I was young and male and I believed the hype, and in the last year of school I began working with the U.S. Army. I was sent to Kandahar as an interpreter. After I was nearly killed twice, I was transferred to the Department of Procurements in Kabul and ended up doing simultaneous translation for colonels and generals who were advising the Afghan military and police. I reported what looked like corruption in the Afghan procurement process, and then I knew I had to leave. It took three years, until 2014—a week or so after I resigned—for my Special Immigrant Visa to be processed.
My wife and I were initially assigned to Albuquerque, N.M., which was funny, because my Army friends always made fun of the mud huts in Afghanistan and there they were in America, only it was called adobe. When we moved to Chicago, I went to community college and so I took up driving taxis and Ubers. I’d study all week and then sleep in my taxi at the airport, because there was always a three-hour wait for a fare. Then in 2021, I started a business called Kapisa Rugs; it was rebranded as Rugistan in 2024, and we directly source hand-knotted rugs from Afghanistan. It’s not easy with Amazon and other competition, so to keep prices down, I’m here seven days a week. Right now we have two locations, but this is not the goal.
I love rugs. I'll always cherish them. But hopefully, in about a year, it will be profitable enough, and my wife will have taken over and I will be able to fire myself. Some of my high school friends who didn’t join the Army are already doctors here, so I sometimes feel like I haven’t lived up to my capacity in the way I could have in Afghanistan. I am currently completing my master’s of public health at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, and I hope to start medical school in 2028. I joke with my wife that I’ll probably graduate alongside our sons. –As told to B.L.
Sari Beth Rosenberg
My first day of student teaching was supposed to be 9/11. I was 26, in grad school, planning to observe a teacher teaching U.S. history at LaGuardia High School. My alarm-clock radio played Z Morning Zoo, a show known for its goofiness, but the hosts were talking about a plane crashing into the Twin Towers and I thought, “That’s not funny.” I turned on the TV, and that’s when I was like, “Oh my, no, this is actually real.” I got a phone call from one of my best friends who worked on Canal Street near the Twin Towers, and when I saw the first tower buckle, I yelled to her, “You have to run!”
The next semester, I was placed at Stuyvesant High School by what was once the Twin Towers. The air was constantly being tested in the cafeteria. And yet 9/11 never came up in the classroom. In the years that followed, I would have students interview a friend or family member about that day as a lesson in how history is remembered, showing them that they just collected primary sources.
Nowadays, students are more clued into current events on their devices and TikTok, so they’re asking really interesting questions about 9/11, like “Why did we attack Afghanistan?” Many students don’t understand the difference between why we went into Afghanistan in the early 2000s versus Iraq. Many adults don't know the difference if they don't really pay attention to the news or recent current events. How do you understand what’s going on in Iran now if you don’t understand the history of Iraq, Iran, the Middle East?
Kids don’t talk about the fear of terrorists coming from the Middle East. The thing that kids are more scared of today is what they see as domestic terror coming from ICE agents. I’ve had to explain that ICE was created in 2003 as part of the new Department of Homeland Security, which was established in response to 9/11, and now it’s being used to, in my opinion, terrorize communities.
I’m definitely going to bring up the 25th anniversary in class this year. They were born so long after 9/11, it’s history to them. We need to find ways to cover more recent history. In a U.S. history class—or any history class—there’s so much to cover, and we don’t get to the recent history, from 1980 to the present, because it’s not emphasized on tests and also you run out of time. –As told to Olivia B. Waxman
Allison Turkel
On Sept. 11, I was outside of Albuquerque, N.M. I worked for a not-for-profit then called the National Center for Prosecution of Child Abuse, and we were running a conference. And the receptionist where we were holding it said a plane just hit the World Trade Center, and you could go into our break room to watch it on TV. I went in just in time to see the second plane hit. Luckily I was able to reach my dad, who had a meeting downtown that day. I got him right before the phones went out in New York, and then we started driving back. We looked on our map. We tried to avoid missile silos because we thought that those might be under attack or shooting things. We had no idea. I drove crying. Not the whole time, but a lot. It’s a skill.
I lived in the D.C. area at the time, but I grew up in Manhattan, up in Washington Heights. I worked down in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which was actually in the zone. So all of it translates well into how and why I’ve been the Special Master of the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund for the last 3½ years.
We want as many people as possible to know, one, we’re still here. We are in business until 2090. We have as much funding as is necessary to pay every eligible claimant. And two, we serve people beyond first responders. We serve people that lived, worked, went to school in the New York exposure zone, who were at Shanksville and at the Pentagon. We really encourage people if they were there, to register with the VCF. In order to file a claim, folks need to get certified that they have a 9/11 illness from the World Trade Center Health Program, which is our sister program that runs out of HHS. We are receiving over 700 new claims a month.
Since 2011, when we reopened, we have received over 110,000 claims. We've paid out $18.5 billion compensation. [The original VCF closed in 2004 after paying out the $7 billion appropriated for those killed or physically injured on 9/11.] The CDC estimates that in New York alone, over 400,000 people may have been exposed to the toxins.
Remember “America Strong”? “Let everybody return”? “Let's begin to live, work, go to school, start over again”? People went back into the New York zone, and the consequence, of course, is they were exposed to these toxins that have made them ill. And people have died from it. On that day, 2,977 people perished at all three sites and on the planes. Since we reopened, we’ve had 6,100 of our claimants die from exposure to the toxins. And unfortunately, every year there are more people becoming ill. Today, 63% of our claimants have a cancer, and those cancers, because of the unique nature of what people were exposed to, may have long latency periods.
Every Sept. 11, the memorial and museum in New York City does the reading of the names of the victims, and there’s always six moments of silence, to mark the four moments of impact and two tower collapses. This year, they’re adding a seventh, to honor the people that have become ill from the toxins. I think that’ll help spread awareness that so many are still suffering and that the 9/11 VCF is here to help.
Christopher Ashley
I actually didn't behave that great that day. I almost got into a fistfight.
It was the first day of rehearsal for the play Wonder of the World, which I was directing. We canceled rehearsal for that day and the next, and I ended up walking back home to the West Village. Late that night, there was a very drunk man who put himself in front of me and asked if I was an Iraqi. He kept putting himself in front of me, and I kept trying to get away. Then he took a swing at me, and I punched him in the face.
It’s not automatic that people are their best selves in these moments. I think one of the things people do with traumatic situations is move on, so it was really meaningful to me to dig back into the feelings that that day created while directing Come From Away, a musical about 38 planes grounded in Gander, Newfoundland, and the people who took care of strangers at this moment of real terror. Telling that story around the world, onstage, on Apple TV helped me heal.
In 2011, the play’s authors, David Hein and Irene Sankoff, went to a 10th anniversary event reconvening a lot of the people who had been diverted there on 9/11. They expected to be there for a couple of days and ended up staying for weeks and weeks. Claude Elliott, the mayor of Gander, used to joke, "Wait, you guys are making a musical about making sandwiches?”
In the current world we're living in, it almost seems mythical that people would take this good care of each other because there are just so many things that pull us apart and make us suspicious of each other. We're all vulnerable. Nobody’s safely apart behind a wall. We're all going to have to figure out how to share the world and the space together. The world keeps changing, but the show remains about the responsibility we have to each other and the value of kindness and connection. Twenty-five years ago, if more people thought like the people in Gander—“these people are my problem, my responsibility, and I will take care of them, despite the fact that I didn't meet them until today”—I think we'd be in a better place. –As told to O.B.W.
Nancy Gibbs
Moments after 8:46 a.m., attention fixed on one incomprehensible event. As first responders scrambled and survivors fled, the rest of us skidded to a stop and watched.
At TIME, editor Jim Kelly launched a reporting army: correspondents around the world tracked the attacks and reactions in real time. White House correspondent Jay Carney was with President Bush in the press pool; writers and editors in the New York City headquarters headed downtown, or to city hospitals and command centers. My job was to curate and condense it all into a single story for a special issue of the magazine. “I just want you to tell the story of today,” Jim told me. “Think of it as a time capsule.”
In one sense we all saw something different. If you lived in New York City, not only did you see the smoke, you smelled it, tasted it. You heard the sirens, felt the fear. Elsewhere, the alerts jolted large towns and small. Local landmarks shivered and then shut down: Disney World and the Sears Tower, Congress and the Supreme Court, the Space Needle. Also, the entire airspace of the United States.
But at a deeper level, we all saw the same thing, a once unimaginable attack on what we soon started calling the Homeland, as though we were all residents of the same reality. No matter how different our individual experiences of that day, we lived through it together and emerged more united: By October, 60% of people said they trusted the government to do the right thing all or most of the time, a three-decade high.
It’s easier to put a jigsaw puzzle together when you can see the whole picture on the lid of the box. Yes, there were toxic rumors and conspiracies even without the yet-to-be-invented Facebook and X. But compared with what has transpired since then, the information landscape looks practically pristine. The demolition of the business model for traditional news sources corresponded with sinking institutional trust across the board. Journalism’s self-inflicted wounds and technological upheaval radically changed how people make sense of the world. Trust in government now sits around 17%. Trust in the media has hit an all-time low.
If you had told me 25 years ago, as we color-coded the threat level, cast a wide surveillance net, launched a Global War on Terror, that we would manage to avoid further terror attacks, I would have found it hard to believe. But I also couldn’t have imagined the maceration of the media as our news channels filled with content of all kinds streaming in from all corners. This year for the first time, more people globally rely on social and video platforms for news, rather than TV or news websites. As audiences migrate from broadcast and cable, print and radio, to creators on TikTok and YouTube, the very notion of a shared reality feels quaint. Eight in 10 of us say Democrats and Republicans can’t even agree on basic facts, which makes reasoned discussion of everything from security threats to education reform all but impossible.
Twenty-five years ago, like journalists everywhere, I focused on how to tell this story, in the belief that stories are stickier than bloodless fact. But what has happened since makes me wonder if I missed the actual war. Sept. 11 did not cause 21st century truth decay, but it coincided with it. Jolted out of the snug 1990s, people went searching for answers they could trust, tribes they could join, distraction as an antidote to alarm. We no longer hear the same stories and too many leaders are counting on that. We can each collect the puzzle pieces, but it's harder to see the full picture. Even when the country is broadly united around key values—reject political violence, protect the safety net, get money out of politics, regulate AI—the sense of division abides and people on both sides see mainly a caricature of their opponents.
Strong societies need good information; communities benefit from shared stories. On Sept. 11, many of those stories were of quiet, reflexive heroism, sacrifice, service. First responders and random strangers modeled courage under fire, and the rest of us were swept up in a wave of gratitude that helped drain the fear. Those are stories worth retrieving now. –Nancy Gibbs
Keira Unterzuber, Eric Johnson, and Freya Johnson
Keira: My first child was due on Sept. 3, and my doctor was going to induce me on the 13th. So the 11th was any other day, really. I was getting ready for work when my husband, who is a pilot and was home on family leave, said, “Keira, come here.” He explained that a plane had crashed in the World Trade Center, and I said, “But it's so sunny!” He's like, “Yeah, that's really weird.” And while we were watching the TV, the second plane hit. As the morning went on, I started to feel unwell. But then I don’t think anybody felt well that day.
Eric: We live near the Pentagon, and suddenly, it was like somebody pushed over a piano in the room next to us. It shook the whole house. The cats jumped off the bed and hid. I went outside and saw smoke. Sometime in there, Keira said, “I’m having the baby today.” I drove 80 to 90 miles an hour all the way  to the hospital. There was zero traffic. It was eerie, like driving somewhere in the middle of the night. 
Keira: Because of construction, we had to go through the emergency-room entrance and I remember all these emergency medical staff just waiting, and not for me. In the delivery room, Eric started to say he was ready to join the military and go fight the terrorists and because of the mood that he was in, he suggested several new names for the baby: Phoenix, America, Freedom, Liberty. I just said no, no, no. Eventually he picked Freya, who is goddess of war and love and a very strong woman. 
Freya: When I was young, I didn’t really understand the significance of the day. But around the 10th anniversary, I realized, “Oh, this is huge,” and then it became very depressing. On the morning announcements at school, they’d show a video tribute, and those videos were obviously very sad. In middle school, some kid told me that I was the reincarnation of Osama bin Laden. So I used to wish I was born on the 10th or the 12th. I actually didn’t celebrate my birthday from ages 10 to 13. It just felt inappropriate and weird to be so happy when everyone else was not. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve told people my birthday, and it becomes a whole conversation. When I need ID at a bar or when I have to pick up a prescription, and they ask me for my birthday, they’re like, “Really?” I’ve even had people ask me, “What was that like for you?” And I have to say, “Well, I was not even born yet so I was not aware of anything.” I’ve learned to just say my birthday is in September. However, as I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized that I like my birthday. It’s such a beautiful time of year. I’m at the point where I can acknowledge that it was sad, but I can also celebrate myself. All my friends tell me that when they think of 9/11, they think of me as their first thought. 
Keira: When something tragic happens, it’s a beautiful thing to be around a newborn baby. My brother’s wife lost her first husband on the 10th, and his funeral was on the 13th. She adores Freya because, in her world, she’s a bright light at a dark moment. We have a lot of friends who say that year after year: She was the shining light that day. –As told to B.L.

articles.title: NATO has no plans to deploy nuclear weapons to additional countries — Polish official
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. NATO is not considering the deployment of nuclear warheads to additional countries as part of its Nuclear Sharing program, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said.
"As of today, the deployment of nuclear warheads beyond the places already hosting them is not on the [NATO] agenda," he told RMF FM.
However, the Polish defense official clarified that Warsaw sought to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence concept and that it was one of the issues on the agenda. "For the first time, we have been able to make sure that NATO countries are willing to include Poland in the nuclear sharing program, which is a very serious one," Zalewski noted.
On August 27, Zalewski said at a press conference at the NATO headquarters in Brussels that Poland had neither the desire nor plans to host nuclear weapons. He explained that Warsaw would like to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence strategy without having nuclear arms stationed in the country.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki said in an interview with Polsat television in mid-February that Warsaw should seek access to nuclear weapons. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, in turn, stressed that the authorities were not considering such an option. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke of the country’s interest in the "nuclear umbrella" project proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron.

articles.title: Trump seeks repayment from Europe for past Ukraine aid
articles.body:
- President Trump said the U.S. has "virtually unlimited" munitions and is producing weapons "at levels never seen before" amid Iran war stockpile reports.
- Trump said he will seek repayment from European countries for Ukraine aid, though the U.S. already runs a NATO-backed program where allies pay for U.S. weapons sent to Ukraine.
President Donald Trump said Wednesday the United States has “virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition” and is manufacturing munitions “at levels never seen before,” pushing back against months of reporting that the war with Iran has strained U.S. weapons stockpiles.
Trump made the claims in a Truth Social post published at 7:56 p.m. on September 3, in which he also said the United States would soon resume munitions sales to allies after prioritizing its own stockpiles during the conflict.
“For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place,” Trump wrote. “In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen. We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin.”
The post is the latest in a series of denials Trump has issued since March, when reports first surfaced that the intensity of U.S. operations against Iran was drawing down stocks of key munitions. The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post reported in early March that Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine had raised concerns about depleted stockpiles ahead of the war’s start. Trump called those reports a “disgrace” at the time and said the U.S. had a “virtually unlimited supply” of certain munitions.
Similar reports resurfaced in July, when The New York Times, NBC News, CBS News and CNN reported that nearly two weeks of daily strikes on Iran had drawn down supplies of defensive interceptors, including Patriot and THAAD missiles, protecting U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz disputed the reporting on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that month, saying anyone leaking such information “deserve[s] to be in jail.”
In August, Reuters reported that the U.S. Army had used “virtually all” of its inventories of Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles during the five-month conflict, citing people familiar with internal military data. Trump responded at the time by calling the U.S. munitions stockpile “massive” and vowing to hunt down “treasonous” leakers.
In Wednesday’s post, Trump also said the Biden administration had given Ukraine and NATO “far more Munitions” at no cost than the U.S. has used in Iran.
“Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for, If they were only asked, but we will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!” Trump wrote.
U.S. military aid to Ukraine under the Biden administration totaled roughly $131 billion, according to figures compiled by the Atlantic Council, most of it disbursed in 2022. European countries have collectively provided more than $227 billion in total aid to Ukraine as of 2025, the same figures show, exceeding the U.S. contribution.
Since July 2025, the United States and NATO have operated the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, a mechanism under which European allies and Canada, not the United States, pay for U.S.-manufactured weapons shipped to Ukraine. The program was established through an agreement between Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. As of October 2025, 26 countries had contributed more than $4 billion through the initiative, according to the Atlantic Council.

articles.title: Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel
articles.body:
Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel
The German government approved nearly €800 million ($930 million) in weapons exports to Israel between January and June, Der Spiegel reports, citing a government response to a parliamentary inquiry. The sum is already four times higher than the total value Berlin greenlighted last year.
Around one-fifth of the exports was linked to German-Israeli defense-industry cooperation benefiting the German Armed Forces, according to the government. Just over two-thirds of the approved value is tied to the INS Drakon, a nearly 70-meter-long Dolphin II-class submarine built for Israel by German shipbuilder TKMS. The vessel, which can remain submerged for weeks, left Kiel on Tuesday and is reportedly on its way to Israel.
Berlin said the remainder covered equipment not classified as ‘weapons of war’, including small arms, ammunition, explosives, and drones, according to Der Spiegel.
The Left Party accused Berlin of “boundless double standards” over the deals.
“As [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz was supposedly outraged by [Israeli Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir’s inhumane statements, his federal government was pushing ahead with cooperation with a government and an army facing genocide charges before the International Criminal Court, supporting settler violence in the West Bank, and continuing to occupy southern Lebanon,” MP Lea Reisner said.
The controversial Israeli minister stated last month that he considers the enclave “to be ours” and urged the IDF to carry out dozens of “targeted assassinations” there every night, claiming that some in the Palestinian enclave “are not people.”
Germany’s War Weapons Control Act requires licenses to “always be denied” where weapons risk being used in “peace-disturbing acts” or where Germany’s obligations under international law could be impaired.
Berlin temporarily halted weapons exports to Israel in August 2025 over West Jerusalem’s plans to occupy Gaza City, but lifted the restrictions in November after a US-backed ceasefire with Hamas. Israeli forces have since continued operations in Gaza and against Hezbollah in Lebanon, where they still occupy parts of the south.
Germany is meanwhile expanding military cooperation with Israel. On Wednesday, the German Navy said it had successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic with a range of up to 500 kilometers. Germany has no ballistic missiles of its own, with Taurus cruise missiles being its longest-range missile systems.
Germany’s unwavering support for Israel, which is facing genocide accusations before the International Court of Justice in a case filed by South Africa, has arguably cost Berlin international support, as it failed to secure a seat on the Security Council in June.

articles.title: Pentagon limits classified access amid Iran war concerns - report
articles.body:
The Pentagon has restricted access to decades of classified military documents on an internal computer system, The Washington Post reported on Wednesday, days after the newspaper reported that senior US commanders had raised concerns about sustaining large-scale military operations against Iran.
Documents associated with the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB) were removed from an internal web portal on the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke to The Washington Post on condition of anonymity.
It was not immediately clear whether the documents remained available to US personnel through other means or how the reduction in access could affect military planning, according to the report.
SIPRNet contains information classified as "secret," while top-secret information is held on more highly classified networks with fewer people granted access.
US military leaders raised concerns over Iran operations
The SDOB contains information on the location and availability of US warships, military units, weapons systems, and other resources. It also allows senior military leaders to formally register reservations about orders while continuing to carry them out through a process known as "non-concurring," The Washington Post reported.
The Jerusalem Post previously reported, citing the Washington Post, that several senior US military leaders raised concerns in the classified August 14 edition of the SDOB about continuing operations against Iran.
The officials warned that prolonging the war could weaken the US military's ability to respond to threats elsewhere. The SDOB reportedly called for some US troops deployed in the Middle East to remain in the region through September, while others would remain until 2027.
Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, head of US European Command; Gen. Francis Donovan, head of US Southern Command; Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command; and Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, were among those who registered reservations with a "non-concur," according to people familiar with the discussion who spoke to the Washington Post.
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach and acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve agreed with Hegseth's plan to extend some unit deployments but emphasized that doing so would carry significant risks, according to the report.
Pentagon declines to discuss access change
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declined to discuss the reported change with the Washington Post on Wednesday but did not dispute that it had occurred.
"As we have previously stated, the Department of War does not publicly discuss internal operational deliberative processes, including the management, handling, or access protocols for the Secretary of War Orders Book (SWOB)," Parnell said in a statement to the newspaper.
"The success of our service members is Secretary Hegseth's top priority, and for that reason, decisions regarding operational processes, force posture, and deliberative staffing are managed through appropriate security channels to ensure mission security and operational integrity," he added.
Following the Washington Post's Sunday report, Parnell said on social media that much of what the newspaper published was "inaccurate," though he did not specify which details he disputed.
"Non-concurs are standard," Parnell said. "The Secretary sees them constantly. That's how you run a real military. We are in great shape around the world."
Restricted access could complicate military planning
A former defense official who routinely reviewed the documents told the Washington Post that removing the SDOB from SIPRNet or moving it to systems with higher levels of classification would "dramatically reduce the number of people who have direct access to it."
Commanders and their staff rely on access to the SDOB for time-sensitive decisions and notifications, the former official told the newspaper.
Moving aircraft and weapons from one command to another, for example, requires urgent logistical work to redirect equipment and resources. Restricting access to the relevant information could make that process slower and more difficult, according to the former official.
The change does not make it impossible for personnel to access strategic and operational documents, but doing so is now "certainly more difficult," the former official said.

articles.title: Ukrainian helicopter gets new AI-assisted gun module against Shaheds
articles.body:
- The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation delivered a Khyzhak combat module for aviation use, funded through a joint project with Uklon.
- The module fires a stabilized 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and uses AI-assisted tracking to help engage drones, including Shahed-type strike drones.
The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation says it has delivered a remotely operated “Khyzhak” combat module for use in Ukrainian aviation, and that the system is now being used against Russian targets.
The foundation announced the delivery on social media, saying it purchased the module through a joint project with the ride-hailing company Uklon called “Pidsvity Voroha 2.0” (“Light Up the Enemy 2.0”). Video accompanying the post shows the module mounted on a helicopter and used against Russian Shahed-type strike drones.
“We are complicating flights for Russian Shaheds,” the foundation wrote. “The video shows the remotely controlled Khyzhak combat module, which the Foundation delivered for aviation. We purchased it as part of a joint project with Uklon, ‘Pidsvity Voroha 2.0.’ And now this module is successfully working against enemy targets, thank you for that!”
The Khyzhak module is built around a 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and can rotate 360 degrees horizontally and elevate up to 75 degrees vertically. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense codified the module and cleared it for use in the Armed Forces. The ministry said the machine guns mounted on the module can be loaded with either Soviet-pattern or NATO-standard 7.62 mm ammunition and that the platform is stabilized, allowing accurate fire while the vehicle carrying it is moving.
The module’s developers designed it to be modular. It can be installed on robotic ground platforms, mounted stationary, adapted for use on vehicles, or fitted to naval systems. The version shown in the foundation’s video represents an adaptation for aviation.
The module includes an artificial intelligence system for automatic target recognition and tracking, including automatic detection of drones. That capability allows operators to use the Khyzhak to engage small first-person-view drones as well as larger Shahed-type drones, which are roughly the size of a small Cessna aircraft, at close range.
The foundation did not disclose how many Khyzhak modules it has funded, which unit or units are operating the system, or the cost of the purchase made through the Uklon partnership.

articles.title: Trump congratulates Hegseth on ‘good job’ after deadly Iran wedding strike
articles.body:
Trump congratulates Hegseth on ‘good job’ after deadly Iran wedding strike
US President Donald Trump has congratulated Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the latest American strikes on Iran, despite one of the attacks hitting a wedding and killing several civilians.
Iranian authorities said two women and two children aged four and 16 were killed when a US munition hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, on Tuesday. At least 67 others were wounded, many of them women and children.
According to weapons experts cited by AP and the New York Times, the fragments recovered at the site belonged to an American air-delivered guided munition, most likely a JSOW.
The Iranian Red Crescent has since asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the Kuhestak strike, while Iran’s UN envoy has urged the Security Council to condemn it.
US Central Command has said it is looking into the reports while insisting that American forces do not target civilians.
“You did a good job last night in Iran, by the way. You knocked the hell out of them,” Trump told Hegseth during an event at the White House on Wednesday. “We’re winning that one very big, by the way, in case you haven’t noticed,” he added, claiming that much of Iran’s naval and air capability has been destroyed.
Tehran responded to the latest wave of attacks by launching its own ballistic missiles and drones at US military facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the UAE, as well as Erbil in Kurdistan Region, Iraq.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later claimed to have killed “a number of enemy elements” and destroyed several drones in a missile and UAV attack on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base.
Kuwait acknowledged that its air defenses had intercepted incoming missiles and drones but reported no casualties. Jordan said ten of 13 ballistic missiles that entered its airspace were intercepted.
Tuesday’s wedding strike follows several other incidents in which US attacks have caused heavy civilian casualties in Iran. On the opening day of the war in February, a US strike hit an elementary school in Minab, killing 175 people, most of them children. On the same day, a US strike also killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children, in the southern Iranian city of Lamerd.
Tehran has accused Washington of war crimes throughout the conflict, reporting up to 3,000 civilian casualties since the US and Israel launched their campaign against the Islamic Republic in February.

Iran's Army says struck U.S. bases in UAE, Kuwait with drones, missiles
articles.body:
TEHRAN/KUWAIT CITY/ABU DHABI, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Army said Thursday that its forces have struck U.S. military bases in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Kuwait with missiles and kamikaze drones earlier in the day.
In a statement on its website, the army said the strikes were in revenge for the Iranian military personnel and civilians killed in recent U.S. attacks against Iran.
It added that its forces targeted the U.S. Army's satellite communications systems, equipment warehouses, and a fighter aircraft hangar at the Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base in Kuwait, causing damage to the communications systems and the hangar.
The army said it also struck the U.S. troops and radar systems at the Al Minhad Air Base in the UAE, stressing that its forces' responses to any attack by the U.S. Army will be "harsh and devastating, and will continue until achieving the ultimate victory and punishing the aggressor."
On Wednesday, U.S. Central Command said in a post on social media platform X that its forces had "successfully completed a wave of strikes against Iranian military targets," citing "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
Iran responded by attacking U.S. bases and assets in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, and the UAE.
In a Thursday post on X, Hossein Kermanpour, head of the Iranian health ministry's public relations, said 18 people were killed and 142 others injured in the U.S. attack against Iran between Aug. 30 and Sept. 2.
Kuwait on Thursday condemned repeated Iranian attacks on the country, saying the latest strike at dawn posed a "direct threat" to its security and stability.
In a statement on X, the Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry said the attacks constituted a flagrant violation of the country's sovereignty and a grave breach of international law, the UN Charter, and UN Security Council Resolution 2817.
It described the continued attacks as a "dangerous escalation" that threatens regional security and stability and undermines diplomatic efforts to de-escalate and reduce tensions.
Kuwait reserves its full right to take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its sovereignty, maintain its security and defend its territory and vital installations against any aggression or threat, the ministry said.
Also on Thursday, UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan received a phone call from U.S. President Donald Trump, during which they discussed bilateral cooperation and regional developments, the Emirates News Agency (WAM) reported.
The two leaders exchanged views on issues of common concern, particularly developments in the Middle East and ongoing efforts to address them, according to WAM. ■

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Strike Russia’s $60 Million Kasta-2E2 Radar in Zaporizhzhia
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Drones Strike Russia’s $60 Million Kasta-2E2 Radar in Zaporizhzhia
Ukrainian drones struck a Russian Kasta-2E2 radar station in the Zaporizhzhia region, with the hit confirmed through objective monitoring, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
According to the General Staff, the strike took place on September 1 near the settlement of Vyshneve in the Zaporizhzhia region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian drones struck both the radar’s antenna and the equipment station of the vehicle operating the Russian system. The General Staff did not provide further details on the extent of the damage.
The Kasta-2E2, also designated 39N6, is a Russian mobile three-coordinate radar system designed to detect and track aerial targets flying at low and extremely low altitudes. The system determines the coordinates of detected targets and transmits the data to air defense command posts.
The radar is capable of detecting aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles, including targets operating at very low altitudes. Its detection range extends from approximately 5 to 150 kilometers (3 to 93 miles), while its altitude coverage reaches up to 6 kilometers (3.7 miles).
A small drone flying at an altitude of around 60 meters can reportedly be detected by the Kasta-2E2 from a distance of approximately 30 to 44 kilometers (19 to 27 miles), depending on the height of the radar’s antenna mast, which can be raised to as high as 50 meters.
Depending on its configuration, the estimated cost of a Kasta-2E2 radar system starts at approximately $60 million.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces targeted multiple Russian military sites in the occupied Donetsk region and Russia’s Bryansk region on September 1 and overnight into September 2. The military also confirmed that earlier operations had destroyed a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet and a Ka-27 helicopter.
