Ukraine Urges EU to Block Russian Ballistic Production With New Sanctions
Ukraine has formally proposed a specialized "anti-ballistic" sanctions package to European partners designed to prevent Russia from manufacturing ballistic missiles.
The initiative was presented by Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha during his visit to Ireland, where he attended an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in the Gymnich format, according to the press service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian estimates show that Russian forces currently hold approximately 600 to 630 ballistic missiles in stock, with a production capacity of around 100 missiles per month, potentially reaching up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually.
“After every massive attack on Ukraine, new sanctions packages must be implemented so as not to give Russia pauses to adapt,” Sybiha emphasized.
Sybiha discussed the upcoming 22nd EU sanctions package with European officials, stating that it should inflict severe damage on the Russian economy.
Air defense enhancement was another major focus of the discussions. The foreign minister stated that establishing a reliable "air shield" over Ukraine remains a top priority and noted that there is now a "confident understanding of the partners' further steps."
Additionally, Ukraine outlined a list of critical pre-winter requirements to its partners. Kyiv is currently awaiting the delivery of essential equipment alongside financial assistance.
On April 23, 2026, the European Union officially approved its 20th package of sanctions against Russia, introducing over 100 individual restrictions and increasing pressure on the energy sector and the "shadow fleet."
The Council of the EU confirmed the measures, which targeted key economic sectors funding Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, introduced new actions against financial institutions in third countries, and restricted companies supporting the Russian military-industrial complex.
Furthermore, the package established a framework for future bans on maritime transport of Russian petroleum products, expanded the list of restricted vessels, and prohibited terminal services for Russian liquefied natural gas.

articles.title: Badenoch says UK must prepare for possible war by 2030
articles.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said Britain must increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, warning that the country could face a major conflict within the next four years and arguing that higher military spending can no longer be delayed.
In a speech on Britain’s defence on Thursday, the Conservative leader linked the spending requirement to Russia, cyber attacks, threats to critical infrastructure and wider instability, while setting out the case for the £10 billion annual increase in defence spending announced by her party.
Badenoch said: “Before the summer, Keir Starmer was given intelligence that Russia could launch an attack on NATO as soon as 2030. Not enough politicians in Parliament have fully appreciated what that means. By that of course I mean Labour politicians. What this means that within the next 4 years, the UK could be at war with the world’s biggest nuclear armed state. Because under Article 5, an attack on any NATO country is an attack on all of them.”
She also referred to Russian naval activity around Britain and threats to undersea infrastructure, saying: “Vladimir Putin has called Britain Russia’s number one enemy. Russian warships have been sailing through the English Channel and the undersea cables which power our internet and power our entire information and communication network have come under threat. People may not see it in their day to day lives, but hostile states are constantly pushing the boundaries with unconventional warfare.”
Badenoch argued that national security needed to encompass more than conventional military forces, pointing to cyber security, energy infrastructure and national resilience.
She said: “National security is not just about tanks, boots on the ground and planes in the air. It is about our cyber defences, it is about our energy security, it is about our country’s resilience. National security does not just happen we also have to pay for it, and that means spending more money on defence.”
The Conservative leader compared the UK’s position with increased defence investment elsewhere in NATO, citing Poland’s expansion of its armed forces and higher German defence spending. She also referred to Greece already spending around 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence.
Badenoch said: “Being an island might make us feel safer, but it does not prevent conflict from coming to us. And let’s be honest, conflict is coming. We must act now. Because the defence of the nation is the first duty of government.”
She called for defence spending to rise every year until reaching 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, saying: “We need to increase our defence spending every year so we can get to 3% of GDP by 2030, anything after that is too late.”
The Conservatives have proposed increasing annual defence expenditure by around £10 billion by 2029/30 compared with current government plans. The party says the increase would be funded through welfare reductions and reallocating money from other areas of government expenditure, including civil research and development, the British Business Bank and the National Wealth Fund.
Badenoch said: “Finding the money to pay for defence means making tough choices, it means making difficult trade-offs.”
She added: “We have now completed our work to get to 3%.
“And today my team have set out our plan to remove the housing benefit and remove the VAT exemption for Motability, alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos Deal,
“And repurposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target.
“And let’s be clear, 3% is the minimum our country needs to stay safe.”
The speech also connected defence policy with the wider state of the economy, with Badenoch arguing that Britain’s ability to sustain greater military expenditure depends on controlling borrowing and public spending.
She said: “Defence is not separate from the economy. Fiscal responsibility is part of national security.”
Badenoch also repeated the Conservative proposal for a £17 billion Sovereign Defence Fund, which the party says would support military readiness and investment in the British defence industrial base.
The Labour Party was approached for comment on Badenoch’s remarks and the Conservatives’ defence spending proposals, but had not responded at the time of publication.
Closing the defence section of her speech, Badenoch said: “Russia will attack a country it thinks is weak. It will not attack a country it knows is strong.
“We need to be strong. If you want peace, you prepare for war.”

articles.title: Britain wants laser armed ground vehicle drones
articles.body:
Britain is seeking counter-drone technology that could lead to autonomous laser weapons mounted on Army vehicles and, later, uncrewed ground vehicles, with £5 million available immediately through a new Ministry of Defence competition, the department has said.
Project PANOPTES, launched by UK Defence Innovation on behalf of the MOD, is intended to develop an integrated Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System force-protection capability able to deal with massed and low-cost aerial threats without rapidly exhausting conventional ammunition stocks.
The MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
Although the competition is open to a range of technologies, laser directed-energy weapons are specifically identified as an area of interest. The MOD said: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The intended configuration would place the counter-drone capability on a military ground platform. According to the procurement documents: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
The system is intended to protect deployed forces against complex and saturation attacks involving small uncrewed aircraft, including simultaneous threats designed to overwhelm local air defences or force troops to expend comparatively expensive missiles and ammunition.
The MOD stated: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus covers representative Class 1 UAS and other small aerial targets. These could include individual drones as well as repeated, sequential or simultaneous attacks used for surveillance, targeting, disruption or attempts to exhaust defensive systems.
A later objective would move the capability onto an unmanned ground platform. The MOD stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
UK Defence Innovation has confirmed that Project PANOPTES is open to UK-based innovators and that a share of £5 million is available immediately. Stage 1 will act as an initial screening process, with applicants outlining their proposed technology before successful teams are invited to develop more detailed proposals.
The first phase is not intended to produce a complete operational counter-drone system. The MOD said: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
Successful technologies could then be matured through later phases into demonstrable Minimum Viable Products before selected systems are developed into Minimum Deployable Capabilities for an initial operational user group.
The notice states: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record.”
The wider procurement has an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, rising to £150 million including VAT. That figure is not an approved programme budget. The MOD stated: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.”
Stage 1 submissions are due by midday on 23 September. A launch webinar will be held on 9 September to provide potential suppliers with further information on the operational requirement before the competition moves into its subsequent stages.

articles.title: Trump weighs declaring Iran war over as Pentagon extends Middle East deployments
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump is privately considering declaring the war with Iran over, even as the Pentagon quietly extends troop deployments in the Middle East, according to a Wall Street Journal report on Wednesday.
The newspaper reported that Trump has discussed with senior aides "whether to declare the Iran war over," a move the president reportedly "favours." He believes that maintaining intense economic pressure will eventually force Tehran to "either dismantle its nuclear programme or collapse."
The US launched Operation Economic Outcast last week, targeting Iran’s key economic lifelines, including its oil, shipping, aviation, gold, technology and digital asset sectors.
Despite the private discussions, the Pentagon is extending deployments in a sign that the war could drag "well into next year.”
The military is maintaining 50,000 troops and 19 warships, including two aircraft carriers and 13 guided-missile destroyers, to provide the president with operational "flexibility."

Ukraine’s Patriot Arsenal Gets Another Lifeline as Spain Pledges More Missiles
Spain will continue supplying Ukraine with missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said on September 3, reinforcing Madrid’s commitment to one of Kyiv’s most urgently needed defenses against Russian ballistic missile strikes, according to euDebates.tv on September 3.
Ukraine has repeatedly urged its partners in recent months to increase deliveries of Patriot interceptors as Russian forces continue using ballistic missiles in large-scale strikes against cities and critical infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Asked whether Spain would continue providing the missiles, Albares gave a direct answer.
“We have been doing this for a long time, and we will continue to do so,” the Spanish foreign minister said during an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
The commitment is particularly significant because Patriot remains one of Ukraine’s most important systems for intercepting ballistic missiles, while stocks of the specialized interceptors required for those engagements remain limited.
Albares had met Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha a day earlier, on September 2, on the sidelines of the EU foreign ministers’ gathering in Wicklow.
Their discussions focused on continued assistance to Ukraine, protection of civilians and the defense of critical infrastructure.
During the meeting, Albares reaffirmed Madrid’s support for Ukraine and its intention to increase missile deliveries.
Previously, Spain transferred five Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles to Ukraine from an air defense artillery regiment based at a Marine Corps facility in Valencia.
After that, reports emerged that NATO and European Union countries were urging Spain and Greece to provide Ukraine with Patriot interceptor missiles, focusing on PAC-2 stocks that are approaching the end of their shelf life.
The requests were made over the summer as Ukraine faces growing demand for air defense interceptors amid intensified Russian missile strikes. One option under discussion would see Norway purchase the missiles from Spain and Greece before transferring them to Ukraine.

articles.title: Nigeria confirms US troop withdrawal
articles.body:
Nigeria confirms US troop withdrawal
Nigeria has confirmed that around 200 US troops deployed to support its fight against armed groups will begin leaving the West African country, with most expected to withdraw by late September.
A smaller advisory and intelligence team will remain, while cooperation in training and information sharing will continue, Nigerian military spokesperson Major General Samaila Uba said on Tuesday. “The deployment of United States personnel was tied to specific operational and counterterrorism objectives,” Uba said, according to AP.
The troops arrived in February to provide intelligence, targeting, and training support. Washington subsequently deployed MQ-9 Reaper surveillance drones to Bauchi Airfield in northeastern Nigeria. The mission came after US President Donald Trump accused the Nigerian authorities of failing to protect Christians and threatened military action.
Nigeria rejected claims that Christians were being systematically targeted, saying jihadist violence, banditry, and communal conflicts affect citizens of different faiths.
The two countries conducted coordinated airstrikes against alleged Islamic State fighters in Sokoto State in December 2025. In May, Nigeria’s Defense Headquarters and US Africa Command said a joint operation in the Lake Chad Basin killed senior Islamic State figure Abu-Bilal al-Minuki. Trump described him as the group’s second-highest-ranking leader globally.
US Africa Command chief General Dagvin Anderson announced in July that most of the American troops had been withdrawn, saying the campaign had successfully degraded Islamic State’s leadership and disrupted its wider network. Samuel Memeh, chairman of Nigeria’s Democratic Leadership Alliance, disputed that assessment. Memeh told RT that the deployment had produced no significant improvement in security and argued that foreign forces alone could not defeat the country’s armed groups.
Nigeria continues to face overlapping threats from Boko Haram and its Islamic State-affiliated offshoot in the northeast, armed bandits operating across the northwest and central regions, and intercommunal violence. More than 40,000 people have been killed since the insurgency began in 2009, UN News reported in January.
Major attacks continued during the US deployment. On August 21, gunmen attacked several communities in Niger State, reportedly killing 30 people and abducting hundreds of worshippers from a mosque. Residents put the number of captives as high as 600, although the authorities said the figure had not been verified. At least 2,000 people reportedly fled into neighboring Benin.
Lagos-based security consultancy SBM Intelligence said in a report last month that at least 7,825 people were abducted across Africa’s most populous nation between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase from the previous 12-month period.

articles.title: Ousted Ukrainian defense chief launches Palantir-backed company
articles.body:
Ousted Ukrainian defense chief launches Palantir-backed company
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has announced the launch of a new military technology company, with Palantir CEO Alex Karp set to become its lead investor.
Fedorov has remained highly active in business and politics since Vladimir Zelensky dismissed him in mid-July amid reported tensions with then-commander-in-chief Aleksandr Syrsky. The former minister has also grown increasingly critical of Zelensky, claiming he was removed over his anti-corruption efforts and calling for elections, which have been repeatedly postponed under martial law.
Last week, Fedorov unexpectedly emerged as an adviser on “defense innovations” to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. He said his role would involve helping Rome “develop modern warfare technologies” and “improve the defense sector.”
This week, Fedorov announced building “our own defense tech company” with the CEO of Palantir, a US data-mining and military tech company, which has been providing AI solutions for the Ukrainian military, set to become its key investor. Fedorov shared a video of him meeting with Karp, with the tech mogul showering the ex-minister with praise.
“We’ve worked together for a half decade. I have been absolutely inspired by what you and the Ukrainians have pulled off and very and super delighted that we could play a part. And you and your colleagues are launching a company that I think will be defining for the world, bringing your knowledge and acumen about the art of war as a product to allied countries,” Karp told Fedorov.
The ties between Fedorov and Karp span well beyond the ex-minister’s six-month tenure as defense minister. Before assuming the post in mid-February, he oversaw Ukraine’s digital transformation in various capacities. Immediately after his dismissal, Fedorov claimed to have been offered a job by Karp.
While Western and Ukrainian media have widely portrayed Fedorov as a military visionary focused on drone warfare, the uptick in long-range strikes against Russia during his tenure was primarily built upon the expansion of drone production in Western Europe secured under his predecessors. Fedorov’s repeated pledges to reform Ukraine’s chaotic mobilization drive did not materialize, with the practice of grabbing random men in the streets to force them into the military arguably growing even more violent under Fedorov.
The anti-graft crusade supposedly led by Fedorov has remained questionable at best. Multiple media reports suggest he focused more on wresting contracts away from companies associated with Zelensky’s inner circle and steering them to companies linked to him personally than on truly battling corruption. Federov’s background has further fueled suspicion. Before entering Zelensky’s government, he considered himself a businessman while repeatedly facing allegations of running online and phone scams, laundering money through online advertising, and engaging in other fraudulent activities.

articles.title: German warship secretly fires ballistic missile in Atlantic
articles.body:
A German warship has fired an Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile during a live test in the North Atlantic, with the German Navy saying the launch demonstrated a strike capability with a potential range beyond anything it had previously operated.
German media reports, citing a German Navy spokesman, said two German frigates had deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the test on Tuesday night. Images from the exercise show a containerised launcher positioned on the deck of a German vessel.
The messaging here could hardly be clearer. By disclosing a test that had deliberately been kept secret, NATO was sending a direct signal to Moscow: European forces are developing longer-range strike options, and not every capability will be visible before it is ready.
NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said the test had been kept secret until after it was completed and involved a German frigate firing the missile in the North Atlantic.
The command stated: “Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.”
Kept secret. Now revealed. 🚀🇩🇪
The German Navy just tested the Israeli 🇮🇱 LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.
NATO 3.0 looks like this:
Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious… pic.twitter.com/K8x2JE61Gs
— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) September 2, 2026
It added: “NATO 3.0 looks like this: Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious capabilities and keeping a few cards close to the chest. Deterrence just got a little more interesting.”
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, said: “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement.”
Kaack added that the system “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
In his original statement, the German Navy chief said the trial opened a new chapter for maritime deterrence and readiness, stating that the system could be operated successfully from German units and that its possible reach exceeded previous German naval capabilities.
The test was conducted with Israel Aerospace Industries’ LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System. According to IAI, the missile has a range of around 400 kilometres and an accuracy of within 10 metres, while NATO’s public account of the German test referred to a range of more than 500 kilometres.
Israel Aerospace Industries said the missile was launched from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. According to the company, the missile followed its planned trajectory, navigated to the target and successfully struck it, with both the weapon system and missile meeting the objectives of the trial.
Boaz Levy, Chairman of IAI, said: “This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense. The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany – the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed.”
He added: “This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
IAI chief executive Guy Bar Lev said: “Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany. This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
The German Navy is using its OPEX initiative to trial technologies and operational concepts as part of its Marine 2035 and Beyond programme. The process is intended to allow new systems to be tested rapidly under conditions intended to resemble operational use as closely as possible.
The North Atlantic launch comes as Germany expands its investment in long-range strike and air and missile defence. The country has also begun fielding the Israeli-developed Arrow 3 ballistic missile defence system as part of its wider effort to strengthen national and NATO defensive capabilities.

articles.title: The world is forgetting how to fear nuclear war
articles.body:
The world is forgetting how to fear nuclear war
For decades, mutual deterrence among major powers provided the world with a degree of predictability, with the nuclear factor lying at the heart of this system since the middle of the last century. The great powers restrained one another and, in doing so, restrained themselves.
They understood that overly ambitious geopolitical adventures could carry unacceptable risks, thus “strategic stability” was the reassuring term given to what was, in reality, the capacity for mutual destruction. International institutions grew around this balance like mushrooms around a tree trunk, but beneath all the agreements and diplomatic language lay something much simpler: the fear of the consequences of a direct conflict between major powers. Now, however, that system is falling apart.
Many posit that the problem is precisely the loss of fear as political elites have ceased to believe that nuclear war is genuinely possible and hence the declining restraint we see in the conflict in Ukraine, in the Middle East and, potentially, in Asia.
The apparent solution is therefore to remind everyone just how terrifying nuclear war would be. Restore the fear, the argument goes, and states will once again exercise restraint and become ready to negotiate new rules. There’s logic to this, but there’s also an enormous danger.
What happens if nuclear weapons are actually used? Either they produce precisely the catastrophe humanity has feared for eight decades, with irreparable consequences, or something quite different happens, such as there’s terrible destruction, but the world does’t end and the weapon doesn’t even guarantee victory.
In that case, nuclear weapons could cease to be primarily a political and psychological barrier and become simply another means of warfare, albeit an extraordinarily powerful one. Would this restore fear? Or would states instead accelerate the development of nuclear weapons designed for more effective battlefield use? Well, in the present atmosphere of growing recklessness, either is conceivable.
Nuclear weapons are the most powerful weapons humanity has invented and they were created to fight wars, but we discovered that they could perform another function by preventing the largest and most destructive wars from occurring at all. Today, however, perceptions seem to be returning to their starting point that a weapon is a weapon, even when it is nuclear.
Yet expecting weapons to solve the problems between states places impossible demands on them, particularly when warfare itself is becoming increasingly asymmetrical and all-pervasive.
States are finding it harder to hold on to what they can’t afford to lose. The erosion of borders, once celebrated as one of the great achievements of liberal globalization, is acquiring a much more alarming character.
The digital world is borderless by definition as drones cross dividing lines with increasing ease and mew technologies steadily undermine the ability of states to control and defend their territory and, in extreme circumstances, even to define where meaningful borders lie.
States won’t simply accept this loss of control, so every action produces a reaction, which means the struggle will become fiercer. More importantly, the battlefield will increasingly encompass almost every sphere of human activity.
Under such conditions, what does “strategic stability” even mean, and how can it be maintained?
War itself increasingly resembles not a means of resolving conflicts but a permanent form of interaction, even coexistence and there may be no decisive victory or defeat, but only repeated attempts to exhaust an opponent economically, militarily, politically, and psychologically.
However, prolonged attrition produces two contradictory effects. States become more experienced and capable of enduring confrontation, but at the same time, fatigue accumulates, along with the temptation to end an apparently endless struggle by reaching for the most decisive and destructive argument available.
The world is losing the systemic safeguards that once limited such impulses and it increasingly resembles a hunting ground during open season.
So what, then, can we hold on to? For now, perhaps only common sense and an accurate assessment of the relationship between our ambitions and our actual capabilities. It’s a fragile lifeline, but it may be enough to prevent us from feeding the flames and instead keep us clear of them.
At least until the value of restraint, including self-restraint, is once again understood by everyone.

548 Drones Target Moscow Region in One of Largest Attacks in Two Years, Russia Says
Russia reported one of its largest drone attacks on the Moscow region in two years, with Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin announcing on September 3 that 548 UAVs had been directed toward the capital region between 8:00 a.m. on September 2 and noon on September 3, according to Russian state media outlets TASS and Interfax.
Interfax reported Sobyanin's statement in full, which was published at 12:22 p.m. on September 3. TASS characterized the attack in a separate post as one of the largest in the Moscow region over the past two years.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Between September 2 at 08:00 and September 3 at 12:00, 548 UAVs flew toward the Moscow region," Sobyanin wrote in his channel on the Max messenger. "The majority were destroyed at distant frontiers. 143 drones were destroyed on the approach to Moscow."
The figures emerged from a series of incremental updates published through the night and into the morning of September 3. Interfax reported that Sobyanin initially announced 10 drones shot down on approach to Moscow, a figure that later climbed to 27, then 37, then 86, before the final midday tally reached 143.
Russian authorities offered no independent breakdown of drone types, flight paths, or intercept locations to allow the claims to be independently verified.
The 143 drones destroyed near Moscow represent roughly one in four of the total figure claimed for the entire region; Russian officials stated only that the remainder were eliminated "at distant frontiers," without further detail.
The attack also disrupted civilian aviation. Russia's federal aviation authority, Rosaviatsia, reported operational changes at Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports, according to Fontanka and Regions.ru, with potential knock-on effects on flight schedules across all three facilities
Vedomosti also confirmed the disruptions, citing Sobyanin's statements on air defense activity.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned international airlines, insurers, and aviation operators that Russian airspace was becoming increasingly unsafe because of drone activity linked to the war.
He argued that Moscow’s failure to properly notify carriers about aerial hazards was effectively closing its own skies, stating that “the Russian sky will de facto be closed.”

articles.title: Estonian defense minister quits after wasting €70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine
articles.body:
Estonian defense minister quits after wasting €70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine
Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur has announced his resignation after it emerged that Tallinn had paid some €70 million ($81 million) in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine to a company with no track record of producing such ammunition.
The scandal erupted on Wednesday after the Eesti Ekspress newspaper reported on the botched procurement and the ensuing legal dispute. In August 2024, Tallinn signed a contract with Italian-registered Datasel, owned by Indian company Neco Defence Munitions, to supply artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The government paid €15 million upfront despite neither company having any previous record of manufacturing artillery shells.
A second deal followed in October, with Estonia paying another €10 million in advance. The first batch was due to reach Ukraine in November, but Datasel reported problems and repeatedly delayed delivery.
Despite the setbacks, Estonia signed two more contracts with the company, eventually bringing total advance payments to around €70 million. The money came from the EU’s European Peace Facility, which has been extensively used to fund weapons and other military assistance for Kiev. Tallinn is now disputing the contracts in a case before the European Court of Arbitration in Strasbourg in a bid to get money back.
The government acknowledged the blunder, with Pevkur proclaiming the readiness to take the “political responsibility” and announcing his resignation. The outgoing minister, who will stay in the role until a replacement is picked, however, appeared to shift the blame for the affair on the country’s procurement authority, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK).
“The defense minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defense minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defense minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine,” Pevkur explained.
The RKIK boss, Elmar Vaher, acknowledged that his agency was to blame for the scandal, yet shifted responsibility to his predecessor, Magnus-Valdemar Saar.
“I have been familiar with the matter since January. I cannot see inside people’s heads to know how they were thinking and what the main arguments behind their decisions were,” Vaher told the ERR broadcaster. “The decision was made by RKIK’s former director general.”
It remained unclear to what extent the contracts remained unfulfilled, since Estonian officials provided conflicting accounts on the matter. Pevkur said that “tens of millions of euros’ worth of the ammunition” were delivered and are currently sitting “in a warehouse in a European country.” The shells, however, were “not of sufficient quality” to send them into Ukraine, according to the outgoing minister. The defense ministry’s secretary general, Kaimo Kuusk, described the consignment as “wholly incomplete,” while the Eesti Ekspress report called the munitions “useless” and faulty.

articles.title: Kiev demands global flight ban over Russia
articles.body:
Kiev demands global flight ban over Russia
Kiev has demanded that the UN aviation watchdog effectively shut Russian airspace to civilian traffic after Vladimir Zelensky threatened that Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign would make flying over the country increasingly dangerous.
Ukrainian newspaper Zerkalo Nedeli reported on Wednesday that Infrastructure Minister Nikolay Kalashnik had sent a letter to Juan Carlos Salazar, secretary general of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), calling for action against flights through Russian airspace.
The letter urged the watchdog to “encourage aviation authorities, air navigation service providers and airlines” operating in Russia to take measures to “protect” civilian aircraft, including a complete ban on flights through Russian airspace by carriers from ICAO member states. 
“The presence of civilian aircraft in Russian airspace may entail particularly high risks,” Kalashnik reportedly wrote in the letter obtained by the outlet.
ICAO later issued a general statement on aviation safety but mentioned neither Russia nor Ukraine and did not directly address Kiev’s demand. Instead, it appealed to all member states to “assess the safety of airspace controlled by them and take all appropriate measures.”
Kiev’s demand followed an explicit threat from Zelensky to foreign airlines, insurers and governments on Tuesday that continued Ukrainian drone attacks would put civilian aviation in Russia at risk. 
“The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said, urging carriers to reconsider flights to Moscow, St. Petersburg and other major Russian destinations.
Russian President Vladimir Putin described Zelensky’s warning as a move toward “state terrorism” and vowed that Moscow would respond if Kiev’s threats resulted in tragedy. “Let no one doubt that,” he said.
Ukraine has intensified long-range drone strikes on Russia in recent months, repeatedly grounding flights and causing prolonged disruptions at airports as air defenses respond to incoming UAVs. The attacks have also targeted Russian ports, energy facilities and civilian infrastructure, including e-commerce warehouses.
Drones have also struck residential areas, including high-rise apartment buildings and houses.
An attack last month on the Black Sea resort of Gelendzhik in southern Russia killed at least eight people, including four children, and wounded dozens more. Another strike on industrial and civilian sites in Nizhnekamsk, in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan, killed 13 people, while a July 18 attack on a Wildberries warehouse in the town of Kotovsk in Tambov Region left seven workers dead.
Moscow has described the intensified Ukrainian strikes as indiscriminate terrorist attacks intended to distract from Kiev’s battlefield setbacks and has responded with renewed long-range strikes on Ukraine. The Russian military maintains that it does not target purely civilian facilities, saying its attacks are directed at military, defense-industrial and dual-use sites.

articles.title: Schiess Sworn in as New Space Force Chief: ‘We Must Grow with Intention’
articles.body:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md.—Gen. Douglas A. Schiess assumed leadership of the Space Force on Sept. 3, succeeding Gen. B. Chance Saltzman as Chief of Space Operations during a change of responsibility ceremony here.
Schiess is just the third CSO in the Space Force’s history since the service was created in 2019. In his first address to Guardians, he emphasized the important role space has come to play in modern military operations—and the growing threats it attracts from adversaries intent on targeting space assets in orbit and on the ground.
“Every day, our potential adversaries advance their efforts to disrupt, degrade, and destroy our space capabilities, and they try to add to their own capacity to exploit space to their advantage,” Schiess said. “We cannot, we will not let that happen.”
A career space operator, Schiess has performed a number of missions in his career including missile warning, GPS, command and control, and launch. In 2023, he became the first commander of U.S. Space Forces-Space, USSF’s component to the U.S. Space Command combatant command. Most recently, he served as deputy CSO for operations, developing and implementing the policies that guide Space Force operations around the world.
That experience, he said, will inform the way he leads Guardians trained “to operate in the cold, dark vacuum of space” from operations centers on the ground that are also under threat—as evidenced in ongoing operations in the Middle East, where Iran has targeted ground-based space and missile defense infrastructure.
“Our Guardians operate from the ground, some in harm’s way—some in harm’s way today—and they require battlefield skills and the warrior mentality as much as our Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and Coast Guardsmen in our sister services,” he said.
Schiess’ emphasis on the growing threats and the warfighting contributions of Guardians continue themes that his predecessor, Saltzman, repeated often throughout his tenure.
Over the past four years, Saltzman helped grow the Space Force from 8,000 uniformed Guardians to 10,000—and he has positioned the force for even more expansion in the coming years. The service is on a path to double in size to 20,000 Guardians over the next five years, and its $71 billion budget request for fiscal 2027 is more than twice what USSF requested last year, as demand increases for space capabilities.
Speaking during the ceremony, Saltzman said he’s proud of the progress the Space Force has made, evidenced in recent months by its delivery of “critical effects” during multiple operations.
“We delivered critical effects on time and on target under fire, and we sustained that effort,” Saltzman said. “When called to action, the U.S. Space Force was ready, combat capable, and mission effective, and that about says it all.”
Saltzman praised Schiess’ leadership, operational experience, and genuine concern for Guardians, their families, and the joint and allied partners they serve alongside.
“He knows how to build teams, how to drive performance, and how to coax bureaucracies into mission success,” Saltzman said. “He has the expertise to make wise decisions. . . . He cares deeply for the people that do the work.”
In his first message to the force, issued shortly after his swearing in, Schiess harkened back to the Space Force’s early days and looked ahead to the future, calling on Guardians to “capitalize on our foundation and evolve to meet the demands of a new era.”
“As we drive our deliberate growth and execution, we will arm our Guardians to acquire, field, operate, and exploit the full spectrum of capabilities required to secure decisive space superiority,” he said. “Integrating into the Joint Force demands a rapid scaling of both our manpower and space capabilities. We must grow with intention, leveraging our industry partnerships to advance our weapon systems and the way we fight.”
Along with Schiess’ ascension to the service chief job this week, the Department of the Air Force also welcomed its assistant secretary for space acquisition and integration, Erich Hernandez-Baquero, who was sworn in at the Pentagon on Aug. 31. Hernandez-Baquero, who will oversee a growing space acquisition portfolio, fills a position that has been vacant since January 2025, though several officials have served in an acting capacity.

EU Countries Pledge More Air Defense to Protect Ukraine From Russian Missile Attacks
Several European Union member states pledged additional air defense systems for Ukraine during an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers and invited non-EU partners in Ireland, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, according to Ukrinform correspondent on September 2.

articles.title: ‘West wants to dictate’: Lavrov on ‘Fuhrer Ursula’ and NATO’s drive to divide Eurasia (KEY REMARKS)
articles.body:
‘West wants to dictate’: Lavrov on ‘Fuhrer Ursula’ and NATO’s drive to divide Eurasia (KEY REMARKS)
The EU and NATO are pursuing an increasingly aggressive campaign to attempt to divide Eurasia, contain Russia and China, and preserve Western global dominance, while hurting themselves in the process, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Thursday, Lavrov also said Moscow would not “beg” European nations to lift sanctions and accused the West of seeking to freeze rather than resolve the Ukraine conflict.
Addressing a lecture organized by the Russian Znanie Society, Lavrov presented the confrontation with the West as part of a broader struggle over the emerging multipolar world order. He argued that Western powers are trying to counter the rise of new economic and political centers while Russia is seeking closer cooperation across Eurasia based on “equality, mutual benefit, and honest dialogue.”
Here are the key takeaways from Lavrov’s address.
West ‘needs an enemy’
The EU and NATO are pursuing anti-Russia policies “even more fiercely, if not frantically” in an attempt to split the Eurasian continent, Lavrov said. He pointed to “walls and trenches” being built along EU borders with Russia, mocking claims that such measures are needed to prevent an alleged Russian invasion.
“This is sick imagination, but I think it is not so much sick imagination as deliberate policy,” he said.
According to Lavrov, both NATO and the EU need Russia to remain an enemy in order to justify their policies at home. “If this artificially created image of an enemy in the form of Russia disappears, the overwhelming majority of governments in the EU and NATO countries will simply be swept away by voters,” he stated.
He went on to accuse Europe of being unable to cooperate “honestly,” arguing that for more than 500 years it had been “the main source” of global upheaval, including two world wars. Europe, he said, is attempting to preserve what it sees as its right to global hegemony.
“Europe has never lived by its own means and its own mind,” Lavrov said. “It has always lived at the expense of others.”
‘Neo-Nazi spirit’ in Europe
The foreign minister said that a “neo-Nazi spirit” remains “very, very resilient” in parts of Europe and singled out Germany, where he said the “metastases of Nazism” were re-emerging.
Lavrov pointed to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s pledge to make Germany Europe’s leading military power “again,” saying the choice of word had left him “stunned.”
“If this person does not understand what the word ‘again’ means in this context, then this is extremely dangerous for Europe,” Lavrov said, accusing the region of once again becoming a source of ideas of “national and racial superiority.”
‘Dictate’ rather than ‘negotiate’
Lavrov linked Western policy in Europe to persistent “neo-colonial habits” elsewhere in the world. Western diplomacy, he argued, is increasingly based not on reaching agreements but on coercion.
“The West does not want to negotiate, it wants to dictate,” he said, adding that diplomacy has effectively been “replaced by sanctions.”
He accused Western states of seeking to undermine the consensus-based architecture built around the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which he praised for emphasizing consensus, mutual respect, and mutual benefit. According to the minister, Washington and its allies are instead creating smaller groupings designed to erode ASEAN’s central role.
He cited AUKUS – the US, UK, and Australia – as well as various “trilateral” and “quadrilateral” arrangements, and pointed to NATO’s expanding infrastructure in Asia. Lavrov said these structures ultimately serve a strategy of containing China and, “along with it,” Russia.
Multipolar alternative
Russia’s answer, Lavrov said, is to strengthen open regional platforms rather than build closed military groupings. He cited the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the Eurasian Economic Union, ASEAN, BRICS, and other structures whose cooperation Moscow wants to deepen.
He highlighted the “ASEAN plus partners” model, saying its participants have equal rights and decisions are based on inclusive principles rather than diktat.
Lavrov linked these efforts to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s proposal for a “Greater Eurasian Partnership” open to all states on the continent and based on shared economic and development interests. He described the broader shift toward a multipolar world as an objective historical process that the West cannot stop.
EU ‘shot itself in the foot’
Lavrov also argued that the EU has inflicted severe economic damage on itself by abandoning Russian energy and accepting the destruction of the Nord Stream pipelines, describing the EU’s response to the sabotage as “self-humiliation.”
The bloc has effectively “shot itself in the foot and in the head,” he said, noting that Russian gas had been at least three times cheaper than current European prices. Soaring energy costs are now pushing industry to the US, where energy is three to four times cheaper, he added.
The EU is thus voluntarily squandering its economic advantages while transforming itself from an economic association into an “openly aggressive anti-Russian military bloc” supporting NATO.
Russia will not ‘beg’ Europe
Moscow, however, will not “beg” European nations to lift sanctions or restore economic ties, Lavrov said.
He argued that European leaders had assumed Russia valued its economic relationship with the EU so highly that it would eventually come “running and begging” for sanctions to be removed.
“That will not happen,” Lavrov said. “It is absolutely not in the genetic code of our people. We have, if you like, our own pride.” Russia has enough countries willing to cooperate “honestly,” he added, and does not need to seek reconciliation with Europe on its terms.
‘Fuhrer Ursula’
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen – “we call her Fuhrer Ursula,” Lavrov said – is stripping national governments of their powers and concentrating them in Brussels.
He stated that von der Leyen was trying to pull into the European Commission powers that EU members had never transferred to Brussels and which “remain with national governments.”
Lavrov also recalled von der Leyen saying Europeans would have to “suffer” from substantially higher energy prices so that Ukraine could defend “our European values.”
“Nobody asked her what those European values were,” he said, pointing to restrictions on the Russian language and the Ukrainian Orthodox Church. “If the legislative ban on the Russian language in education, culture, everyday life, and the media reflects European values, then welcome back to Nazism for Europe,” Lavrov said.
West wants to ‘freeze’ Ukraine conflict
Turning directly to Ukraine, Lavrov said Western governments had abandoned – or at least played down – their previous rhetoric about inflicting a “strategic defeat” on Russia and were instead seeking an immediate halt to fighting along the current front line.
Under that scenario, he said, Western countries would deploy “stabilization forces” to the territory remaining under Kiev’s control and provide security guarantees while refusing to recognize Russian control of Crimea, Donbass, and Novorossiya.
“They do not want to settle this conflict, but to freeze it, preserving this threat on our borders,” Lavrov added. Accepting such an outcome would also amount to abandoning Russia’s stated goal of “denazification,” he argued, saying Moscow would not agree to preserve an anti-Russian government in Kiev.
“We would betray our ancestors who defeated Nazism in 1945,” he said. “I do not think our people are ready for that.”

Ukraine is considering involving businesses in the production and supply of certain types of air defense systems
Kyiv • UNN
At the Staff meeting, tasks were set for businesses in the production of air defense systems. Ukraine will ramp up production of interceptor drones and inexpensive missiles.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the Staff meeting addressed the potential for engaging businesses in the production of certain types of air defense systems, reports UNN.

"We will also act asymmetrically. The relevant operations have been approved," the President concluded.

articles.title: Air defenses down 135 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Air defenses down 135 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this in a Telegram post.
Beginning at 18:00 on Wednesday, September 2, the enemy attacked Ukraine with 163 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (about half of them jet-powered), S8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodya-type decoy drones launched from the directions of Millerovo and Oryol, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The aerial attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:30 on Thursday, September 3, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 135 UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera drones, and other types of UAVs.
Hits were recorded at 15 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
As reported by Ukrinform, 17 people, including three children, were injured in a Russian attack on Odesa overnight on September 3.

articles.title: UN's Sudan probe says foreign fighters fuelling conflict
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN's Sudan probe says foreign fighters fuelling conflict
Foreign fighters and support networks are fuelling the conflict in Sudan and worsening violence against civilians, a UN-backed investigation warned Thursday.
The United Nations' independent fact-finding mission on Sudan said foreign involvement was strengthening the military capabilities of the country's warring parties, enabling increasingly sophisticated military operations, with devastating consequences for ordinary people.
Since April 2023, the conflict between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and forced millions to flee their homes.
In a report, the probe documented the recruitment, training and deployment of foreign personnel to support the RSF, with transnational entities also facilitating the transfer of weapons, ammunition, military technology and logistical support.
It also said there were reasonable grounds to believe that the regular army used foreign-supplied drones in its operations that harmed civilians and civilian infrastructure.
"This external support has not brought greater protection for civilians," said the fact-finding mission's chairman Mohamad Chande Othman.
"Instead, civilians are paying the price through attacks on homes, hospitals, schools, markets and places of refuge."
The UN Human Rights Council established the probe in October 2023, to begin gathering evidence of violations in Sudan.
The independent investigative team does not speak on behalf of the United Nations.
Colombian contingent
The investigation documented the deployment of up to 2,000 ex-military Colombian contractors who directly operated combat drones, artillery and advanced weapons alongside RSF units.
Witnesses also reported fighters from South Sudan, Chad and Ethiopia, "including women, serving primarily in frontline, rather than technical roles", identified by language, accent "and, in some cases uniforms", the report said.
Private entities, intermediaries and recruiters operating from countries including Colombia and the United Arab Emirates used transit locations in Chad, Libya and Somalia to facilitate the delivery of personnel, training, weapons and logistics to the RSF in Sudan, the report said.
It found that foreign suppliers had boosted the RSF and the army's drone capabilities, allowing them to strike far beyond the front lines.
The mission found reasonable grounds to believe that the army and RSF attacks it documented may amount to war crimes.
Responding to the report, the United Arab Emirates insisted in a statement it was "not involved in the civil war in Sudan, nor has it provided arms or any related material to any party in Sudan since the outbreak of the conflict", and strongly condemned violations of international law by all sides.
The United States last month urged the UN Security Council to expand an arms embargo on the Darfur region to cover all of Sudan -- a call echoed by the fact-finding mission.
"Protecting Sudan's civilians requires action not only against those fighting the war, but also against the individuals, entities and networks that enable it to continue," said Chande Othman.

articles.title: Ukraine gets first Skyranger 35 systems on Leopard 1 tanks
articles.body:
- Ukraine's 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment has reportedly received the first Rheinmetall Skyranger 35 air defense systems mounted on Leopard 1 chassis.
- The contract, signed in the second half of 2025, is financed by an EU country using proceeds from frozen Russian assets.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces have shown footage of what appears to be one of the first Skyranger 35 short-range air defense systems mounted on a Leopard 1 tank chassis to reach Ukrainian units.
GAU, an account that tracks German military assistance to Ukraine, identified the unit in the footage as Ukraine’s 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment, part of the Ground Forces. The account said the regiment appears to have taken delivery of the first Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 systems built by Rheinmetall.
Rheinmetall announced the contract for the systems in October 2025, saying an unnamed European Union country would finance the deal using proceeds from frozen Russian assets under the EU’s Windfall Profit Mechanism. The company put the order’s value in the hundreds of millions of euros and said production and integration would take place at Rheinmetall Italia’s headquarters in Rome. Ukraine had already fielded earlier Skyranger 35 systems mounted on truck chassis; the Leopard 1 version is a separate, tracked variant.
The Skyranger 35 is built around a KDG 35/1000 revolver cannon firing 35x228mm ammunition at a rate of 1,000 rounds per minute, with an effective range up to 4,000 meters (2.5 miles). The system fires airburst rounds that detonate near a target and scatter tungsten sub-projectiles, a design intended to improve hit probability against small, fast-moving threats such as Shahed-type drones and FPVs. Rheinmetall has said the turret shares a high degree of commonality with the company’s Oerlikon Revolver Gun Mk 3 and could eventually be fitted with guided missiles.
Rheinmetall first showed the Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 publicly in September 2024, at a demonstration event at the Erprobungszentrum Ochsenboden test site in Switzerland. That demonstrator used a Leopard 1A5BE hull with an unmanned turret carrying 252 rounds, with the two-person crew, a commander and a gunner, seated in the front of the hull. Representatives from defense ministries and industry in 26 countries attended.
Germany’s own military has ordered 19 Skyranger systems and has discussed acquiring several hundred more, following reports of unidentified drones appearing in European airspace. Ukraine’s version reaching the field ahead of Germany’s own fielding was noted at the time the October contract was announced.
Rheinmetall has previously delivered Skyranger 35 units to Ukraine mounted on wheeled truck platforms. The Leopard 1 chassis gives the new variant tracked mobility and armor protection not available on the truck-based version, allowing it to operate closer to the front line. Ukraine has received roughly 170 Leopard 1 tanks from Germany and other partners since 2023, with about 25 confirmed damaged or destroyed, according to the open-source tracking project Oryx.

articles.title: What Each F-35 Variant Really Costs Right Now
articles.body:
The base cost of an F-35A, the Air Force variant of the Joint Strike Fighter, is going up 11.5 percent from $82.5 million to $92 million for the latest lots of the fifth-generation aircraft, Air & Space Forces Magazine has confirmed.
A spokesperson for the F-35 Joint Program Office gave cost estimates for each F-35 variant, averaged across Lots 18 and 19, in current-year dollars. A recent Pentagon acquisition report gave the estimates in 2012 dollars, when the program was rebaselined. The new figures give insight how inflation is affecting the program.
Manufacturer Lockheed Martin lists the price of F-35 variants for Lots 15 through 17 on its website.
The totals are average flyaway costs, which refer to all the basic costs it takes to produce one aircraft. The JPO confirmed those price tags include the cost of the jets’ engines and radars, which are provided to manufacturer Lockheed Martin as government-furnished equipment.
The cost of the F-35A went up the most in recent lots, at 11.5 percent, with the F-35B almost identical in terms of percentage growth. The F-35C went up the least, at just 8.5 percent.
But the F-35A remains the cheapest and least complex variant of the three. The F-35B—the short takeoff and vertical landing variant flown by the Marine Corps—is the most expensive and complicated, given its unique swiveling engine nozzle and hovering capabilities. And the F-35C, flown by both the Marine Corps and the Navy, is closer in price to the F-35B and has bigger wings than the F-35A to help with carrier landings, as well as folding wingtips to help with storage in close quarters.
The revelation of the price tags for the F-35s’ upcoming lots—the highest in the nearly $2 trillion program’s history—follows the Pentagon’s release of a modernized selected acquisition report which said the total estimated acquisition cost for the F-35, including both airframes and engines, had grown more than 10 percent to $536.2 billion.
The selected acquisition report, which was released in August, pointed to inflation and critical upgrades as causes of the F-35’s cost growth. But the report only included flyways costs for the three variants in 2012 dollars, leaving the full effects of inflation unclear. Those costs were:
- $78 million for the F-35A, up 7.3 percent from the previous report in 2023.
- $110.3 million for the F-35B, up 10.5 percent from the previous report.
- $93.4 million for the F-35C, up 6.6 percent from the previous report.
The fact that the actual costs are seeing greater percentage increases could suggest inflation is having a significant effect on the jet’s price tag.
Lockheed officials have been sounding warnings about the growing effects of inflation on the F-35 for some time now.
Greg Ulmer, then-president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, told Defense One in July 2024 that keeping the F-35’s price under the rate of inflation would be challenging for Lots 18 and 19.
“Inflation is real,” Ulmer said at the Farnborough Air Show in England. “The cost of raw materials has gone up. The cost of everything has gone up, so there is just inflation pressure in the system.”
The JPO, Lockheed, and other F-35 contractors have also been working on adding more capabilities to the jet, including additional computing and processing power under the Technology Refresh 3 program and additional weapons, sensor, and sensor fusion capabilities as part of the Block 4 effort.
The JPO pointed to information in the selected acquisition report when asked for comment on the Lots 18 and 19 cost growth. Lockheed Martin said in a response to a query that the recent acquisition report shows the program is moving into full-rate production, resuming high-volume development deliveries, and growing globally.
“It also shows that the hard work has shifted from proving the basic aircraft to executing major modernization, improving fleet readiness, and controlling long-term sustainment and integration costs,” a Lockheed spokesperson said.
The JPO had previously declined to release the cost for each variant in current-year dollars and said those numbers were considered controlled unclassified information. The office eventually released the figures after further queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The JPO and Lockheed Martin in September 2025 struck a final “definitized” deal for Lots 18 and 19, which would buy 296 fighters for nearly $24.3 billion. That deal was for just the airframe and did not include engine costs, meaning the average cost of just the airframe across all variants will be $82.4 million.

articles.title: Russia Is Paying for the War with Its Future Economy
articles.body:
Andriy Dubas, President of the Association of Ukrainian Banks
For several years, massive government spending related to the war was one of the main drivers of the Russian economy. Military contracts ensured demand for businesses, supported employment, household incomes, and consumption. Now, this model is producing significantly weaker results: economic growth is slowing, the cost of capital remains high, and budgetary and production constraints are becoming more visible.
This is clearly evident from GDP trends. After growing by 4.9% in 2024, the Russian economy expanded by only 1% in 2025. In 2026, the Russian Ministry of Economic Development expects growth of just 0.4%, while the Bank of Russia forecasts growth in the range of 0–1%.
Government procurement supports demand; resources are concentrated in military sectors
The Bank of Russia explicitly identifies the consumer sector and the portion of the manufacturing industry focused on government procurement as key drivers of economic growth. This explains why significant government spending has long allowed Russia to sustain economic activity despite sanctions and other restrictions.
This model concentrates resources in sectors that serve government contracts. Meanwhile, parts of the civilian economy face more challenging conditions.
The need to maintain a balance between the military and civilian sectors is already being discussed within Russia itself. Putin’s special representative, Boris Titov, has warned against an excessive concentration of the economy on the needs of the military-industrial complex.
This is an important signal: while military demand remains significant, its ability to drive growth across the entire economy is gradually weakening.
High borrowing costs are accompanied by production constraints.
Another factor is the high cost of financing. Following a prolonged period of tight monetary policy, the Bank of Russia’s key rate stood at 14% in July. For businesses, this means expensive loans and more challenging conditions for new investments.
In August, the manufacturing PMI fell to 48.8 points. Companies reported declines in production and new orders, weaker demand, and rising costs for fuel and imports.
The Bank of Russia is already anticipating a further economic slowdown due to a “temporary loss of capacity” in manufacturing and logistics. This is a fundamentally important point: the issue is no longer just about demand or the cost of borrowing, but about the economy’s ability to produce and supply goods.
The consequences of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy and logistics infrastructure are emerging as a separate factor. In particular, Russia has already revised its oil production forecast for 2026 downward, and Reuters cites the effects of the war and strikes on oil refineries among the reasons.
Budgetary pressure is becoming increasingly evident
The changes are most evident in public finances. According to preliminary data from the Russian Ministry of Finance, the federal budget deficit for January–July 2026 amounted to 6.455 trillion rubles, or 2.8% of GDP. The current annual plan calls for a deficit of 3.786 trillion rubles. The Ministry of Finance itself attributes a significant portion of the accumulated deficit to front-loading of expenditures.
Oil and gas revenues to the federal budget fell by 16.8% year-over-year over the seven-month period, to 4.595 trillion rubles. During the same period, expenditures rose by 14.5% to 28.567 trillion rubles.
Military and security spending remains substantial. The 2026 budget allocates approximately 16.84 trillion rubles for defense, security, and law enforcement combined.
The pressure is also evident at the regional level. According to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, in 65 of 85 Russian regions, real budget revenues at the end of 2025 were lower than in 2021. Among the reasons are reductions in federal transfers and corporate income tax revenues.
The Russian economy has so far managed to maintain its export revenues, large domestic market, and ability to reallocate significant budgetary resources. However, an ever-increasing portion of these resources is being directed toward the war effort, which limits opportunities for civilian investment, modernization, and regional development.
The cost of the war is becoming increasingly visible for Russia. In fact, it is already paying for it with its own future.
