articles.title: Iran struggles to restrict Hormuz traffic after US strikes hit maritime capabilities
articles.body:
The Islamic Republic’s ability to surveil the Strait of Hormuz and lay mines in the vital waterway has likely been significantly degraded by American attacks, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed, noting that increased oil flows through the strait on September 1 suggest Iran is having difficulty preventing some commercial vessels from using the southern route.
United States officials told Axios on Wednesday that approximately 40 vessels carrying millions of barrels of oil transited the strait on September 1.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also confirmed that oil tankers transported over 17 million barrels of oil through the strait on August 31, the highest volume of oil exports through the waterway since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The figure of 17 million barrels is close to pre-war levels, which averaged 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025.
These developments, according to ISW, suggest that Iran is having difficulty preventing some commercial vessels from using the southern route.
Additionally, ISW reported growing indications that Iranian forces are facing operational constraints preventing them from efficiently identifying vessels and laying mines in the strait.
IRGC turns to alternative methods as Hormuz surveillance is degraded
According to ISW, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) recently attempted to use shore-based rocket launchers instead of fast-attack craft to deploy mines.
It has also reportedly used fast-attack craft to physically identify vessels because Iran has only a few functioning radars capable of covering the southern route.
ISW assessed that these less-optimal methods suggest that US strikes have degraded some of Iran’s maritime surveillance and mine-laying capabilities.
Though the IRGC has repeatedly claimed that vessels are striking naval mines in the strait, ISW’s assessment of the claims likely forms part of an effort to preserve the perception that the southern route remains dangerous. US Central Command previously reported that US forces had cleared naval mines from the strait.
CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said last week that US forces had cleared an effective pathway for ships to leave the Persian Gulf, adding that the mines had been “highly degraded.”
However, Ebrahim Zolfaghari, an Iranian military officer and spokesman, claimed on Wednesday that new mines had been laid.
“During last night’s operation, more naval mines were laid along the illicit routes south of the Strait of Hormuz. The only thing CENTCOM could do in response was rename the strait using Photoshop,” he wrote on X/Twitter. “Problem solved! You can just use Photoshop to get the oil tankers through, too!”
Iran appears to be investing in rebuilding its radar systems, ISW noted, citing a claim by US President Donald Trump that Iran had nearly rebuilt some of its radar systems before the US struck them again on September 1.
CENTCOM strikes targets on September 1
CENTCOM confirmed that its September 1 strikes targeted Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.
ISW noted that Iran is likely to continue attempting to reconstitute these capabilities because control of the Strait of Hormuz remains one of Tehran’s core objectives.
With Iran’s radars degraded, ISW suggested that the regime would seek alternative ways to attempt control over the strait.
An unnamed American source told Saudi-based Al Arabiya on Wednesday that CENTCOM’s Tuesday night strikes were a preemptive response to the Islamic Republic considering disabling undersea cables.

articles.title: Civil rights groups campaign against deepening US-Israel defense cooperation
articles.body:
Dozens of civil rights and advocacy groups are urging Congress to scrap a defense bill provision that would deepen US-Israeli military technology ties, according to a letter seen by Reuters, at a time of growing US skepticism toward the longtime ally.
The provision would deepen cooperation between the US and Israeli defense sectors by accelerating joint military technology development and other partnerships. The bill passed the House of Representatives in July and awaits Senate action.
The provision of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, known as Section 219, seeks to set up frameworks for joint ventures, licensing agreements and US-based co-production partnerships with the Israeli industry.
In Thursday's letter addressed to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, 56 groups said deeper integration with Israel's defense sector would be "exceptionally dangerous" and urged lawmakers to remove the provision.
The groups include Amnesty International USA and the civil rights network National Lawyers Guild as well as Arab and Jewish advocacy groups.
"At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support to Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the US defense-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous," said the letter, which has not been previously reported.
Israel is one of Washington's closest allies in the Middle East, and the two countries cooperate extensively on defense and intelligence issues. Supporters say deeper ties could help speed military innovation and technology development.
A spokesperson from the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off US military support within a decade. In a June letter to a US congressman, he wrote that the time has come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."
US public support for Israel declines
US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries, and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of US support for Israel.
The Islamist militant Hamas group, in an October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, killed nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals and took hundreds hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed in Israel's subsequent assault on Gaza, according to Gaza health officials.
The letter criticizes Israel for its potential violations of international humanitarian law in its war in Gaza and rising settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It says such developments should prevent any discussion of deepening military ties.
US-Israel military aid agreement nears 2028 expiration
A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion in annual US military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028, and conversations are under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
Some members of Congress have already tried to strip the provision from the fiscal 2027 NDAA. Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California introduced an amendment to block it, but it did not make it into the House version of the bill.
Once the House and Senate write their versions of the NDAA, members of the two chambers work out a compromise version of the bill, which must pass both chambers - typically near the end of the calendar year - before it can be sent to the White House for President Donald Trump to sign into law or veto.

articles.title: Arctic limbo: What you need to know about the Russian ship seized by Norway
articles.body:
Arctic limbo: What you need to know about the Russian ship seized by Norway
Norway has seized a Russian research vessel in Svalbard at the request of Kiev, prompting Russian President Vladimir Putin to denounce the capture of civilian vessels as “state terrorism.”
The vessel, called the Professor Molchanov, was detained while docked in Barentsburg, a Russian-operated settlement on the Norwegian-administered Arctic archipelago. The ship has been barred from leaving after a local court granted a request by Ukraine’s state-owned energy company Naftogaz.
Moscow has since summoned Norway’s ambassador in protest and vowed to challenge the seizure.
Why was a Russian state vessel in Norway in the first place, why does Kiev want it, and what could happen to the ship now?
What exactly happened
The Professor Molchanov arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday on a scheduled voyage from Murmansk carrying scientists, passengers and supplies for the Russian settlements on the Norwegian-administered Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
Norwegian officials first boarded the vessel for what Svalbard Governor Lars Fause described as an ordinary border and customs inspection, of a kind the ship had undergone numerous times before.
On Wednesday, Norwegian police, accompanied by an interpreter, boarded the ship again and read a court order to its captain, barring the vessel from leaving. Nobody aboard was arrested.
The order was issued on August 31 by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court after an application from Ukraine’s Naftogaz.
What happened to the passengers and crew
The exact number of people on board when the ship arrived in Barentsburg has not been officially confirmed. The Professor Molchanov can accommodate up to 80 people, including at least 20 crew members and as many as 60 scientists and other expedition personnel.
Norwegian media have reported that around 50 passengers and crew were affected by the seizure.
Russian officials have said that 21 people remained on board. They have been supplied with everything they need and continue working, with no Norwegian police or officials stationed on the vessel.
Those who had already gone ashore were not detained and have been able to continue their planned work. They include participants in the Arctic Biennale art-and-science project.
The seizure has, however, left some passengers without their planned transport back to Russia. Norwegian authorities have said they are working with Arktikugol to resolve the situation for those affected, but no alternative route has yet been announced.
The Professor Molchanov
The ship, named after renowned Soviet meteorologist Pavel Molchanov, is a Russian state-owned, ice-strengthened research vessel with more than four decades of experience operating in polar waters.
Built in Finland for the Soviet hydrometeorological service and launched in late 1982, the 71-meter-long ship was designed for Arctic oceanographic and weather research. It carries four laboratories on board and can accommodate dozens of researchers alongside its crew.
The ship continues to be actively used in Arctic research, including studies of weather, marine ecosystems, microbiology, biodiversity and environmental conditions in the Barents and Kara seas.
Why is goes to Svalbard
The voyage to Svalbard was part of a regular route between Murmansk and Barentsburg, a Russian mining settlement where the state-owned Arktikugol trust has operated for decades.
Since 2025, the Professor Molchanov has carried scientists, Arktikugol employees, contractors, family members and supplies to Barentsburg and another Russian settlement called Pyramida. Ten round trips were planned for 2026.
It is currently the only vessel providing a direct passenger connection between the Russian mainland and the archipelago after direct air links between Russia and Svalbard ended in 2020.
While Svalbard is under Norwegian sovereignty, it is governed by the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which grants nationals of signatory countries rights to conduct commercial and scientific activities on the archipelago.
Why Ukraine wants the ship
The seizure of the vessel stems from a long-running dispute over Crimea. Ukraine’s Naftogaz has claimed that it lost energy assets after the peninsula’s reunification with Russia in 2014 and took the case to an arbitration tribunal in The Hague.
In 2023, the tribunal ordered Russia to pay around $4.22 billion, plus interest and legal costs, ruling that Naftogaz’s assets in Crimea could be treated as Ukrainian “investments” in Russian territory and were protected under a bilateral treaty.
Moscow has rejected the ruling, arguing that the tribunal had no jurisdiction over the dispute and that the treaty did not apply to assets that had already been located in Crimea before its reunification with Russia.
Nevertheless, Naftogaz has since tried to collect the award by targeting Russian state property abroad. It has pursued assets in several Western countries, including Finland, Britain and France, and says the arbitration award can also be enforced in Norway.
According to Reuters, lawyers acting for Naftogaz had been monitoring the Professor Molchanov for months before seeking its seizure.
Will Kiev actually get the ship?
Not automatically. The current order only prevents the Professor Molchanov from leaving Barentsburg while the case proceeds. The vessel remains Russian property and has not yet been transferred to Ukraine.
Naftogaz ultimately wants Russian assets seized abroad to be sold, with the proceeds used to cover part of the $4.22 billion award. According to Reuters, its lawyers sought not only the arrest of the Professor Molchanov, but also its eventual compulsory sale.
However, even if the ship were to be sold, it would cover only a tiny fraction of Kiev’s multibillion-dollar claim.
Russia has also said it will challenge whether the ship can be seized or sold at all. While Naftogaz has claimed that the vessel has a commercial function, Moscow has stressed that it is state-owned, operated by Roshydromet, and used for scientific research and supplying Russian settlements in the Arctic.
Moscow’s response
Moscow has protested the seizure and demanded that Norway release the vessel. On Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador Heidi Olufsen and delivered a “strong protest” over the detention of the ship.
The ministry stressed that the vessel was carrying out a scheduled trip between Murmansk and Barentsburg and was transporting scientists, Arktikugol employees, and supplies needed by Russian settlements on Svalbard.
It accused Oslo of using the restrictions against Russia to undermine Moscow’s longstanding presence on the archipelago, saying Russian organizations and citizens there had effectively been placed in a “state of blockade.”
The ministry also accused Norway of violating the 1920 Svalbard Treaty and said Russian authorities would work to have the seizure lifted.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described the detention as another example of Western “piracy,” while Far East and Arctic Development Minister Aleksey Chekunkov called it “legal nihilism and lawlessness” and said Moscow would challenge the decision.
President Vladimir Putin described the capture of civilian vessels, attacks on merchant ships and threats against civilian aircraft as manifestations of “state terrorism.” He added that Western countries which ignore such actions risk becoming “accomplices in international terrorism.”
Part of a broader campaign against Russian vessels
Western countries have increasingly moved beyond sanctions and begun physically detaining or seizing vessels they accuse of helping Russia bypass restrictions on its trade, claiming the ships are part of a so-called “shadow fleet.”
A number of ships linked to Russia have been held in European waters since 2025, including tankers and cargo vessels detained by Germany, Estonia, France, Belgium, Sweden, and Britain.
Moscow has repeatedly decried the seizures while dismissing the “shadow fleet” designation as legally meaningless.
Putin warned in August that attempts to seize Russian ships and sell their cargo amounted to “piracy and robbery” and said Moscow could respond in kind against vessels carrying cargo for countries involved in such actions.
An attempt to limit Russia in the Arctic?
Russian officials and experts have linked the seizure to a wider Western effort to weaken Moscow’s position in the Arctic. Murmansk Governor Andrey Chibis accused Norwegian officials of trying to “push us out of Svalbard,” stressing that Russia has longstanding economic and scientific interests on the archipelago and that such efforts would fail.
Arctic expert Aleksey Fadeev similarly described the detention as another attempt by Western countries to pressure Russia under the pretext of confiscating property for Ukraine, warning that it could further increase tensions between Moscow and NATO states in the region.
Military analyst Aleksandr Stepanov warned the seizure could set a precedent for disrupting Russian maritime access not only around Svalbard but across northern waters more broadly.
Russian experts have also described the arrest as a potential blow to Russia’s ability to conduct Arctic research, noting that the Professor Molchanov is used for climate, weather, and environmental studies with relevance beyond Russia itself.

articles.title: Leonid Slutsky was promised second place in the September elections, sources tell Meduza. Frustrated that the Kremlin stopped helping, he’s now saying LDPR belongs to the security services instead.
articles.body:
Leonid Slutsky was promised second place in the September elections, sources tell Meduza. Frustrated that the Kremlin stopped helping, he’s now saying LDPR belongs to the security services instead.
Leonid Slutsky, who leads Russia’s Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), has begun casting it as a “party of security officials” rather than as a party of the Kremlin’s civilian staff. That is how Slutsky describes the party in private conversations with allies and with businesspeople close to the Liberal Democrats, and even in public campaign materials.
A post on LDPR’s Facebook page says security officials are running for the party in elections to the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of parliament. Slutsky made the same point on his VKontakte page. The party’s social media posts read (errors as in the original):
Our team is made up of heroes and builders. LDPR’s list of State Duma candidates includes 111 people who know firsthand what it means to defend the Motherland. They are veterans of the “special military operation,” volunteers, and security officials. Among them are brigade commander Alexey Vereshchagin and Sergei Antoshin, leader of “Bars-Bryansk.” Our guys on the front lines are correcting past mistakes today, strengthening the Russian World.
Two LDPR members and a strategist who works with the political bloc of Russia’s Presidential Administration told Meduza about the shift in positioning.
The party changed its image because Slutsky is unhappy with the work of the political bloc headed by Sergei Kiriyenko. The reason for his displeasure is the party’s declining ratings and the fear that comes with them — that LDPR will fail to take the coveted second place, or even third.
“[At the political bloc] they promised second place, but they’re not delivering. It didn’t work out in the presidential election, and they’re not helping in the Duma election,” said one party member, summing up Slutsky’s complaints.
The same member said Slutsky now coordinates the campaign not with Alexander Kharichev, head of the Social Monitoring Directorate, but with Andrey Yarin, head of the Domestic Policy Directorate.
Under the Kremlin’s informal division of labor, Kharichev — who is close to the head of the political bloc — oversees election campaigns; Yarin handles day-to-day “operational” matters with regional authorities. Yarin has always been seen as closer to the security officials than to Kiriyenko’s team.
After the full-scale invasion began and Vladimir Zhirinovsky, LDPR’s founder, died in 2022, the Presidential Administration’s political bloc did try to pull LDPR into second place in regional elections. It managed to secure that result only last year, when LDPR finished second in seven of the 11 regions electing legislatures.
In the 2024 presidential election, LDPR’s new leader finished only fourth, behind not just Russian President Vladimir Putin but also Communist Party (KPRF) nominee Nikolai Kharitonov and Vladislav Davankov of the New People party. That happened even though the political bloc had sent Andrey Polosin, an experienced political strategist close to Kiriyenko, to help Slutsky, and even though the leaders of KPRF and New People took no part in the campaign.
According to the strategist working with the political bloc, “that’s when the mutual grievances between Slutsky and Kiriyenko’s team began.”
“Andrey [Polosin] did good work, but Slutsky and [Maria Voropayeva, the head of the party’s staff] complained about him to Kharichev constantly. They tried complaining to Kiriyenko, too. At some point SVK stopped talking to him and handed Slutsky off to Kharichev — that stung as well,” the strategist said. “Though at a congress or a public event Kiriyenko will, of course, say hello and toss out a line.”
The political bloc’s complaint, which Meduza has reported before, is that Slutsky cannot pull off the role of a public politician and that he himself “doesn’t understand this,” according to the strategist who works with the Presidential Administration and another source close to the Kremlin. Even so, Slutsky is seriously trying to become the party’s frontman: he has led and continues to lead LDPR’s lists in regional legislative elections.
“In the Russian system, it’s not a problem for a loyal party to be run by an uncharismatic man — no,” said a political strategist who works with the Kremlin. “You can be smarter about it: push other, more public figures to the front. Or just work with slogans and branding and try to take second place that way, especially when your interests line up with the Presidential Administration’s. But that doesn’t suit Slutsky’s vanity.”
The party is repeating that mistake in the current campaign, he said: its leader takes part in debate after debate and puts himself front and center in LDPR’s campaign videos, in which he urges voters to “save Russia” by voting for the party.
Another prominent LDPR figure appears in one of those videos: Viktor Bout, an arms dealer convicted in the United States, whom Russia exchanged in 2022 for basketball player Brittney Griner, who had been detained at Sheremetyevo Airport with hashish oil for a vape pen. Bout is on the federal portion of the party’s State Duma list, but in this ad he, for some reason, plays an ordinary businessman.
A source in the party said the campaign built around Slutsky is aimed mainly at a loyalist, patriotic electorate, and he sees no problem with that. He acknowledged, though, that internal polling shows Slutsky’s name recognition is low even among LDPR sympathizers.
After Zhirinovsky’s death, LDPR continued to use his image in some regional elections, and it remained the centerpiece of Slutsky’s 2024 presidential campaign messaging. In the current State Duma campaign, though, the founder’s name is almost absent.
Under Zhirinovsky, LDPR eagerly played up the issue of “fighting migrants.” By the early 2010s, however, the party had scaled back its use of the “Russian question” in its messaging at the Kremlin’s prompting. Under Slutsky, LDPR returned to anti-migrant appeals, riding a wave of xenophobic sentiment that grew among Russians in the 2020s.
Now the party’s leadership is unhappy with the political bloc’s unspoken ban on flirting with nationalist ideas. Still, posts with xenophobic appeals continue to go up on LDPR’s social media accounts.
“It [the nationalist theme] would give us a good boost, but Slutsky apparently didn’t get the go-ahead. Maybe he couldn’t have. And yet he presented himself as someone the Presidential Administration supports and helps in every way!” said a party member critical of the LDPR leader.
Both he and the strategist working with the Presidential Administration believe that recasting the Liberal Democrats as a party of security officials, and Slutsky’s outreach to Yarin, who is close to the security officials, are meant to paper over, within the party, the evident lack of understanding between Slutsky’s team and the political bloc’s leadership.
“Slutsky came into the party leadership as the political bloc’s man. If something is wrong in his relationship with Kiriyenko, [Slutsky, for appearances,] needs a new patron — real or imagined — who will deliver the necessary result. The security officials and Yarin became just that. And Slutsky really does go to Yarin — on day-to-day party business. But it’s Kharichev who oversees the elections,” said the strategist who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc.
Meduza’s sources do not rule out that LDPR could finish not second but as low as fourth in the State Duma elections. Second place, by their account, will go to KPRF, and New People may contend for third.
The party A Just Russia, in their view, will make it into the State Duma only if the political bloc receives instructions to that effect from Putin. “In the polling, public and internal alike, they don’t clear the threshold. The story with [A Just Russia leader Sergei] Mironov will only push their ratings down. But there’s no clarity yet on whether they’ll be in parliament. If the president wants to keep the current lineup of Duma factions, A Just Russia will get help,” said the strategist working with the Presidential Administration.
In his view, the Kremlin will not put in the effort to pull LDPR up to second or third place: “If they get to third on their own — which is realistic — no problem. If they don’t, that’s their problem. They’ve been helped every way possible for years as it is.”
LDPR had not responded to Meduza’s request for comment at the time of publication.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Dhesi presses PM on pathway to three per cent
articles.body:
The Prime Minister has told the Commons that he has already committed to a pathway to spending three per cent of gross domestic product on defence, in response to a question pressing him to do so urgently rather than waiting for a future fiscal event.
Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the Defence Committee, put the question at Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday.
He said: “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level, especially from Russia, but also that we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or a priority. That is why it is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than being sorry later. Indeed, defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just will not be enough.
“Rather than kicking the can down the road, waiting for a fiscal event in a future year, will the Prime Minister urgently commit to charting a pathway to reaching 3% of GDP being spent on defence by 2030? As his Chancellor rightly noted, that is critical to keeping our country safe.”
Andy Burnham replied: “I have made that commitment, I have made it very clearly, and I have done so for a considerable time. I was in Ukraine last week for a very specific reason: to repeat it on the world stage. My hon. Friend can be absolutely sure of that.”
He went on: “Alongside our commitment to defence, we also have to build the resilience of Britain. We need to ensure that the maximum amount of the funding committed to the defence investment plan goes back into the reindustrialisation of our communities. We should do more to maintain sovereign manufacturing and production capability here, and that will be a theme of my Government. We will make sure that British taxpayers’ money goes to supporting industry in our own country, to make us more resilient going into the future.”
The exchange turns on a distinction between committing to a figure and setting out how it will be reached. Dhesi’s question asked for a pathway, and specifically for one that does not wait on a future fiscal event, which is the point on which the government has previously declined to be drawn.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, has argued that announcing a spending figure without setting out how it will be funded invites a loss of market confidence and rising borrowing costs. He has said he has every confidence the Defence Investment Plan will be fully funded, and has not ruled out tax rises as part of the answer.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has previously put the cost of reaching three per cent at an additional £17.3 billion in 2029-30. Behind the domestic argument sits NATO’s push towards 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence by 2035, agreed at the alliance summit in The Hague.
The second half of Burnham’s answer picks up a theme the government, current and former, has been developing through the Defence Industrial Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to defence over four years.
The department has pointed to figures published last month showing that spending with industry supported 274,000 jobs across the United Kingdom in 2024/25, with £31.9 billion spent, including 12,200 direct jobs in Scotland where shipbuilding and submarines account for 7,900 of them. Jobs supported by spending on weapons and ammunition manufacturing rose 51 per cent across the country over the same period, an increase the department attributes to the drive to rebuild what it calls an always on pipeline of munitions supply.

articles.title: Son of Iran's former vice president received over $2 million in Canadian gov't contracts - report
articles.body:
The son of Iran's former vice president received over $2 million in contracts from the Canadian government as he worked to further the regime's missile program and help it evade sanctions, Global News reported on Wednesday, citing obtained documents.
According to the report, 45-year-old Mohammad Reza Ghafouri Fard, son of Iranian politician and former vice president Hassan Ghafouri Fard, operated under the pseudonym Sal Ghafouri while living in Edmonton.
He received the government contracts while participating in an official Canadian trade mission to Latin America, Global News reported, with the intention of the funds being to help Fard “propose legislation” to Canada's government.
Fard is already the subject of a long-running investigation by the Canadian government into his suspected ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the report added.
Global News cited a recently declassified Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) report, which said Fard was “involved in the research and development of Iranian military technologies.”
Specifically, he assisted the regime in its attempts to "confront American aircraft" through the development of an anti-aircraft missile system and jamming system, having participated in a “covert procurement structure” designed to procure components for such projects.
Canada: Fard admitted to participating in activities beneficial to regime
The CSIS report cited by Global News further claimed that Fard “admitted to active participation in procurement activities that benefited the Iranian military, including the IRGC.”
CSIS noted in its report that Fard had traveled to Iran in 2015 to meet with members of Iran's Intelligence and Security Ministry on two separate occasions, during which he "provided details of his employment in Canada."
“During the second meeting, he was given detailed instructions and warnings, as they related to police or intelligence services approaching him while living in Canada,” CSIS was cited as saying.

articles.title: West trying to draw India into ‘games’ against China – Lavrov
articles.body:
West trying to draw India into ‘games’ against China – Lavrov
Western countries are trying to draw India into a confrontation with China by pushing a more military role for the Quad grouping, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok. 
Lavrov said India feels “very uncomfortable” in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) grouping, arguing that the US and Japan have sought to add a military component to it. 
“They are conducting maritime security exercises and are keen to draw our Indian friends into games against another great friend of ours – the People’s Republic of China,” Lavrov said.
The Quad grouping of India, the US, Japan, and Australia focuses on cooperation in the Indo-Pacific. Its activities cover areas ranging from trade and critical technologies to maritime security, with the four countries also taking part in the annual Malabar naval exercise.
At a meeting hosted by India in May, Quad foreign ministers launched a maritime surveillance initiative aimed at increasing information sharing and maritime domain awareness. India is also due to host the grouping’s next Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission, intended to improve interoperability and knowledge-sharing.
📹 Germany Wants To Be Europe’s Top Military Force ‘Again’... Lavrov Points To Nazi Past, Calls It ‘Extremely Dangerous’

Lavrov linked the grouping to what he described as a broader Western effort to weaken the central role of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) by creating smaller blocs in the region.
He said Western countries are also trying to establish a “second Quad,” comprising the US, Japan, Australia, and the Philippines – instead of India – with the aim of fragmenting ASEAN unity.
The four countries already cooperate in a separate defense format, sometimes referred to as the SQUAD. Their defense ministers agreed last year to deepen maritime and air activities and strengthen what they described as regional deterrence and response capabilities.

articles.title: External involvement fuelling Sudan war, new report finds
articles.body:
Outside forces fuel Sudan war, new report finds
Foreign recruitment and external support networks are fuelling the brutal conflict in Sudan, independent UN human rights investigators said on Thursday in a new report, calling for accountability as fighting continues between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
This action is strengthening the military capabilities of the warring parties and enabling increasingly sophisticated military operations with devastating consequences for civilians, according to the report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan.
The report documented the involvement of transnational entities operating in several countries in recruiting, training, and deploying foreign personnel to support the RSF, as well as facilitating the transfer of weapons, ammunition, and military technology, and providing logistical support.
It also concluded that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the SAF used foreign-supplied drones in operations that harmed civilians and civilian objects.
Civilians bearing the brunt
The mission pointed to the "strict international legal obligations" incumbent upon States linked to these supply chains, which require them to exercise due diligence, investigate and stop illicit mercenary and supply networks operating from or through their territories, prevent violations, and enforce the UN arms embargo.
“The consequences of this external support are being felt most acutely by civilians,” said Mohamad Chande Othman, Chair of the Fact-Finding Mission.
“This external support has not brought greater protection for civilians. Instead, civilians are paying the price through attacks on homes, hospitals, schools, markets and places of refuge.”
The mission said it had documented the deployment of up to 2,000 former Colombian military contractors who were directly involved in operating combat drones, artillery and advanced weapons alongside RSF units in Darfur and Kordofan.
The report concluded that there are reasonable grounds to believe that private entities, logistical facilitators, and recruiters operating from countries including Colombia and the United Arab Emirates used transit points in Chad, southeastern Libya, and the Somalian city of Bosaso to facilitate the delivery of personnel, training, weapons, and logistical supplies to the RSF in Sudan.
Drone capabilities expanded
Mona Rishmawi, an expert member of the mission, said it had identified “a transnational chain of networks spanning several countries” that provided the RSF with foreign personnel, training, weapons and logistics.
“This support fed into RSF operations in Zamzam camp and later during the takeover of El-Fasher, where the Mission documented grave human rights and international humanitarian law violations and international crimes, including conduct displaying hallmarks of genocide,” she said.
The report also found that foreign suppliers have substantially enhanced the drone capabilities of both the RSF and the SAF, enabling them to strike far beyond front lines.
Translate warnings into action
The investigators called on States to enforce the arms embargo on Darfur, halt military transfers where there is a substantial risk of contributing to serious violations, investigate individuals and entities involved in illicit support networks, and strengthen accountability measures.
They also urged the Security Council to extend the arms embargo to cover all of Sudan.
Mr. Osman recalled that the international community has received repeated warnings about the violations in Sudan.
“Those warnings must now translate into action,” he said.
"Protecting civilians in Sudan requires taking action not only against those waging this war, but also against the individuals, entities, and networks that enable its continuation."

articles.title: India, Sri Lanka, and Israel’s overlooked Indian Ocean opportunity  - opinion
articles.body:
While Sri Lanka is not an obvious priority in Israel’s Asian policy, with India, Japan, and Singapore receiving far more strategic attention, it has considerable potential because of its location, its development needs and the direction its relationship with India is heading.
During my recent visit, this became particularly clear. The island sits close to major sea lanes and within India’s immediate maritime security environment. For New Delhi, Sri Lanka is not simply another neighbor. Access to its ports and maritime infrastructure carries significance beyond bilateral relations.
Indian concerns about China’s research and survey vessels illustrate this sensitivity. The issue is not simply Chinese commercial investment. New Delhi is also attentive to the possibility that external actors could gain access to ports, infrastructure, or oceanographic information with potential dual-use applications close to India’s coastline.
Sri Lanka should not be reduced to another arena of India-China competition. Colombo has strong reasons to maintain relations with multiple partners, including China. Any Israeli strategy framed primarily around containing Beijing would misunderstand Sri Lanka’s interests and risk narrowing the space for cooperation.
India’s own approach has become broader. During Sri Lanka’s economic crisis in 2022, New Delhi provided some $4 billion in assistance. Since then, the relationship has moved beyond emergency support toward longer-term cooperation in energy, infrastructure, digital connectivity, trade, and security.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s April 2025 visit marked an important step. The two countries signed agreements on electricity interconnection, digital transformation and development, and, for the first time, a formal memorandum of understanding (MoU) on Defence Cooperation.
India, Sri Lanka and the United Arab Emirates also agreed to cooperate on developing Trincomalee as an energy hub.
The defense agreement did not create bilateral security cooperation: India and Sri Lanka already had substantial ties in training, naval visits, exercises, and capacity-building. Yet the MoU gave this relationship a more formal framework. Cooperation includes joint exercises, maritime surveillance, hydrography, capacity-building, and the provision of defense platforms and assets.
SLINEX is a regular bilateral naval exercise, and in April 2026 the two navies conducted their fourth bilateral diving exercise in Colombo, including complex underwater operations. Sri Lankan personnel have also participated in India’s wider IOS Sagar initiative.
Taken together, these developments suggest that India is progressively embedding Sri Lanka within a wider Indian-led maritime security architecture. This does not mean that Colombo is surrendering its strategic autonomy or that India is constructing a formal alliance system. India continues to prefer flexible partnerships. But New Delhi increasingly sees regional security as something built through training, maritime domain awareness, interoperability, capacity-building, and institutional cooperation.
For Israel, this creates an opportunity that deserves attention.
For years, Israel-India relations have been viewed primarily through defense cooperation, technology, and an expanding strategic convergence. Those ties remain important. But as India’s regional role grows, Israel should consider whether that partnership can also provide a basis for selective cooperation with third countries.
Sri Lanka offers a useful test case; there is evidence of Sri Lankan interest in expanding relations with Israel. In August 2026, Sri Lanka’s new ambassador to Israel identified agricultural technology, defense, and trade as areas in which Colombo would like to deepen cooperation.
Agriculture is an obvious starting point. India and Israel have spent years developing Centers of Excellence that combine Israeli agricultural technology with Indian institutions, local adaptation, and training. A similar trilateral initiative could bring together Israeli technology, Indian implementation experience, and Sri Lankan development priorities.
The potential goes further.
Maritime security is one area where Israeli capabilities could complement rather than compete with India’s regional role. Israel has relevant experience in sensors, electro-optics, unmanned systems, and maritime infrastructure protection. Cybersecurity and artificial intelligence are also important as ports, energy facilities, and digital systems become connected and vulnerable.
Israel’s comparative advantage lies not in establishing a military presence in Sri Lanka but in providing niche capabilities, technology, and practical solutions. India brings geographical proximity, political weight,and military-to-military engagement. Israel can contribute specialized expertise in maritime surveillance, cyber defense, AI, and critical-infrastructure protection.
This does not require a formal India-Israel-Sri Lanka strategic triangle. A more realistic model would be functional trilateralism: concrete projects addressing Sri Lankan needs. The India-UAE-Sri Lanka cooperation around Trincomalee provides a useful precedent, illustrating that third-country participation can complement Indian interests rather than challenge them.
Israel must also recognize Sri Lanka’s political sensitivities. Colombo has historically supported the Palestinian cause and continues to support a two-state solution. Treating Sri Lanka merely as another market for defense technology would therefore be politically shortsighted. A broader relationship combining agriculture, water, technology, trade, and carefully calibrated security cooperation would be more sustainable.
The larger lesson extends beyond Sri Lanka. As India becomes more influential across the Indian Ocean, Israel should think about India not only as a bilateral strategic partner but also as a platform for regional cooperation.
For decades, the focus has been on what India and Israel can do together. The next question is what their accumulated experience and complementary capabilities might allow them to do together elsewhere.
Sri Lanka may be one of the best places to begin.

articles.title: Norway seizes Russian Arctic science vessel at Kiev’s request
articles.body:
Norway seizes Russian Arctic science vessel at Kiev’s request
The Norwegian authorities have seized a Russian research vessel in Svalbard at the request of Ukraine’s state-owned energy company, Naftogaz, amid growing tensions between Moscow and NATO states over access to and control of the Arctic.
The Professor Molchanov was detained on Wednesday while docked in Barentsburg, a Russian settlement on the Norwegian-administered archipelago. The Governor of Svalbard said the move followed an August 31 order by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court granting Naftogaz the right to seize the ship. The vessel has been barred from leaving Barentsburg until further notice.
The crew and passengers aboard the vessel learned about the seizure from media reports, a TASS correspondent traveling with the expedition said. Russian Far East and Arctic Development Minister Aleksey Chekunkov said on Thursday that the crew is safe, adding that lawyers for the Arktikugol trust would soon issue a legal response and intended to challenge the seizure order.
The Professor Molchanov is a Russian state-owned research vessel operated by the country’s hydrometeorological service, Roshydromet. Alongside scientific expeditions, it has served since last year as a regular passenger and cargo link between Murmansk and Barentsburg, transporting scientists, employees of the state-owned Arktikugol, contractors, their families, and supplies to the Russian settlements on Svalbard.
Direct air links between Russia and Svalbard ceased in 2020, while direct maritime passenger service was restored in 2025. The Professor Molchanov is currently the only vessel operating the route, with ten round trips between Murmansk and Barentsburg planned for 2026.
Under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, Norway exercises sovereignty over the archipelago, while signatory nations are granted equal rights to engage in commercial and scientific activities there. Russia has maintained a presence on Svalbard for decades, with Arktikugol serving as its principal economic operator on the islands.
Naftogaz said it sought the seizure as part of an international effort to enforce a Hague arbitration award over assets it lost in Crimea following the peninsula’s reunification with Russia in 2014.
Russia has rejected the arbitration tribunal’s jurisdiction over the dispute, arguing that the Crimean assets in question could not qualify as Ukrainian investments made on Russian territory under the relevant bilateral investment treaty.
Acting Naftogaz chief Sergey Fedorenko praised the move as “another important step toward restoring justice,” pledging to continue the hunt for Russian assets worldwide.
Naftogaz, which claims that Moscow currently owes it around $4.22 billion, plus interest and legal costs, has pursued Russian state property elsewhere in Europe. The Finnish authorities froze a number of Russian-owned properties in 2024 at the company’s request. The Kremlin vowed to challenge the measures, and the Russian Foreign Ministry denounced them as illegitimate and warned of possible retaliatory steps.
The latest seizure comes just weeks after Moscow issued unusually explicit warnings against Western attempts to detain Russian vessels.
President Vladimir Putin described plans to seize Russian ships and sell their property as “piracy and robbery,” warning that Moscow would respond in kind in any part of the world it considers appropriate. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia would choose its own targets, including vessels operating in the interests of countries that made these seizures their policy.
Tensions have been mounting in the Arctic. In an article published earlier this week, Lavrov accused NATO states of seeking to turn the region into a “new front” against Russia and its partners. He pointed to large-scale Western military exercises and expanding command infrastructure near Russia’s northern borders, warning that the buildup increased the risk of an armed confrontation with potentially disastrous consequences.
Lavrov maintained that Moscow wants the Arctic to remain an area of peace and cooperation, but warned that Russia would defend its interests “by all available means” if confronted with hostile actions.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Security service and defence intelligence deputy heads to be dismissed over standoff between employees

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated that the deputy heads of the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) are to be dismissed over an incident involving a shootout between employees of the two agencies.
Source: Zelenskyy's evening address
Quote: "Two individuals implicated in the shooting have been formally named as suspects – a Security Service officer and a Defence Intelligence officer. All the other circumstances of what happened are also being investigated, from the very first day of this entire situation."
Details: Zelenskyy said he had discussed the situation with Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
Zelenskyy said the actions of the heads of both agencies will be assessed based on the results of an internal investigation. Decisions regarding the deputy heads of the SSU and DIU have already been taken.
Quote: "Personnel decisions have already been made in both agencies – the deputy heads who bear responsibility for this situation will be dismissed. This is entirely fair – both agencies must be held accountable; both acted in a way that is absolutely unacceptable."
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps The Russian Volunteer Corps is a military and political organisation established in 2022 that consists of Russian volunteers who have been fighting for Ukraine since 2014 said that its deputy commander for combat operations, Stepan Kaplunov, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of the building where he was living.
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Security Service of Ukraine in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance.

articles.title: German police probing suspected arson attack against arms manufacturers
articles.body:
German police probing suspected arson attack against arms manufacturers
German police have launched an investigation into a suspected arson attack near the Munich premises of defense contractors Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing, detaining two Bulgarian nationals in connection with the incident.
Two incendiary devices were thrown from a car at a construction site around midnight on Thursday, Bavarian police said. One ignited and was extinguished by officers, while a bomb disposal team defused the second. No injuries or significant damage were reported.
Police shortly afterward detained a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, both Bulgarian citizens.
The motive remains unclear, although police noted that “several defense companies are located” at the site. Because a political motive cannot be ruled out, the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office and the Bavarian Central Office for Combating Extremism and Terrorism have taken over the investigation.
Die Welt later reported, citing a police spokesperson, that a letter claiming responsibility had appeared on a platform linked to left-wing extremists.
Several defense contractors are based near the site, including Rohde & Schwarz, which supplies radio and communications equipment to German security agencies and the military, and drone manufacturer Helsing.
Since the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, EU officials have repeatedly alleged Russian involvement in suspected sabotage and other incidents described as ‘hybrid attacks,’ although Moscow has denied responsibility and conclusive evidence has not been publicly presented.
In another high-profile case, an explosive-laden drone was discovered between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Tuesday that authorities believe Russia was behind the incident.
Berlin subsequently announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, along with other measures.
Moscow has rejected the allegations. Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Berlin of seeking to distract from its domestic economic problems by “planting the evidence” to implicate Russia.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova likewise dismissed the accusations as an “absolutely trumped-up and far-fetched” pretext for closing the Russian facilities.

articles.title: Foreign support, drones fuel Sudan war and possible war crimes, UN probe says
articles.body:
Foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan's conflict and expanding the warring parties' ability to strike deep into civilian areas, a United Nations fact-finding mission said in a report published on Thursday, warning that some attacks may amount to war crimes.
Sudan's war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Sudan's military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) ahead of a planned transition to civilian rule. The conflict has devastated the country, displaced more than 14 million people and created what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The UN mission said investigators found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network involving individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, military equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel.
The UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia, the RSF and Sudan's military did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.
UAE, Chad deny allegations
The UAE rejected allegations that it had provided military, logistical, financial or political support to the RSF, and Chad said it remained neutral in the war and denied knowledge of weapons transfers through its territory, according to the report.
The UN mission also said it obtained evidence that Colombian contractors played a significant role in operating and maintaining drone systems and other advanced weapons used by the RSF. It estimated the total number of Colombian contractors involved could approach 2,000 and said some were present during operations around al-Fashir in Darfur.
Colombia told investigators it opposed mercenarism and was taking steps to address the participation of Colombian nationals in foreign conflicts.
Mass killings of non‑Arab communities when the RSF captured al‑Fashir bore hallmarks that point to genocide, the UN mission said in a previous report in February.
In the past, the RSF has denied such abuses, saying the accounts have been manufactured by its enemies and making counter-accusations against them.
The mission said its investigation into external support for Sudan's military was at an early stage but had found evidence that foreign-supplied combat drones and loitering munitions, which can hover over an area before striking a target, had expanded the army's long-range strike capabilities.
It said some of those weapons were used in attacks on civilian locations, including Yabus Market in Blue Nile State.
Drone warfare violated international human rights law, UN says
The report found both sides committed serious violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in their drone operations, with some conduct amounting to war crimes. Both sides have previously denied allegations of human rights abuses.
Expanded range, persistence and increasingly sophisticated capabilities enabled Sudan's military and the RSF to strike far beyond immediate front lines, and evidence points to both sides carrying out drone attacks that killed civilians and hit hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.
More than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes between January and May 2026, according to figures cited by the report.
Between May and July 2026, repeated RSF drone attacks damaged electricity and fuel facilities in the North Kordofan capital of El Obeid, which was under SAF control as RSF pressure intensified in June this year. Strikes disrupted water supplies, healthcare, transport and other basic services in a city already under severe strain and partial siege, the mission said.
Among the cases highlighted in the report were SAF strikes on Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur that investigators said killed at least 70 people and left the facility non-functional.
The mission reiterated calls for enforcement of the Darfur arms embargo and urged the UN Security Council to extend it across all of Sudan.

articles.title: UK seeks vehicle-mounted laser defence against drone swarms
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence has opened a competition for new counter-drone technologies intended to protect deployed troops from mass and low-cost aerial threats, with particular interest in laser directed-energy weapons and a requirement for an eventual system capable of autonomous operation from an Army vehicle, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The tender notice published on 2 September begins an iterative procurement process through the Commercial X Dynamic Market. The wider procurement carries an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, or £150 million including VAT, although the MOD makes clear that this funding has not yet been approved and later stages will depend on future funding decisions.
Setting out the operational requirement, the MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
On existing counter-UAS approaches, the notice states: “Current approaches are constrained by limited magazine depth, high cost-per-engagement, limited manoeuvrability, workforce intensity and the difficulty of adapting capabilities at pace as UAS threats evolve.” The MOD added: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The first phase will focus on technologies which already exist and could be accelerated towards a deployable system rather than procuring a finished counter-UAS capability immediately. The MOD stated: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
For later phases, the department said: “Over later Phases, the Authority’s intent, aligned with their Integrated Procurement Model, is to identify and rapidly mature promising technologies as demonstrable Minimum Viable Products (MVPs). The Authority may then, at its discretion (and the criteria detailed below) select projects to be iteratively developed, integrated and proven as Minimum Deployable Capabilities (MDCs) for an initial operational user group.”
The notice continues: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record. Suppliers will be notified of the criteria, selection processes, and competition format as these Phases arise.”
The intended configuration is also set out in the requirement. The MOD stated: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
On the attacks the system is expected to counter, the department said: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus is on representative Class 1 uncrewed aerial systems and related small aerial threats, covering single attacks as well as repeated, sequential and simultaneous profiles. The notice states that this includes threats intended to disrupt operations, conduct surveillance, target fixed or mobile assets, overwhelm local defences or force the disproportionate use of high-cost munitions.
The MOD also plans for the system to move beyond a crewed Army vehicle. It stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
Stage 1 will assess whether industry proposals can meet the problem statements, with suppliers required to submit an evidence-based high-level programme plan supported by demonstrations, modelling, analysis and testing where appropriate. The MOD states: “No contract shall be awarded at this stage, but success is required to continue to Stage 2. All suppliers who demonstrate achievement of the threshold criteria shall be invited to Stage 2.”
Stage 2 will require successful suppliers to develop their initial proposals into fully costed and contractable projects running for around six months. Contracts at this point will be awarded according to evaluation scores and available funding within a £5 million limit, with technical factors expected to account for between 60% and 80% of the assessment and commercial factors between 20% and 40%.
Stage 3 could involve either a further competition or negotiation of a single direct award depending on how many suppliers remain. The MOD says contracts at that stage will cover scaling and production alongside testing, assurance, safety and security, with break points where aspects of the system cannot be demonstrated within the required timescales.
The department states: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.” It adds: “The intention is to begin Stage 1 with immediate effect, but future stages will not proceed until funding has been allocated and approved.”
The MOD also warns suppliers that later funding is not guaranteed, stating: “There is no guarantee that future funding will be allocated or approved and the Authority may cancel the procurement process at any time. Bidders proceed knowing and accepting this risk that no effort shall be compensated.”

articles.title: Taiwan deploys Ching Tien I cruise missile
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force has completed mass production and deployed its Ching Tien I long-range supersonic cruise missile, while an upgraded version is reportedly being developed with a range exceeding 2,000 kilometers.
The ministry's proposed 2027 budget includes a program for the Air Force to contract the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology to provide follow-on support for the weapon system through 2031, per Liberty Times. The funding covers routine maintenance and periodic inspections, indicating the system has moved into operational service.
Ching Tien I, formerly known as the Yun Feng missile, uses a ramjet engine and can reach speeds of up to Mach 3. It has an estimated range of 1,200 to 1,500 kilometers, potentially allowing it to strike military targets in central and eastern China.
Because of its large size and earlier design, the first-generation missile is deployed primarily from fixed underground positions and mountain shelters, Liberty Times reported. The military is now pursuing an upgraded version designed to address the vulnerability of fixed-site deployment.
Ching Tien II is reportedly being developed as a road-mobile system, with plans to mount the missile on a European-made 12-by-12 heavy truck chassis. The military is also evaluating the possibility of using railway tracks for deployment and launch.
The upgraded missile is expected to feature improved propulsion technology, including a scramjet engine and solid-fuel rocket propulsion, according to Liberty Times. Its top speed is expected to exceed Mach 5, while its range could increase to more than 2,000 kilometers.
Such performance could put targets including Beijing and Wuhan within the missile's range. The system is expected to become a major component of the nation’s asymmetric deterrence capabilities.

articles.title: Construction of British deep space radar to begin in 2027
articles.body:
Construction of the British site for the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability will begin in April 2027 under a contract the United States Space Force signed with Northrop Grumman in August 2024, with planning permission sought in March this year and initial authority to operate already issued, according to a written answer published this week.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what progress had been made on establishing the capability, referring to paragraph 81 of the Defence Investment Plan.
Mr Pollard said: “The Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) is a ground-based radar system that will provide 24/7, all-weather capabilities to detect, track, identify and characterise objects up to Geostationary Earth Orbit. DARC will require three permanent radar sites and a radar operations centre to provide 360-degree coverage: in Australia, the UK and the US. Construction of sites in Australia (Exmouth) and the US (IROC, Eglin) have been completed.”
He said: “The USSF signed a contract with Northrop Grumman on 23 August 2024 for construction of the UK site starting April 2027.”
On the regulatory position, he said the department has completed an environmental impact assessment including a landscape and visual impact assessment, to ensure the project has minimal impact on the local skyline, and that this formed part of a town planning application submitted to the local planning authority in March 2026.
He added: “The Defence Electromagnetic Authority, working with the Office of Communications, has issued an initial Authority to Operate. MOD and the Civil Aviation Authority is completing the necessary safety of flight procedures for local airspace.”
What DARC does
Most existing radars are optimised for low Earth orbit, where the majority of satellites and debris sit a few hundred kilometres up, and objects in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres have been tracked largely by optical telescopes, which depend on clear skies and darkness. A radar capable of reaching that altitude works regardless of weather or time of day, which is what the reference to 24/7 all-weather capability in the answer describes. The three sites, spread across Australia, Britain and the United States, provide continuous coverage of the geostationary belt as the Earth turns.
Geostationary orbit holds communications satellites, missile warning satellites and a substantial share of the space infrastructure military operations depend on, and both Russia and China have demonstrated satellites capable of manoeuvring close to others, which is a behaviour that cannot be characterised without being able to see it happening.
The United Kingdom site is at Cawdor Barracks in Pembrokeshire, west Wales, an existing defence site the Army had been due to vacate. The answer’s references to the local skyline and to safety of flight procedures for local airspace reflect the physical scale of the installation, which involves large parabolic dish antennas across a substantial footprint.
The programme is a trilateral effort under the AUKUS partnership, jointly funded by the three nations, with the American site at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and the Australian site at Exmouth in Western Australia, which the answer confirms are both complete.
Britain’s wider space programme sits under UK Space Command, established at RAF High Wycombe in 2021, which brings together military space operations alongside the existing space domain awareness assets including the Fylingdales radar in North Yorkshire, itself part of the American ballistic missile early warning system.

articles.title: Brain implants fuel U.S.-China bioscience rivalry
articles.body:
Brain implants like those being developed by Elon Musk's Neuralink are becoming the latest friction point in the intensifying U.S.-China rivalry in the life sciences.
Why it matters: The devices are bringing new hope to patients with strokes, Parkinson's disease and other neurological conditions. And tech billionaires have fueled advances by pouring billions into biotech startups focused on linking the brain with computers.
But a new national security analysis says U.S. development efforts are being overtaken by Beijing's full-court press around manufacturing, data and commercialization.
The consequences could extend beyond health care, affecting U.S. military capabilities and the ability to train the next generation of AI models, according to the analysis.
The report was produced by the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology, which was created by Congress to review how biotechnology can affect national security.
State of play: Brain-computer interfaces, or BCIs, are going mainstream. Companies like Neuralink, Precision Neuroscience, Paradromics and Synchron are testing new applications, like helping to restore communication for people who have lost the ability to speak.
Rapid advances in artificial intelligence are reducing the time it takes to calibrate a device to a patient's brain signals and use them for functions like controlling a prosthetic part.
And China leveled up the field this spring, when its National Medical Products Administration issued what's thought to be the world's first commercial approval of a BCI designed to revive hand movement in people with spinal cord injuries.
The approval was part of a strategy that designated BCIs as a national "future industry," alongside quantum computing and 6G wireless communications systems.
The commission analysis says regulatory bottlenecks and funding concerns are drying up the U.S. pipeline for BCIs and shifting the playing field in China's favor, noting that new treatments for neurological conditions take an average of more than 11 years to reach approval.
It calls for the Food and Drug Administration to develop a clearer pathway for bringing implants to market, and for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to come up with a way to pay for devices once they're through regulatory approvals.
"China is moving strategic technologies like BCI faster than the United States can," Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.), the chair of the national security commission, tells Axios.
"Our government needs a coordinated biotechnology strategy to promote U.S. innovation and commercialization of what promises to be a truly revolutionary platform technology for health and national security."
Between the lines: BCIs are another example of how technology is outpacing regulation — and posing thorny ethical and privacy issues.
There's the basic question of who controls the device and data, and whether privacy laws like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act even apply.
Giving patients more control over their data may require new laws or regulations that could limit developers' ability to improve algorithms that decode brain signals, the Government Accountability Office has noted.
But more consumer autonomy could provide safeguards that extend beyond medical settings and protect against data being accessed to make insurance or workplace decisions, or to study how people subconsciously respond to advertising or other messages.
China currently has no neural-data-specific privacy or security regulations, per the commission analysis.
Reality check: Brain implants remain a work in progress. Many fail within their first year, and experts say manufacturing improvements like new materials, coatings and batteries could address signal degradation and extend power life.
It's also difficult to recruit patients for clinical trials who have profound disabilities but still are healthy enough to withstand brain surgery.
What we're watching: Whether brain implants areincluded in the Trump administration's RAPID program — a joint effort between FDA and CMS to expedite Medicare coverage of certain "breakthrough" devices.
Longer term, BCIs could be adapted for nonmedical purposes, like controlling swarms of drones through operators' thoughts.

Russian Ballistic Missiles Destroy Warehouse Holding Ai Weiwei Artwork Near Kyiv
A warehouse housing an installation by internationally renowned Chinese artist Ai Weiwei was destroyed during a Russian missile attack on the Kyiv region on July 19, the artist said.
He stated that the warehouse, located in the Bucha district on the outskirts of Kyiv, was hit by two ballistic missiles during the Russian attack.

The facility contained Ai’s installation Three Perfectly Proportioned Spheres and Camouflage Uniforms Painted White. The extent of the damage to the artwork itself remains unclear.
World-renowned Chinese dissident artist and sculptor Ai Weiwei presented his first major installation in Ukraine in fall 2025. Titled Three Perfectly Proportioned Spheres and Camouflage Uniforms Painted White, the work explores themes of war and concealment, as well as the tension between ideals of rational order and the realities of contemporary war.
Created specifically for its presentation in Ukraine, the installation was unveiled at Pavilion 13, a multidisciplinary cultural venue. The work reflects Ai’s longstanding humanist and pacifist perspective, shaped by his experiences with state repression and his broader artistic exploration of violence, displacement, and political power.
Ai Weiwei is widely regarded as one of the most prominent figures in contemporary art, combining artistic practice with outspoken criticism of authoritarianism and political repression.
His work has been exhibited at major international events and institutions, including the Venice Biennale, Documenta, and the São Paulo Biennial. Ai’s personal history has also been shaped by persecution by the Chinese authorities, beginning with the targeting of his family.
The reported destruction of the warehouse comes as Ukraine’s cultural sector continues to document the impact of Russia’s war on art and cultural heritage.
