articles.title: Former Biden adviser Hochstein rejects Lapid's claim Israel blocked a US-Saudi nuclear agreement
articles.body:
Former Biden administration senior adviser Amos Hochstein rejected opposition leader Yair Lapid’s claim that Israel had previously succeeded in blocking a US-Saudi nuclear agreement, saying Washington’s negotiations with Riyadh were conducted independently and only gained momentum after the Bennett-Lapid government left office.
“Did Israel at some point manage to stop the US from doing a nuclear deal with the Saudis?” Hochstein was asked by The Jerusalem Post.
“The easy answer, and the simplest answer, is absolutely not,” he said.
Hochstein, who served as a senior adviser to former president Joe Biden and was the administration’s lead negotiator on the nuclear component of the proposed US-Saudi agreement, said the talks were conducted directly between Washington and Riyadh.
“We negotiated a comprehensive agreement with the kingdom, and at no time did Israel, or any other country, block that deal,” he said.
Lapid slams US-Saudi nuclear agreement
His comments came in response to Lapid’s criticism on X of the nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia submitted to Congress this week. Lapid called the agreement “one of the biggest and most dangerous failures of Israeli foreign policy of all time,” arguing that the Trump administration was pursuing what it considered the US interest, but that the agreement would symbolize Israel’s declining influence in Washington.
Both as foreign minister and prime minister, and later as opposition leader, Lapid warned senior US officials and members of Congress about the prospect of Saudi Arabia receiving uranium-enrichment capabilities as part of a civilian nuclear program.
“A normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia is a welcome development, but not at the price of a nuclear arms race throughout the Middle East. Netanyahu has spent his entire life fighting precisely against such moves. These are the foundations of our nuclear strategy,” Lapid said in September 2023, at the height of normalization talks between Israel and Saudi Arabia under then-prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Joe Biden.
“Strong democracies do not abandon their security interests for the sake of politics. It is dangerous and irresponsible. Israel must not agree to any form of uranium enrichment in Saudi Arabia".
Despite Lapid’s public opposition to the deal, Hochstein pushed back on the broader suggestion that Israel could determine or block US foreign policy.
“Israel can have input, and it could express its interests to the United States, but it cannot block or initiate any American policy,” Hochstein said. “That is done by the United States.”
According to Hochstein, the process that ultimately produced the Biden administration’s proposed nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia began in earnest in 2023, as the administration sought to establish a broader normalization framework between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
He pointed to Biden’s July 2022 visit to Israel, followed by his trip to Jeddah, as an important starting point for the wider diplomatic effort. However, Hochstein stressed that the nuclear agreement itself was not being negotiated at that stage.
“The seed of the normalization negotiations started during that trip to Saudi Arabia in Jeddah in 2022 and picked up in earnest in 2023," he said.
The talks were led by Hochstein, Brett McGurk, and other senior US officials. They included a nuclear component alongside discussions on economic, defense, and security arrangements.
The nuclear agreement was negotiated as part of a much wider normalization package, Hochstein explained, though each agreement was handled separately.
“The normalization was the umbrella, but each of the agreements that we negotiated was separate,” he said.
Hochstein said the Biden administration reached a final agreement on the nuclear component toward the end of 2024. The broader package ultimately did not materialize, preventing the agreement from moving forward at that time.
Based on his understanding, he added, the agreement recently reached by the Trump administration is “largely based” on the framework negotiated under Biden.
“I haven't seen the full text of it yet, so I can't fully comment on that,” Hochstein cautioned.
Hochstein voiced support for the principle of a US-Saudi nuclear agreement.
“On its own, a nuclear agreement between the United States and Saudi is a good thing,” he said. “It is a good development and a good policy for the United States and for the region.”
He argued that Saudi Arabia’s importance as a US ally made the issue particularly significant, while emphasizing that his support depended on the agreement meeting American nonproliferation and security requirements.
“I am fully supportive, and I think there's bipartisan support for that idea, as long as the deal is done in a way that lives up to American standards of security verification and so on,” Hochstein said. “I hope this deal has” those safeguards.
Brett McGurk says Saudi framework agreement not completed in 2022
Brett McGurk, who was former president Biden's National Security Council coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa and was involved in the negotiations with Saudi Arabia, told the Post that "these agreements (between Saudi Arabia and the US) were not complete in 2022 and negotiations were just getting underway during the Lapid-Bennett government period.”
McGurk added that “Their government, of course, was extremely helpful in getting the Saudi process started. But the process gained momentum in early 2023".

Russia Threw Six FPV Drones at Ukraine’s Armed Robot—It Completed the Mission Anyway
Ukraine’s Droid TW-12.7 unmanned ground vehicle survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its combat mission before a sixth hit finally disabled the platform, according to a DevDroid press release shared with UNITED24 Media on September 2.
Soldiers from the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion deployed the UGV during a remotely conducted operation against a concentration of Russian troops.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
As the Droid TW-12.7 approached the position, two FPV drones struck the vehicle almost simultaneously. One of the hits damaged its aiming module, but the platform remained mobile and continued the mission.
Operators adapted to the damage by aiming in the direction of the weapon barrel and opened fire on the target. Two additional FPV drones struck the UGV during the engagement, but it remained operational long enough to complete its primary task.
The vehicle then began withdrawing and survived a fifth FPV strike while continuing to move. A sixth drone eventually disabled it on the return route.
DevDroid said the Russian troop concentration was cleared and enemy forces suffered losses. The entire operation was carried out remotely, allowing Ukrainian personnel to avoid direct contact with Russian troops.
“In this engagement, the enemy was able to stop the Droid only with the sixth FPV drone, but they still failed to prevent it from completing the mission. For us, this is what survivability means in practice: after being hit, a system must not simply remain mobile—it must retain enough functionality for its operators to complete the mission and achieve the intended result,” DevDroid CEO Yurii Poritskyi said.
The Droid TW-12.7 is a Ukrainian reconnaissance-and-strike UGV developed by DevDroid. It is equipped with a remotely operated turret carrying a 12.7 mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun, as well as an integrated ballistic computer and AI-assisted targeting functions.
The platform is designed to engage personnel, vehicles, and lightly armored targets while allowing Ukrainian troops to conduct dangerous frontline missions from a safer distance.

Zelensky calls the strike a message to US
Ukrainska Pravda first reported the fire at the plant, citing its own sources, before official confirmation became available.

articles.title: ICAO notes growing risk of weapons use against civil aircraft

WASHINGTON, September 3. /TASS/. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) said that risks of weapons being used against civil aircraft are growing all over the world.
"ICAO is observing heightened risks of civil aircraft being targeted or caught in crossfire, and while the aviation industry is able to reroute flights and maintain operations during conflicts, this operational flexibility does not address the fundamental security threat," the Canada-based organization said in a statement obtained by TASS.

articles.title: U.S. Marine Corps orders 14 more MRADR radar systems
articles.body:
- The Marine Corps awarded Dynetics a $40.8 million modification to build 14 more Medium Range Air Defense Radar systems, with work through August 2028.
- The contract also covers retrofitting four existing MRADR prototypes and four MELPS sensor systems, alongside logistics and software support.
The U.S. Marine Corps has awarded Dynetics a $40.8 million contract modification to build 14 additional Medium Range Air Defense Radar production-representative systems, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The hybrid other transaction agreement modification also funds depot-level technical manual support, program management, engineering change proposals, logistics support and software support. It further requires Dynetics to retrofit four existing MRADR prototype systems and four Marine Expeditionary Long Range Persistent Sensor, or MELPS, systems. Work will be performed primarily in Huntsville, Alabama, accounting for 87.5% of the effort, with the remainder done in Woodlake, California. The contract is expected to be completed by August 2028.
The Marine Corps funded the award with $2,972,730 in fiscal 2025 procurement funds, $31,295,685 in fiscal 2026 procurement funds and $1,500,000 in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds, all obligated at the time of award. The Marine Corps procured the modification under 10 U.S. Code 4022 as a follow-on to an earlier prototype agreement. Marine Corps Systems Command in Quantico, Virginia, is managing the contract.
Dynetics, a Leidos company based in Huntsville, has built the MRADR program since 2023. The Marine Corps first awarded the company a $32 million contract that November to develop four MRADR prototype systems over two years, drawing on sensor work Dynetics had previously done on the MELPS program for the Office of Naval Research. In August 2025, the Marine Corps placed a follow-on order worth roughly $24.9 million for six MRADR production-representative model systems. The new $40.8 million modification adds 14 more of those production-representative units to the program.
MRADR is designed to give Marine units a mobile, 360-degree radar capable of detecting, tracking and identifying aerial threats, including cruise missiles and crewed and uncrewed aircraft. The system relies on digitized antennas, receivers and digital signal processing to build a persistent air picture while producing minimal electromagnetic emissions, a design intended to make the radar harder for adversaries to locate and target.
The Marine Corps intends to integrate MRADR with other ground-based air defense systems already in its inventory, including the AN/TPS-80 Ground/Air Task-Oriented Radar, known as G/ATOR, and the Medium-Range Intercept Capability system. Together, those systems are meant to give Marine expeditionary units layered detection and engagement capability against helicopters, fixed-wing aircraft, cruise missiles, rockets and drones.

Russia’s LUKOIL Refinery Producing Up to 11% of Country’s Gasoline Shuts Down Following Ukraine Strike
Russia’s LUKOIL-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez oil refinery in Kstovo has completely halted operations for repairs following a Ukrainian drone attack on August 26, according to an analysis of satellite imagery by Dnipro Osint.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Satellite images taken after the attack show at least four sites of intense burning across the refinery complex, indicating multiple drone impacts.
According to Dnipro Osint, the strikes caused significant damage to technical overpasses and columns associated with the AVT-4, AVT-5, and AVT-1 primary crude-processing units. A vacuum gas oil hydrotreatment unit used in secondary refining was also damaged.
The extent of the damage has forced the refinery to completely suspend operations while repairs are carried out, Dnipro Osint reported.
The Kstovo refinery, operated by LUKOIL-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, has an annual processing capacity of approximately 17 million metric tons of crude oil. According to Dnipro Osint, the facility accounts for up to 11% of Russia’s gasoline production.
Before repeated Ukrainian drone strikes, it produced about 5 million metric tons of gasoline and more than 5 million metric tons of diesel per year, along with roughly 2 million metric tons of fuel oil and around 500,000 metric tons of bitumen.
The August 26 operation also targeted a major Wildberries logistics center in Russia’s Tambov region. Ukrainian defense technology company Fire Point said FP-1 long-range drones were used to strike both the logistics hub and the Kstovo refinery.
Initial reports of a fire at the Wildberries facility in Kotovsk emerged shortly after 1 am, with local residents reporting at least 10 explosions before a major blaze broke out at the site.
The reported shutdown in Kstovo comes as Ukrainian strikes continue to disrupt operations at other major Russian refineries. Russia’s Kirishi oil refinery in the Leningrad region, the country’s second-largest by processing capacity, also suspended all crude processing following a Ukrainian drone attack on August 30.

The nationalist said he was detained by the SBU Security Service and obliged to sign a confession that he collaborated with Russian intelligence. He later retracted the statement.
The street clash occurred in central Kyiv on Tuesday after the activist's home in Kyiv was searched. SBU officers fired on members of the HUR unit. The SBU has said it was acting to prevent a Moscow-inspired plot to assassinate Russian anti-Kremlin activists in Kyiv.

SBU, HUR agencies clash violently over dispute
"An assessment of the heads of these two agencies - the SBU and the HUR - will be made based on the results of an internal investigation. It is completely fair that both sides be brought to account. Both acted precisely in a way that should not have happened," he said.

articles.title: Russia remained India’s top oil supplier in August
articles.body:
Russia remained India’s top oil supplier in August
Russia remained India’s largest supplier of crude oil in August, selling around 2.1 million barrels per day (bpd), or 45% of the country’s total imports, data from maritime intelligence firm Kpler shows.
Russian shipments were down from a record 2.8 million bpd in July, when they accounted for more than half of India’s crude purchases. However, India’s overall imports also declined to around 4.6 million bpd in August, nearly 8% below the more than 5 million bpd bought the previous month.
Indian refiners ramped up purchases in May, June, and July to guard against potential supply shortages amid the conflict in the Middle East. The August decline reflected some normalization after months of heavy buying, scheduled maintenance at Indian refineries, and lower availability of Russian crude, according to Kpler.
“August was less a story of India voluntarily stepping away from Russian oil than of Russia having fewer barrels to offer,” Abu Dhabi-based commodity analyst Natalia Katona told the Financial Express. Lower Russian seaborne exports and stronger competition from Chinese refiners for available cargoes also weighed on supplies to India, she said. 
The United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela were among India’s other leading oil suppliers during the month. Venezuelan shipments rose sharply, reaching their highest level since 2020, according to Kpler data. 
Russian oil has remained an important part of India’s energy mix as it seeks to secure supplies amid disruptions affecting shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. India imports around 90% of the crude oil it consumes.
The purchases have continued despite the prospect of new US tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which cleared the US Senate last month, would allow tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the five biggest buyers of Russian oil. The bill has US President Donald Trump’s backing but still has to pass the House. 
India maintains that its oil purchases are guided by affordability, availability, and national energy security rather than geopolitical considerations.

Norway Seizes Russian Vessel in Arctic Svalbard at Ukraine's Request, Drawing Putin's Fury
Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the remote Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at Ukraine's request. The move drew condemnation from the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, who on September 3 compared it to "state terrorism," Associated Press reported.
A Norwegian court ordered the seizure to help Ukraine's state energy company Naftogaz recover a $4.22 billion arbitration award. The award stems from Russia's 2014 illegal annexation of Crimea and its seizure of Ukrainian energy assets, including gas fields and pipelines.

After Russia refused to pay the 2023 award, Naftogaz began petitioning national courts for orders to seize Russian commercial assets abroad.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, is used for commercial expedition cruises, including to Svalbard. The archipelago lies more than 500 miles (about 800 kilometers) north of the Norwegian mainland and is known for its snow-covered mountains, fjords, and glaciers.
"This is another important step towards restoring justice for Russia's unlawful seizure of Naftogaz assets in Crimea," Naftogaz CEO Sergii Fedorenko stated.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," he added. "We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world."
Putin, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on September 3, criticized the seizure. He also condemned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's warning to foreign airlines to avoid Russian airspace because of Ukrainian long-range drone attacks.
